lessons.title: What Probability and Statistics Are
lessons.content:
Imagine you are standing at a tea stall near your school gate. Every afternoon the stall owner, Karim bhai, wonders the same thing: how many cups of tea should I prepare? If he makes too few, customers walk away. If he makes too many, the tea goes cold and he loses money. He cannot see the future, but he has something almost as good: memory of the past. On rainy days more people come. On Fridays fewer people come. On exam days the crowd is huge. Without knowing it, Karim bhai is doing probability and statistics in his head. This course turns that kind of smart guessing into clear, careful maths.

What the two words mean: Probability is the maths of chance. It answers questions like "how likely is it to rain tomorrow?" or "what is the chance this coin lands heads?". Statistics is the science of data. It answers questions like "what is the average score of this class?" or "do students who sleep more get better marks?". The two are like two sides of one coin. Probability starts from a known rule and predicts what data will look like. Statistics starts from data and tries to guess the rule behind it.

A tiny example of each: Suppose you know a coin is fair. Probability tells you that in 100 tosses you should expect about 50 heads. Now flip the story. Suppose someone hands you a strange coin, and in 100 tosses you see 80 heads. Statistics helps you decide whether the coin is probably unfair, and by how much. Probability goes from rule to data. Statistics goes from data back to the rule. In this course you will learn both directions, and you will see that they need each other.

Why a computer science student needs this: Almost everything modern in computing has chance and data inside it. A spam filter decides whether an email is spam using probabilities of words. A recommendation system on YouTube or Daraz guesses what you might like next. Machine learning is mostly statistics with a lot of computing power. Network engineers use probability to plan how many users a server can handle. Game designers use random numbers to make games fair and fun. Even testing software uses statistics: if 3 out of 1,000 users see a crash, is the new version really worse than the old one? If you want to work in data science, AI, networking, or research, this course is a foundation stone.

Data: Data is simply recorded facts. The marks of 40 students, the heights of players in a cricket team, the number of bKash transactions per minute, or the colour of cars passing a road. One piece of data, like "Rahim scored 72", is called an observation. A collection of observations is a data set. Statistics is all about turning a messy pile of data into useful understanding.

Population and sample: The population is the whole group you care about. If you want to know the average height of all university students in Bangladesh, the population is every single one of them, which could be millions of people. Measuring everyone is usually impossible or too costly. So we pick a smaller group, called a sample, maybe 500 students, and measure them carefully. Then we use the sample to say something about the population. A number that describes a population, like the true average height, is called a parameter. A number calculated from a sample, like the average height of our 500 students, is called a statistic. A simple memory trick: Population goes with Parameter, Sample goes with Statistic.

Why samples work: Think of tasting rice while it cooks. Your mother does not eat the whole pot to check if it needs more salt. She stirs it well and tastes one spoonful. If the pot is well mixed, one spoonful tells her about the whole pot. A good sample works the same way. The key is the stirring, which in statistics means choosing the sample randomly, so that every member has a fair chance to be picked. If you only taste the top layer of an unstirred pot, you may get a wrong idea. That is what we call a biased sample.

Variables: A variable is a characteristic that can change from one person or thing to another. Age, blood group, mobile operator, monthly income, and number of siblings are all variables. Variables come in two big families. Qualitative (or categorical) variables put things into groups or labels, like blood group A, B, AB or O, or mobile operator Grameenphone, Robi, Banglalink or Teletalk. Quantitative (or numerical) variables are numbers that you can do maths with, like height or income.

Discrete and continuous: Quantitative variables split again into two kinds. Discrete variables take separate, countable values, usually whole numbers: number of siblings (0, 1, 2, 3), number of goals in a match, number of emails received today. You cannot have 2.5 siblings. Continuous variables can take any value in a range, including fractions: height (165.3 cm), weight, time taken to run 100 metres, temperature. Between any two heights there is always another possible height. This difference matters a lot later, because discrete and continuous variables use different tools. Discrete ones use sums, continuous ones use areas under curves.

Scales of measurement: Statisticians also describe data by its level of measurement. There are four classic levels. Nominal data are just names or labels with no order, like blood group or district name. Ordinal data have an order but the gaps are not equal, like exam grades A+, A, A-, or a survey answer "poor, okay, good, excellent". Interval data have equal gaps but no true zero, like temperature in Celsius: 20 degrees is not "twice as hot" as 10 degrees, because 0 degrees does not mean "no heat". Ratio data have equal gaps and a true zero, like height, weight, income or age. With ratio data you can say "twice as much": 40 kg really is twice 20 kg. Knowing the level tells you which calculations make sense. Taking the average of district names makes no sense, but taking the average of incomes does.

Descriptive statistics: This branch is about summarizing and showing the data you have. Making a table of marks, drawing a bar chart of favourite fruits, finding the average, the middle value, or how spread out the numbers are. Descriptive statistics does not try to go beyond the data. It just describes. Lessons 2 to 5 of this course are all about this.

Inferential statistics: This branch is about making conclusions that go beyond the data, from a sample to a population. Election polls, medicine trials, quality checks in a factory, and A/B tests on websites all use inference. Because we only see part of the population, our conclusions always carry some uncertainty, and probability is the tool that measures that uncertainty. Lessons 17 to 24 cover inference: sampling, estimation, confidence intervals and hypothesis tests.

Where probability fits: Between description and inference sits probability theory, lessons 6 to 16. It gives us the language of chance: events, random variables and distributions like the binomial, Poisson and normal. Without probability, inference would be just guessing. With probability, we can say things like "we are 95% confident the true average lies between 160 and 164 cm".

Real-life example 1, a cricket team: Suppose the Bangladesh team analyst has the scores of a batsman in his last 20 innings. First she cleans the data: two matches were washed out by rain, so those are removed. Then she describes it: average score, highest score, how often he crosses 50. That is descriptive statistics. Next she asks a bigger question: is his true batting ability better on slow pitches? She cannot watch him play every possible future match, so the 20 innings are a sample of his ability. Using inference, she checks whether the difference between slow and fast pitches is big enough to be real or could just be luck. Finally, she might estimate the probability that he scores at least 30 in the next match. All three parts of this course show up in one cricket conversation.

Real-life example 2, a mobile app survey: A Dhaka startup builds a food delivery app and wants to know if users are happy. There are 2 lakh users, which is the population. The team sends a short survey to 1,000 randomly chosen users, which is the sample. The questions collect different kinds of variables: city (nominal), satisfaction level from 1 to 5 stars (ordinal), number of orders last month (discrete), and average delivery time in minutes (continuous). From the sample they find that 72% are satisfied. That 72% is a statistic. They use it to estimate the parameter, the true satisfaction rate of all 2 lakh users, with some margin of error. If they had only surveyed their office friends, the result would be biased and useless.

Small history note: Probability theory grew partly out of gambling questions. In the 1600s, the French mathematicians Blaise Pascal and Pierre de Fermat exchanged letters about how to fairly split the prize money of an unfinished game of chance. Their ideas became the start of modern probability. Statistics, on the other hand, grew from governments counting people, crops and taxes. The word "statistics" is connected to the word "state". Today both fields have merged into one powerful toolbox.

Common mistakes students make: First, mixing up population and sample. Always ask, "Am I talking about everyone or just the ones I measured?" Second, calling numbers quantitative when they are really labels. A roll number or a phone number is a number, but it is a label: the average of phone numbers means nothing. Third, thinking a bigger sample always fixes everything. A huge biased sample is still biased. Asking 1 lakh Facebook users only reaches people who use Facebook. Fourth, confusing discrete and continuous. Ask yourself whether the variable is counted (discrete) or measured (continuous).

What exams usually ask: Define population, sample, parameter and statistic with examples. Classify given variables as qualitative or quantitative, discrete or continuous. Identify the scale of measurement (nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio) for a list of variables. Explain the difference between descriptive and inferential statistics. These are easy marks if you practise with a few examples.

A quick self-check: Classify these. Number of students in a class: quantitative, discrete, ratio. Blood group: qualitative, nominal. Temperature in Celsius: quantitative, continuous, interval. Customer rating of a restaurant (1 to 5 stars): ordinal. Time to download a file: quantitative, continuous, ratio. If you got these right, you already speak the basic language of statistics.

Recap: Probability is the maths of chance, statistics is the science of data. A population is everyone, a sample is the few we measure, parameters describe populations and statistics describe samples. Variables are qualitative or quantitative, and quantitative ones are discrete or continuous. Data can be nominal, ordinal, interval or ratio. Descriptive statistics summarizes, inferential statistics generalizes, and probability is the bridge. Next lesson, we will take a pile of raw data and turn it into tables and pictures that tell a story at a glance.
key_points: Probability is the maths of chance; statistics is the science of learning from data.
Population = the whole group; sample = the part we actually measure.
A parameter describes a population; a statistic is calculated from a sample.
Variables are qualitative (labels) or quantitative (numbers); quantitative ones are discrete (counted) or continuous (measured).
Four scales of measurement: nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio.
Descriptive statistics summarizes data; inferential statistics draws conclusions about a population from a sample.
A random sample is like stirring the pot before tasting; a biased sample gives misleading answers.
lessons.tip: Every time you see a number in the news, ask: who was measured, how many, and how were they chosen? This one habit makes statistics feel real.
lessons.task: Write down 6 variables about your family (for example age, blood group, phone operator, number of shoes, height, favourite food). Label each as qualitative or quantitative, discrete or continuous, and give its scale of measurement.

quiz.q: A survey of 500 students finds their average height is 162 cm. What is 162 cm?
quiz.explain: It is calculated from a sample, so it is a statistic. The true average of all students would be the parameter.

quiz.q: Which variable is continuous?
quiz.explain: Time is measured and can take any value in a range, so it is continuous. The others are counted or are labels.

quiz.q: Exam grades A+, A, A-, B are which scale?
quiz.explain: Grades have a clear order but the gaps between them are not equal numbers, so they are ordinal.

quiz.q: Temperature in Celsius is interval, not ratio, because...
quiz.explain: 0 degrees Celsius does not mean no heat, so ratios like twice as hot are not meaningful.

quiz.q: Using a sample of 1,000 voters to predict an election result is an example of...
quiz.explain: Going from a sample to a conclusion about the whole population is inference.

lessons.title: Organizing and Showing Data
lessons.content:
Imagine your class teacher hands you a sheet with the maths marks of 30 students, written in the order they sat in class: 45, 72, 68, 55, 90, 38, 61, ... and so on. Can you tell, just by staring, how the class did? Not really. Your eyes jump around, you see a 90 here and a 38 there, but the big picture hides. Now imagine the same marks turned into a neat table that says "8 students scored between 60 and 69" and a bar picture where the tallest bar sits right in the middle. Suddenly you can see the story in two seconds. That is what this lesson is about: organizing and showing data so that patterns pop out.

Raw data: Data in the form it was collected, unsorted and unorganized, is called raw data or ungrouped data. A list of 30 marks in random order is raw data. The first simple step is to sort it, an ordered list is called an array. Sorting already tells you the smallest and largest values, and the range between them. But with hundreds or thousands of values, even a sorted list is too long to read. We need to compress it.

Frequency: The frequency of a value is how many times it appears. Suppose 20 students were asked how many siblings they have, and the answers were: 0, 1, 2, 1, 3, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, 4, 1, 2, 1, 0, 3, 2, 1, 1, 2. Count each value. 0 appears 3 times, 1 appears 8 times, 2 appears 6 times, 3 appears 2 times, and 4 appears once. Check: 3 + 8 + 6 + 2 + 1 = 20, which matches the number of students. A table with values in one column and frequencies in the other is called a frequency distribution table. In the old days people counted using tally marks: four straight lines and a fifth line crossing them for each group of five. It is still a great trick when counting by hand.

Grouped data and class intervals: For continuous data like heights, or data with many different values like marks out of 100, listing every value is useless, because almost every value would have frequency 1. Instead we group values into class intervals, like 30-39, 40-49, 50-59, and so on. Each interval is called a class. The lower class limit of 40-49 is 40 and the upper class limit is 49. The class width (or class size) is the gap between the lower limits of two neighbouring classes, here 10. The class mark or midpoint is the average of the limits: (40 + 49) / 2 = 44.5. The midpoint represents the whole class when we do calculations later.

How many classes and how wide: There is no single fixed rule, but a common guideline is to use about 5 to 15 classes. Too few classes hide the shape, too many make it bumpy and noisy. A simple recipe: find the range (largest minus smallest), decide on a number of classes, then class width is roughly range divided by number of classes, rounded up to a nice number. For example, if marks go from 31 to 95, the range is 64. With 7 classes, 64 / 7 is about 9.1, so we choose width 10 and start at 30: 30-39, 40-49, ..., 90-99. Some books also mention Sturges' rule, which suggests about 1 + 3.322 log10(n) classes for n values. For n = 100 this gives about 7.6, so 7 or 8 classes.

Inclusive and exclusive classes: Classes like 30-39, 40-49 are called inclusive, because both limits belong to the class. But for continuous data, where would 39.5 go? There is a gap between 39 and 40. To fix this we use class boundaries, found by going half a unit outward: 29.5-39.5, 39.5-49.5, and so on. Another style is exclusive classes, like 30-40, 40-50, where the convention is that the upper limit is not included, so 40 belongs to 40-50. Exams often ask you to convert inclusive classes into boundaries before drawing a histogram, so remember the half-unit trick.

Relative and cumulative frequency: The relative frequency of a class is its frequency divided by the total. If 8 out of 40 students scored 60-69, the relative frequency is 8 / 40 = 0.2, or 20%. Relative frequencies always add up to 1 (or 100%). They are handy when comparing two groups of different sizes. The cumulative frequency of a class is the running total up to and including that class. If classes have frequencies 2, 5, 8, 12, 9, 4, then cumulative frequencies are 2, 7, 15, 27, 36, 40. The last cumulative frequency always equals the total. Cumulative frequency answers questions like "how many students scored less than 70?" instantly.

A complete worked table: Suppose 40 students' marks are grouped like this. Class 30-39: frequency 2. Class 40-49: 5. Class 50-59: 8. Class 60-69: 12. Class 70-79: 9. Class 80-89: 4. Midpoints are 34.5, 44.5, 54.5, 64.5, 74.5 and 84.5. Relative frequencies are 0.05, 0.125, 0.2, 0.3, 0.225, 0.1, which add to 1. Cumulative frequencies are 2, 7, 15, 27, 36, 40. From this one table you already know the most crowded class is 60-69, and 15 students (37.5%) scored below 60.

Bar charts: Now to pictures. A bar chart shows categories along one axis and frequencies as bar heights. It is perfect for qualitative or discrete data, like favourite mobile operator or number of siblings. The bars have gaps between them, because the categories are separate. The order of bars can be anything for nominal data, though sorting from tallest to shortest makes it easier to read.

Pie charts: A pie chart shows how a whole is split into parts. Each category gets a slice, and the angle of the slice is its relative frequency times 360 degrees. If 30% of students like biryani, that slice gets 0.3 x 360 = 108 degrees. Pie charts are good when there are a few categories and you care about share of the whole. They are bad when there are many small slices, or when you want to compare similar values, because human eyes are poor at comparing angles. Many statisticians prefer bar charts for this reason.

Histograms: A histogram looks like a bar chart but is for continuous or grouped numerical data. The horizontal axis is a number line with class boundaries, and the bars touch each other, because the classes are continuous with no gaps. The height of each bar is the frequency (when all classes have equal width). A histogram shows the shape of the data: is it a nice hill in the middle, does it lean to one side, does it have two peaks? If class widths are unequal, the height should be frequency density, which is frequency divided by class width, so that the area of each bar represents its frequency. That is a classic exam trap.

Frequency polygon: Take a histogram, put a dot at the top middle of each bar (at the class midpoint), and join the dots with straight lines. To close the shape, add one empty class with zero frequency at each end. This line shape is a frequency polygon. It is useful for comparing two distributions on the same graph, for example the marks of two sections, since two polygons can overlap without hiding each other, unlike two histograms.

Ogive (cumulative frequency curve): An ogive plots cumulative frequency against the upper class boundary. For our marks table, the points are (39.5, 2), (49.5, 7), (59.5, 15), (69.5, 27), (79.5, 36), (89.5, 40), starting from (29.5, 0). Join them with a smooth curve or straight lines. The curve always rises from left to right and looks like a stretched S. The ogive is very useful: to find the median, go to half the total on the vertical axis, which is 20, move across to the curve and down to read the mark. Quartiles and percentiles can be read the same way. This type is called a "less than" ogive; a "more than" ogive uses lower boundaries and falls instead.

Stem-and-leaf plot: This is a clever display that keeps the actual numbers. Split each number into a stem (all but the last digit) and a leaf (the last digit). For marks 45, 47, 52, 58, 58, 61, 63, 67, 69, 72: stem 4 has leaves 5 7, stem 5 has leaves 2 8 8, stem 6 has leaves 1 3 7 9, stem 7 has leaf 2. Written in rows, it looks like a sideways histogram, but you can still read every original value. It is great for small data sets you sort by hand.

Other common charts: A line graph shows how a value changes over time, like daily COVID cases or the dollar-taka rate across months. A dot plot puts one dot per observation above a number line. A scatter plot shows two numerical variables at once, like study hours and marks; we will use it in the correlation lesson. Choosing the right chart is part of the skill: categories go in bar or pie charts, distributions of numbers go in histograms, changes over time go in line graphs.

Real-life example 1, a shop's daily sales: A mobile recharge shop in Mirpur records how many customers come each hour from 9 am to 9 pm for a month. The owner makes a frequency table of customers per hour and a line graph of the average for each hour of the day. The line shows two peaks, one around 1 pm and a bigger one around 7 pm when people return from work. So he decides to have two people at the counter only from 6 to 9 pm. A simple table and a line graph saved him salary money and kept customers happy.

Real-life example 2, an app's load times: A developer at a Bangladeshi fintech app collects how long the home screen takes to load for 1,000 users. She makes a histogram with classes of 0.5 seconds. Most bars sit between 1 and 2.5 seconds, but there is a long tail on the right, with a small bump around 6 seconds. Looking deeper, she finds that the bump is from users on slow 2G networks in rural areas. Without the histogram, the average alone would have hidden that group. The picture told her exactly where to optimize.

Lying with graphs: Charts can mislead. A bar chart whose vertical axis starts at 90 instead of 0 makes a change from 92 to 95 look huge. A 3D pie chart makes front slices look bigger than they are. Pictograms where an image is doubled in both width and height look four times bigger, not twice. When you read a chart, always check the axis scales, where the axis starts, and whether the areas match the numbers.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often draw histograms with gaps between bars (wrong), or forget to use class boundaries for inclusive classes. Another mistake is using frequency instead of frequency density when class widths are unequal. In ogives, people plot cumulative frequency against midpoints instead of upper boundaries. Typical exam questions: build a frequency table from raw data with given class width; find relative and cumulative frequencies; draw a histogram, frequency polygon and ogive; read the median or quartiles from an ogive; draw a stem-and-leaf plot; choose and justify a suitable chart.

Recap: Raw data becomes useful once organized. Frequency tables count how often values appear, grouped tables use class intervals with limits, boundaries, widths and midpoints. Relative frequency gives proportions, cumulative frequency gives running totals. Bar and pie charts suit categories, histograms and frequency polygons show the shape of numerical data, ogives answer "how many below" questions, and stem-and-leaf plots keep the real values. Next lesson we squeeze a whole data set into one number that describes its centre: mean, median and mode.
key_points: Raw data is unorganized; sorting it gives an array, and counting gives a frequency table.
Grouped data uses class intervals with limits, boundaries, width and midpoint (class mark).
Relative frequency = frequency / total and adds up to 1; cumulative frequency is a running total.
Bar and pie charts suit categories; in a pie chart, angle = relative frequency x 360 degrees.
Histograms are for continuous data: bars touch; use frequency density when widths are unequal.
A frequency polygon joins midpoints; an ogive plots cumulative frequency against upper boundaries and helps find the median.
Stem-and-leaf plots show shape while keeping every original value.
Check axis scales: charts can mislead when the axis does not start at zero.
lessons.tip: When you draw any chart, first write down the total and check your frequencies add up to it. Half of all chart mistakes are counting mistakes.
lessons.task: Ask 15 friends or family members how many hours they slept last night. Make a frequency table, a stem-and-leaf plot, and a small histogram on paper. Where is the peak?

quiz.q: In a pie chart, a category with relative frequency 0.25 gets what angle?
quiz.explain: 0.25 x 360 = 90 degrees.

quiz.q: What are the class boundaries of the inclusive class 40-49?
quiz.explain: Go half a unit outward on each side: 39.5 and 49.5.

quiz.q: Frequencies are 3, 7, 10, 5. What is the third cumulative frequency?
Which statement about histograms is correct?
options: Bars touch because the classes are continuous
They are only for nominal data
Bar height is always the class midpoint
quiz.explain: Histograms show continuous numerical classes, so the bars touch.

quiz.q: An ogive plots cumulative frequency against...
quiz.explain: A less-than ogive uses the upper class boundaries.

lessons.title: Mean, Median and Mode
lessons.content:
Your cousin asks you, "How did your class do in the maths exam?" You do not want to read out 40 numbers. You want one number that sums it all up, something like "most of us got around 63". That one number is called a measure of central tendency, a value that tells where the centre or typical point of the data sits. There are three famous ones, the mean, the median and the mode, plus a few special means. Each one has a personality: some are sensitive, some are stubborn, and choosing the right one is a real skill.

The arithmetic mean: This is the everyday "average". Add all values and divide by how many there are. In symbols, mean = (x1 + x2 + ... + xn) / n, often written x-bar = sum of x / n. For marks 6, 8, 5, 9, 7, the sum is 35 and n = 5, so the mean is 7. The population mean is written with the Greek letter mu, and the sample mean with x-bar. Think of the mean as the balance point: if you put equal weights at each value on a ruler, the ruler balances exactly at the mean.

A useful property of the mean: The deviations from the mean always add up to zero. For 6, 8, 5, 9, 7 with mean 7, the deviations are -1, +1, -2, +2, 0, which sum to 0. This is why it is the balance point. Another property: if you add a constant to every value, the mean shifts by that constant, and if you multiply every value by a constant, the mean is multiplied too. If every student gets 5 grace marks, the class mean rises by exactly 5.

Mean from a frequency table: When values repeat, multiply each value by its frequency. For siblings data with values 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and frequencies 3, 8, 6, 2, 1, the sum of f times x is 0 + 8 + 12 + 6 + 4 = 30, and the total frequency is 20, so the mean is 30 / 20 = 1.5 siblings. Notice the mean need not be a possible value: nobody has 1.5 siblings, but the average family does.

Mean of grouped data: For grouped data we do not know the exact values, so we pretend every value sits at its class midpoint. Take our marks table from last lesson: midpoints 34.5, 44.5, 54.5, 64.5, 74.5, 84.5 with frequencies 2, 5, 8, 12, 9, 4. The products f times x are 69, 222.5, 436, 774, 670.5 and 338, summing to 2510. Divide by 40 and the mean is 62.75. This is an estimate, because of the midpoint assumption, but it is usually very close. For big numbers, some textbooks use a shortcut called the assumed mean or step-deviation method, which gives the same answer with smaller arithmetic.

Weighted mean: Sometimes values do not count equally. Your CGPA is the perfect example. Suppose you took three courses: a 3-credit course with grade point 4.00, another 3-credit course with 3.50, and a 1.5-credit lab with 3.00. The weighted mean is (3 x 4.00 + 3 x 3.50 + 1.5 x 3.00) / (3 + 3 + 1.5) = (12 + 10.5 + 4.5) / 7.5 = 27 / 7.5 = 3.60. If you had wrongly taken a simple average of 4.00, 3.50 and 3.00 you would get 3.50, which is wrong because the lab has fewer credits. Formula: weighted mean = sum of (w times x) / sum of w.

The median: The median is the middle value after sorting. For 3, 9, 4, 7, 5: sort it to 3, 4, 5, 7, 9, and the middle (3rd) value is 5. If there is an even number of values, take the average of the two middle ones: for 2, 4, 6, 10, the median is (4 + 6) / 2 = 5. A general rule: the median is at position (n + 1) / 2 in the sorted list. The median splits the data into two halves: half the values are below it, half above.

Why the median is stubborn: Imagine 10 people in an office. Nine earn 20,000 taka a month and the owner earns 5,00,000. The mean income is (9 x 20,000 + 5,00,000) / 10 = 6,80,000 / 10 = 68,000 taka. That makes it sound like a typical person earns 68,000, which is false; nine out of ten earn far less. The median is 20,000, which is the honest "typical" salary. We say the median is robust or resistant to outliers. That is why reports on income and house prices usually use the median.

Median of grouped data: Find N / 2, locate the class where the cumulative frequency first reaches N / 2 (the median class), then use: median = L + ((N/2 - F) / f) x h. Here L is the lower boundary of the median class, F is the cumulative frequency before it, f is its frequency and h is its width. For our marks table, N / 2 = 20; cumulative frequencies are 2, 7, 15, 27, ... so the median class is 60-69 with boundary L = 59.5, F = 15, f = 12, h = 10. Median = 59.5 + (5 / 12) x 10 = 59.5 + 4.17 = 63.67, about 63.7. You could also read this from the ogive, as we saw last lesson.

The mode: The mode is the value that appears most often. In 2, 3, 3, 5, 3, 7, 5 the mode is 3. A data set can have one mode (unimodal), two modes (bimodal), more (multimodal), or no mode at all if every value appears once. The mode is the only measure of centre that works for nominal data: you cannot average blood groups, but you can say the most common blood group is O+. Shoe shops love the mode: they stock the most common shoe size the most.

Mode of grouped data: First find the modal class, the one with the highest frequency. Then: mode = L + ((f1 - f0) / ((f1 - f0) + (f1 - f2))) x h, where f1 is the modal class frequency, f0 the one before and f2 the one after. In our table the modal class is 60-69 with f1 = 12, f0 = 8, f2 = 9. Mode = 59.5 + (4 / (4 + 3)) x 10 = 59.5 + 5.71 = 65.21. The formula pulls the mode towards the neighbour with the larger frequency.

The empirical relation: For data that is only moderately skewed, Karl Pearson noticed a rough rule: mode is about 3 x median - 2 x mean. Check it with our table: 3 x 63.67 - 2 x 62.75 = 191.0 - 125.5 = 65.5, close to the 65.21 we calculated. This is only an approximation, but exams like asking you to use it when one of the three is missing.

Geometric mean: The geometric mean of n positive numbers is the nth root of their product. For 2 and 8, GM = square root of 16 = 4. It is the right average for growth rates and ratios. If your savings grow by 10% in one year and 50% the next, the growth factors are 1.1 and 1.5. The average factor is the square root of 1.1 x 1.5 = square root of 1.65, about 1.285, so about 28.5% per year, not the simple average of 30%. Using the arithmetic mean for growth over-states it.

Harmonic mean: The harmonic mean is n divided by the sum of reciprocals. It is the right average for rates like speed when the distance is fixed. A bus goes from Dhaka to Gazipur at 60 km/h and comes back on the same road at 40 km/h. The average speed is not 50. It is 2 / (1/60 + 1/40) = 2 / (5/120) = 48 km/h, because the bus spends more time on the slower trip. For any set of positive numbers, AM is greater than or equal to GM, which is greater than or equal to HM. For 2 and 8: AM = 5, GM = 4, HM = 2 / (1/2 + 1/8) = 3.2.

Which one to choose: Use the mean for roughly symmetric numerical data without extreme values; it uses every value and works well with later maths. Use the median for skewed data or data with outliers, like income, house rent or app response times. Use the mode for categorical data or when you want the most popular choice. Use the GM for growth rates and the HM for rates over fixed amounts. In a perfectly symmetric bell-shaped distribution, mean, median and mode are all equal.

Real-life example 1, response times on a server: A backend engineer at a ride-sharing app looks at 1,000 API response times. Most are around 80 milliseconds, but a few requests stuck behind a database lock took 5 seconds. The mean is 120 ms, pulled up by the slow ones, while the median is 78 ms. Engineers usually report the median along with high percentiles like the 95th or 99th, because the mean hides what normal users feel and also hides how bad the slow tail is. We will meet percentiles in the next lesson.

Real-life example 2, your CGPA and a cricket average: Your university result sheet uses a weighted mean, credit hours are the weights, so a 4-credit course moves your CGPA more than a 1-credit lab. Cricket batting averages are another twist: the average is total runs divided by the number of times out, not the number of innings, so not-out innings add runs without adding to the divisor. Always ask what is being divided by what.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Forgetting to sort before finding the median. Using the simple mean when weights are given. Using lower class limits instead of boundaries in the grouped median and mode formulas. Averaging percentages or speeds without thinking about whether GM or HM is right. Typical exam questions: find mean, median and mode for raw and grouped data; compute a weighted mean; show AM is greater than or equal to GM greater than or equal to HM for given numbers; use the empirical relation; explain which measure suits a given situation and why.

Recap: The mean is the balance point and uses every value but is pulled by outliers. The median is the middle, robust to extreme values. The mode is the most common value and works even for categories. Grouped data uses midpoints for the mean and interpolation formulas for the median and mode. Weighted, geometric and harmonic means handle unequal importance, growth and rates. Next lesson asks a second question: how spread out is the data around its centre?
key_points: Mean = sum / count; it is the balance point and deviations from it sum to zero.
Grouped mean uses class midpoints: mean = sum of f x / sum of f.
Weighted mean = sum of w x / sum of w (CGPA uses credit hours as weights).
Median is the middle of sorted data, at position (n + 1) / 2, and is robust to outliers.
Grouped median = L + ((N/2 - F) / f) x h; grouped mode = L + (f1 - f0) / ((f1 - f0) + (f1 - f2)) x h.
Mode is the most frequent value and the only centre measure for nominal data.
Geometric mean suits growth rates, harmonic mean suits rates like speed; AM >= GM >= HM.
lessons.tip: For every centre question, first ask: are there outliers or is the data skewed? If yes, lean towards the median.

Credits 3, 3, 1 with grade points 4.0, 3.0, 2.0. What is the weighted mean?
A car goes 30 km at 30 km/h and returns 30 km at 60 km/h. Average speed?

lessons.title: Measuring Spread: Range to Standard Deviation
lessons.content:
Two batsmen both have a batting average of 40 over their last five innings. Batsman A scored 38, 42, 40, 39, 41. Batsman B scored 0, 95, 2, 100, 3. Same average, completely different players. A is a steady wall; B is either a hero or a duck. If you only reported the mean, you would miss the most important difference between them. That difference is called dispersion, or spread, or variability: how far the values wander from the centre. This lesson gives you the tools to measure it.

Why spread matters: Knowing the centre alone is like knowing a road's average depth of water is 10 cm. You might happily walk in, and then find a 2-metre hole in the middle. In real life, spread is often what decides things. A factory wants bolts that are all very close to 10 mm, not bolts that average 10 mm while half of them do not fit. A bank wants to know not just the average return of an investment but how much it jumps around, which is risk. A teacher wants to know whether the whole class is at the same level or split into strong and weak groups.

Range: The simplest measure of spread is the range: largest value minus smallest value. For batsman A the range is 42 - 38 = 4; for batsman B it is 100 - 0 = 100. Easy, and already it shows the difference. But the range uses only two values and ignores everything in between, and one wild value can blow it up. For 3, 5, 6, 7, 100 the range is 97, even though four of the five values are close together.

Quartiles: Quartiles cut sorted data into four equal parts. Q1 (the lower quartile) has 25% of the data below it, Q2 is the median (50%), and Q3 (the upper quartile) has 75% below it. One common hand method: find the median, then Q1 is the median of the lower half and Q3 is the median of the upper half. Take 11 sorted values: 3, 5, 7, 8, 9, 11, 13, 15, 17, 20, 25. The median (6th value) is 11. The lower half 3, 5, 7, 8, 9 has median 7, so Q1 = 7. The upper half 13, 15, 17, 20, 25 has median 17, so Q3 = 17. Another common method uses positions (n + 1)/4 and 3(n + 1)/4, here the 3rd and 9th values, giving the same 7 and 17. Different textbooks and software use slightly different rules, so small differences in answers are normal; follow the method your course uses.

Interquartile range: The IQR is Q3 - Q1. In our example IQR = 17 - 7 = 10. It is the spread of the middle 50% of the data, and because it ignores the top and bottom quarters, extreme values cannot disturb it. That makes it the natural partner of the median, just as the standard deviation is the natural partner of the mean. Half of the IQR, (Q3 - Q1) / 2, is called the quartile deviation or semi-interquartile range, which some exams ask for.

Percentiles: Percentiles generalize quartiles. The kth percentile is the value below which k% of the data falls. Q1 is the 25th percentile, the median is the 50th, Q3 is the 75th. If your admission test score is at the 90th percentile, you did better than about 90% of the test takers. That says nothing about your raw marks, only your position. Software engineers use percentiles all the time: "p99 latency is 800 ms" means 99% of requests finished within 800 ms. Deciles cut data into ten parts, so the 1st decile is the 10th percentile.

Box plot and outliers: A box plot (box-and-whisker plot) draws the five-number summary: minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum. A box goes from Q1 to Q3 with a line at the median, and whiskers stretch out to the smallest and largest values that are not outliers. A common rule marks a value as an outlier if it is below Q1 - 1.5 x IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 x IQR. In our example the fences are 7 - 15 = -8 and 17 + 15 = 32, so nothing is an outlier. If the last value were 40 instead of 25, it would be above 32 and would be drawn as a separate dot. A box plot shows centre, spread, skew and outliers in one tiny picture, and it is great for comparing groups side by side.

Mean deviation: Now measures that use every value. The idea: how far, on average, is each value from the mean? Distances must be positive, so we use absolute values. Mean absolute deviation = sum of |x - mean| / n. Take data 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9 with mean 40 / 8 = 5. The absolute deviations are 3, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 2, 4, summing to 12, so the mean deviation is 12 / 8 = 1.5. It is easy to understand, but absolute values are awkward in algebra, so statisticians usually prefer the next measure.

Variance: Instead of absolute values, square the deviations, which also makes them positive. The population variance is sigma squared = sum of (x - mu)^2 / N, the average squared distance from the mean. For our data the deviations -3, -1, -1, -1, 0, 0, 2, 4 have squares 9, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 4, 16, which sum to 32. Variance = 32 / 8 = 4. Squaring gives extra weight to big deviations, which is often what we want, since big misses are worse. The downside is the unit: if the data is in centimetres, variance is in square centimetres.

Standard deviation: To get back to the original units, take the square root of the variance. The standard deviation sigma = square root of variance = square root of 4 = 2. You can read it as "the typical distance from the mean". For batsman A the SD is about 1.4 runs; for batsman B it is about 47 runs. One number shows the whole difference. The SD is the most used measure of spread in all of statistics, and it will appear again and again in the normal distribution, confidence intervals and tests.

A faster formula: Computing every deviation is slow. An equivalent shortcut is variance = (sum of x^2) / N - mean^2, the "mean of the squares minus the square of the mean". For our data, the squares are 4, 16, 16, 16, 25, 25, 49, 81, summing to 232. So variance = 232 / 8 - 5^2 = 29 - 25 = 4. Same answer. For grouped data, use variance = (sum of f x^2) / N - mean^2 with x as class midpoints.

Sample variance and n - 1: When your data is a sample and you want to estimate the population variance, divide by n - 1 instead of n: s squared = sum of (x - x-bar)^2 / (n - 1). For our 8 values, s squared = 32 / 7 = 4.57 and s = 2.14. Why? The sample mean sits in the middle of the sample by construction, so deviations from it are a bit smaller than deviations from the true population mean would be. Dividing by the slightly smaller n - 1 corrects that underestimate on average. This is called Bessel's correction, and the result is an unbiased estimator of the population variance; we will revisit this idea in the estimation lesson. Calculators often have two buttons, sigma n and sigma n-1, for exactly this reason.

Properties of variance and SD: Adding a constant to every value does not change the spread at all; everyone just shifts together. Giving everyone 5 grace marks leaves the SD unchanged. Multiplying every value by a constant c multiplies the SD by |c| and the variance by c squared. Converting heights from metres to centimetres multiplies the SD by 100 and the variance by 10,000. The variance is zero only if all values are identical.

Coefficient of variation: How do you compare spread between data sets with different means or units? Use the CV = (SD / mean) x 100%. Section A has a mean of 60 with SD 12, so CV = 20%. Section B has a mean of 75 with SD 9, so CV = 12%. Section B is relatively more consistent. The CV has no units, so you can even compare the variability of weights in kg with heights in cm. It only makes sense for ratio-scale data with a positive mean.

Real-life example 1, choosing a player: The selectors of a Dhaka Premier League team must pick one opener. Both candidates average 35. Player X has an SD of 8 runs, Player Y has an SD of 30. For a team that needs a steady start, X is the better pick; for a team that needs a gamble to chase a big target, Y might be interesting. The CVs are 23% and 86%. Selectors and fantasy-league players think exactly like this, whether or not they use the word "standard deviation".

Real-life example 2, delivery times: A courier company in Chattogram promises delivery within 3 days. Their average delivery time is 2.1 days, which looks great. But the SD is 1.5 days and the box plot shows many outliers at 6 to 8 days in rainy months. Customers remember the late ones, not the average. The company decides to track the 95th percentile instead of the mean, and sets a goal to bring it under 3 days. Spread, not centre, was the real problem.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Forgetting to square-root the variance when asked for SD. Mixing up dividing by n and n - 1; read the question for "sample" or "population". Forgetting that variance is in squared units. Using the shortcut formula with rounded means, which can cause big rounding errors; keep extra decimals. Typical exam questions: find range, quartiles, IQR and quartile deviation; calculate mean deviation, variance and SD for raw and grouped data; compute and compare coefficients of variation; draw a box plot and identify outliers using the 1.5 x IQR rule; show how SD changes when data is shifted or scaled.

Recap: Spread tells how much data varies around its centre. Range is quick but fragile. Quartiles, percentiles and the IQR describe positions and the middle 50% and are robust, and box plots show them in a picture along with outliers. Mean deviation, variance and standard deviation use every value; the SD is the standard measure, in the same units as the data. Divide by n - 1 for sample variance. The coefficient of variation compares spread across different scales. Next lesson looks at the shape of data: is it lopsided, and how heavy are its tails?
key_points: Range = max - min: quick but sensitive to one extreme value.
Quartiles split sorted data into four parts; IQR = Q3 - Q1 covers the middle 50% and resists outliers.
Outlier rule: below Q1 - 1.5 x IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 x IQR; box plots show the five-number summary.
Variance = average squared deviation from the mean; standard deviation = its square root, in original units.
Shortcut: variance = mean of squares - square of mean.
Sample variance divides by n - 1 (Bessel's correction).
Adding a constant does not change SD; multiplying by c multiplies SD by |c|.
Coefficient of variation = SD / mean x 100% compares spread across different scales.
lessons.tip: Always pair the median with the IQR and the mean with the standard deviation. Reporting a centre without a spread is only half the story.
lessons.task: Time how many seconds it takes you to tie your shoes 8 times. Find the mean, the range, the IQR and the standard deviation (by hand or phone calculator). Is your timing consistent?

lessons.title: Shape of Data: Moments, Skewness and Kurtosis
lessons.content:
Picture three slides in a children's park. The first one is a perfectly symmetric hill: same slope on both sides. The second one has a long, gentle slope going off to the right. The third has its long slope going off to the left. Even if all three hills had the same height and the same middle point, a child would feel the difference instantly. Data has shapes like these too. Knowing the centre and the spread is not enough; we also want to know whether the data leans to one side, and whether it has a sharp peak with heavy tails or a flat top. Those two ideas are called skewness and kurtosis, and they are built from a tool called moments.

What is a moment: The word comes from physics, where a moment measures the turning effect of a force around a point. In statistics, a moment is an average of powers of the data. The rth raw moment (about zero) is m'r = sum of x^r / n. So the first raw moment is just the mean, the second raw moment is the average of the squares, and so on. Central moments are taken about the mean instead of zero: mr = sum of (x - mean)^r / n. Each moment describes a different feature of the shape.

The first four central moments: The first central moment m1 is always zero, because deviations from the mean always sum to zero, as we saw in lesson 3. The second central moment m2 is the variance, the measure of spread. The third central moment m3 measures lopsidedness: cubing keeps the sign of each deviation, so big positive deviations push m3 up and big negative ones push it down. The fourth central moment m4 measures how much weight sits in the tails, because raising to the fourth power makes far-away values count enormously.

Raw to central moments: Exams often give raw moments and ask for central ones. If we write the raw moments as m'1, m'2, m'3, m'4, the relations are: m2 = m'2 - (m'1)^2; m3 = m'3 - 3 m'2 m'1 + 2 (m'1)^3; m4 = m'4 - 4 m'3 m'1 + 6 m'2 (m'1)^2 - 3 (m'1)^4. The first one is the shortcut variance formula you already know. The others come from expanding (x - mean)^3 and (x - mean)^4 with the binomial theorem and averaging. You do not need to memorize the derivation, but practise using the formulas once or twice.

A worked example of moments: Take the data 1, 2, 3, 4, 10. The mean is 20 / 5 = 4. Deviations are -3, -2, -1, 0, 6. Squares are 9, 4, 1, 0, 36, so m2 = 50 / 5 = 10. Cubes are -27, -8, -1, 0, 216, so m3 = 180 / 5 = 36. Notice how the single value 10 dominates m3: its cube, 216, outweighs all the negative cubes together. That is the cube doing its job, signalling a long tail on the right.

Skewness: Skewness describes asymmetry. In a symmetric distribution, the left and right sides are mirror images, and the mean, median and mode coincide. In a positively skewed (right-skewed) distribution, the tail stretches to the right: most values are smallish, a few are very large. Incomes, house prices, waiting times and file sizes are classic examples. Here the large values pull the mean to the right, so typically mean is greater than median, which is greater than mode. In a negatively skewed (left-skewed) distribution, the tail stretches to the left: most values are high and a few are very low, like marks on an easy exam where most students score 80 to 95 but a few score 20. Then typically mean is less than median, which is less than mode. A memory trick: the skew is named after the side of the tail, not the side of the peak.

Moment coefficient of skewness: To get a number without units, divide m3 by the cube of the standard deviation: gamma1 = m3 / (m2)^(3/2). Some textbooks use beta1 = m3^2 / m2^3, and then gamma1 is its square root with the sign of m3. For our data, m2 = 10, so (m2)^(3/2) = 10 x square root of 10, about 31.62, and gamma1 = 36 / 31.62, about 1.14. A positive value means right skew. A value of zero means no skew (as measured by this coefficient), and a negative value means left skew. As a rough guide, values beyond plus or minus 1 are usually called highly skewed.

Pearson's coefficients of skewness: Karl Pearson gave two simpler measures that use the mean, median, mode and SD. The first is Sk1 = (mean - mode) / SD. The second, useful when the mode is unclear, is Sk2 = 3 (mean - median) / SD. Let us use our grouped marks table from lessons 2 and 3: mean 62.75, median 63.67, mode 65.21. The SD of that table, using the grouped formula, is about 13.21. So Sk1 = (62.75 - 65.21) / 13.21, about -0.19, and Sk2 = 3 x (62.75 - 63.67) / 13.21, about -0.21. Both are slightly negative: a gentle left skew, with a few low scorers stretching the tail.

Bowley's coefficient: There is also a quartile-based measure, Bowley's coefficient of skewness: (Q3 + Q1 - 2 Q2) / (Q3 - Q1). It compares the distance from the median to each quartile. If the upper quartile is further away from the median than the lower quartile, the result is positive. Because it uses only quartiles, it is robust to outliers, and it always lies between -1 and +1. With Q1 = 7, Q2 = 11, Q3 = 17 from lesson 4, it gives (17 + 7 - 22) / 10 = 0.2, a mild right skew.

Kurtosis: Kurtosis describes the tails and peak of a distribution compared to a normal (bell-shaped) distribution. The usual measure is beta2 = m4 / m2^2. For a normal distribution, beta2 equals exactly 3. Many software packages report excess kurtosis, gamma2 = beta2 - 3, so that a normal distribution gets 0. Always check which version a table or program is showing.

Three types of kurtosis: A distribution with beta2 greater than 3 is called leptokurtic ("lepto" means slender): it tends to have a sharper peak and heavier tails, so extreme values occur more often than a normal curve would predict. Stock market daily returns are a famous example; big crashes happen more often than a bell curve suggests. A distribution with beta2 equal to 3 is mesokurtic, like the normal. A distribution with beta2 less than 3 is platykurtic ("platy" means flat, like a platypus's flat bill, or a plate): flatter, with lighter tails. A uniform distribution, where every value in a range is equally likely, is platykurtic. Modern statisticians stress that kurtosis is mostly about tails, the chance of extreme values, more than about the pointiness of the peak.

A tiny kurtosis example: Take the data -1, -1, 1, 1. The mean is 0, every deviation is plus or minus 1, so m2 = 1 and m4 = 1. Then beta2 = 1 / 1 = 1, far below 3. This data has no tails at all: everything sits exactly one unit from the mean. In fact, 1 is the smallest possible value of beta2. On the other hand, data where most values are zero but one value is huge, like 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 10, will have a very large beta2, because that single huge deviation dominates the fourth power.

Why moments matter beyond describing: Moments come back later in this course in a more powerful form. For random variables, the mean is the first moment and the variance is the second central moment. The moment generating function, which we meet in lesson 11, packs all the moments of a distribution into one function. And in machine learning, checking skewness tells you when to transform data, for example taking the logarithm of incomes before building a model, which pulls in a long right tail.

Real-life example 1, mobile data usage: A telecom analyst studies the monthly data usage of 10,000 prepaid customers. Most use 2 to 8 GB, but a small number of heavy users stream video all day and use 100 GB or more. The histogram has a long right tail, the mean (12 GB) is much larger than the median (5 GB), and the skewness coefficient is strongly positive. If the company designs its most popular package around the mean, it will overestimate what a typical customer needs. Designing around the median and percentiles works better. The analyst may also take logarithms of usage before running a regression, because the log makes the shape closer to symmetric.

Reading shape without formulas: You can often guess the shape before computing anything. In a box plot, if the right whisker is much longer than the left one and the median line sits closer to Q1, the data is right-skewed. If the whiskers are equal and the median is in the middle of the box, the data is roughly symmetric. With quartiles alone, compare Q3 - Q2 with Q2 - Q1: a bigger upper gap means right skew. For kurtosis, look at the outliers: many far-away points beyond the whiskers hint at heavy tails, while a flat histogram with no outliers hints at light tails. These quick checks help you catch calculation mistakes in the exam hall.

Real-life example 2, exam design: A university teacher sets a test and finds a strongly negatively skewed result: most students got 85 to 98, a few got below 40. The test was too easy to separate strong students from very strong ones. Next semester she adds a few harder questions, and the distribution becomes closer to symmetric, with scores spread across the range. Teachers and admission test designers look at skewness and spread to judge whether an exam is doing its job.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Naming skew after the peak instead of the tail; a right-skewed distribution has its peak on the left. Forgetting that the first central moment is always zero. Mixing up beta2 and excess kurtosis, and calling a beta2 of 2.9 "leptokurtic" when it is slightly platykurtic. Using Pearson's first coefficient when the mode is poorly defined. Typical exam questions: define moments and convert raw moments into central moments; compute beta1, beta2, gamma1, gamma2 and interpret them; calculate Pearson's and Bowley's coefficients; sketch positive, negative and zero skew and order the mean, median and mode; explain leptokurtic, mesokurtic and platykurtic with diagrams.

Recap: Moments are averages of powers of the data. The first central moment is zero, the second is the variance, the third measures skewness and the fourth measures kurtosis. Skewness is named after the tail: right skew pulls the mean above the median, left skew pulls it below. Pearson's coefficients use mean, median, mode and SD, Bowley's uses quartiles, and the moment coefficient uses m3. Kurtosis beta2 = m4 / m2^2 equals 3 for a normal curve, with leptokurtic above and platykurtic below. With this, descriptive statistics is complete. Next we start probability with a key skill: counting the number of ways things can happen.
key_points: Raw moments are averages of x^r; central moments are averages of (x - mean)^r.
First central moment = 0, second = variance, third measures skewness, fourth measures kurtosis.
Skew is named after the tail: right skew usually gives mean > median > mode; left skew the reverse.
Moment coefficient of skewness gamma1 = m3 / m2^(3/2); Pearson's Sk1 = (mean - mode) / SD, Sk2 = 3 (mean - median) / SD.
Bowley's coefficient = (Q3 + Q1 - 2 Q2) / (Q3 - Q1), robust and between -1 and 1.
Kurtosis beta2 = m4 / m2^2 equals 3 for a normal curve; excess kurtosis = beta2 - 3.
Leptokurtic (> 3): heavy tails; mesokurtic (= 3); platykurtic (< 3): light tails.
lessons.tip: Draw a quick sketch every time you compute a skewness value. If the number says positive but your sketch has the long tail on the left, something is wrong.
lessons.task: Write down the ages of 12 people you know (family, neighbours, teachers). Find the mean and median and decide the direction of skew. Then sketch a rough histogram to check.

quiz.explain: The long right tail pulls the mean above the median, which sits above the mode.

quiz.explain: Deviations from the mean always sum to zero.

A distribution has beta2 = 4.5. It is...
quiz.explain: beta2 above 3 means heavier tails than normal: leptokurtic. Kurtosis says nothing certain about symmetry.

lessons.title: Counting: Permutations and Combinations
lessons.content:
Imagine you walk into a tea stall in the morning. The man asks: tea or coffee? With milk or without? With sugar or without? Before he even starts, you could ask a fun question: how many different cups could he possibly make? Two drinks, two milk choices, two sugar choices. That is 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 different cups. You just did counting, the way probability people do it. Counting sounds babyish, but when the numbers get big (how many passwords, how many lottery tickets, how many ways to pick a cricket team), you cannot list everything by hand. You need clever shortcuts. This lesson gives you those shortcuts.

Why counting matters for probability: In the classical idea of probability, which we meet in the next lesson, the chance of an event is (number of favourable outcomes) / (total number of outcomes), as long as every outcome is equally likely. So to find a probability, you often have to count two things: the good outcomes and all outcomes. If you can count well, half of probability becomes easy. Counting also shows up everywhere in computer science: how many possible passwords, how many test cases, how many paths in a grid, how many ways to schedule jobs, and how fast an algorithm grows.

The multiplication rule: If a task is done in steps, and step 1 can be done in n1 ways, step 2 in n2 ways, and so on, and the number of choices at each step does not depend on what you picked earlier, then the whole task can be done in n1 x n2 x ... x nk ways. Example: a shirt shop has 4 colours and 3 sizes. A shirt is (colour, size), so there are 4 x 3 = 12 kinds of shirt. A Bangladeshi car number plate has a city name, a letter class, and digits; each extra digit position multiplies the count by 10. This rule is the root of everything else in this lesson.

The addition rule for counting: If a task can be done in one of several separate ways that cannot happen together, you add. Example: you go from Dhaka to Chattogram by bus (5 companies), train (3 trains) or plane (2 airlines). You pick only one mode, so there are 5 + 3 + 2 = 10 choices. Remember the simple test: "and then" means multiply, "either or" (with no overlap) means add.

Factorial: The number of ways to arrange n different things in a row is n x (n-1) x ... x 2 x 1, written n! and read "n factorial". Why? The first place has n choices, the second has n-1 left, and so on. So 3! = 6, 4! = 24, 5! = 120, 10! = 3,628,800. By definition 0! = 1, which keeps the formulas working (there is exactly one way to arrange nothing). Factorials grow scary fast: 20! is about 2.4 x 10^18. That is why brute-force algorithms that try every ordering, like checking every route for a travelling salesman, become impossible for even 20 or 30 cities.

Permutations: A permutation is an arrangement where order matters. The number of ways to arrange r things chosen from n different things is nPr = n! / (n-r)!. Example: a class of 10 students elects a captain, a vice-captain and a secretary. Order matters because the posts are different. So the count is 10P3 = 10 x 9 x 8 = 720. A quick way to compute nPr: start at n and multiply r numbers going down. 7P2 = 7 x 6 = 42.

Permutations with repetition allowed: If each of r positions can use any of n symbols again and again, the count is n^r. A 4-digit mobile banking PIN using digits 0-9 has 10^4 = 10,000 possibilities. A 6-character password using only lowercase letters has 26^6, which is about 309 million. Add uppercase letters and digits (62 symbols) and it becomes 62^6, about 57 billion. This is the simple math behind "use a longer password with mixed characters".

Permutations with identical items: If some items look the same, swapping them does not create a new arrangement, so we divide. The number of distinct arrangements of n items where one type repeats n1 times, another n2 times, and so on, is n! / (n1! n2! ... nk!). Example: the letters of the word DHAKA. There are 5 letters with A appearing twice, so 5! / 2! = 120 / 2 = 60 arrangements. The word BANANA has 6 letters, with A three times and N twice, so 6! / (3! 2!) = 720 / 12 = 60.

Circular permutations: When people sit around a round table, rotating everyone by one seat gives the same arrangement. So we fix one person and arrange the rest: (n-1)! ways. Five friends at a round table at an iftar party can sit in 4! = 24 different ways. If clockwise and anticlockwise are also considered the same (like beads on a necklace that you can flip), divide again by 2.

Combinations: A combination is a selection where order does not matter. The number of ways to choose r things from n is nCr = n! / (r! (n-r)!). It is also written as "n choose r". Each combination of r items can be arranged in r! orders, so nCr = nPr / r!. Example: choose 3 students from 10 for a quiz team, all with the same role. 10C3 = 720 / 6 = 120. Compare with the 720 for captain, vice-captain and secretary: the posts made order matter.

Useful facts about combinations: nC0 = nCn = 1 (one way to choose nothing, one way to choose everything). nCr = nC(n-r), because choosing who is in is the same as choosing who is out. So 10C8 = 10C2 = 45. And nCr = (n-1)C(r-1) + (n-1)Cr, called Pascal's rule: either a specific person is chosen (then pick r-1 from the other n-1) or not chosen (pick all r from the other n-1).

Pascal's triangle: Write 1 at the top. Each row starts and ends with 1, and every inside number is the sum of the two numbers above it. Rows: 1; 1 1; 1 2 1; 1 3 3 1; 1 4 6 4 1; 1 5 10 10 5 1. Row n (counting from 0) gives nC0, nC1, ..., nCn. So 4C2 = 6 sits in the middle of row 4. These numbers are also the coefficients of the binomial theorem: (a + b)^n = sum of nCr a^(n-r) b^r. For example (a + b)^3 = a^3 + 3a^2 b + 3a b^2 + b^3. Adding a full row gives 2^n, which is the total number of subsets of an n-element set.

Worked problem 1, a committee with conditions: From 6 men and 4 women, form a committee of 5 with at least 2 women. Break it into separate cases and add: exactly 2 women: 4C2 x 6C3 = 6 x 20 = 120. Exactly 3 women: 4C3 x 6C2 = 4 x 15 = 60. Exactly 4 women: 4C4 x 6C1 = 1 x 6 = 6. Total = 186. Check with the complement: all committees are 10C5 = 252; those with 0 women: 6C5 = 6; with 1 woman: 4C1 x 6C4 = 4 x 15 = 60. So 252 - 66 = 186. Same answer, so we trust it.

Worked problem 2, things that must stay together: In how many ways can 5 books be arranged on a shelf if 2 particular books must be next to each other? Tie the two books into one bundle. Now you arrange 4 units: 4! = 24 ways. Inside the bundle, the two books can swap: 2! = 2. Total = 48. If the two must NOT be together, subtract from all arrangements: 5! - 48 = 120 - 48 = 72.

Worked problem 3, cards and probability: A standard deck has 52 cards. How many 5-card hands are there? 52C5 = 2,598,960. How many of them have all 4 aces? Choose the 4 aces (1 way) and any 1 of the other 48 cards: 48 ways. So the probability of getting all four aces in a 5-card hand is 48 / 2,598,960, about 1 in 54,145. This is exactly how counting turns into probability.

Distributing identical things, stars and bars: How many ways can you give 5 identical chocolates to 3 children (some may get none)? Write the 5 chocolates as stars and use 2 bars to split them into 3 groups, like **|*|** meaning 2, 1, 2. You are arranging 5 stars and 2 bars in a row: 7C2 = 21 ways. In general, putting n identical items into k boxes gives (n + k - 1)C(k - 1). If every child must get at least one, first give each one chocolate, then distribute the remaining 2: (2 + 2)C2 = 6.

Real-life example 1, mobile number and PIN security: A bKash PIN has 5 digits, so there are 10^5 = 100,000 possible PINs. If a thief guesses randomly and the account locks after 3 wrong tries, the chance of breaking in is at most 3 / 100,000 = 0.003%. Now think about why the app blocks PINs like 12345: many people pick them, so real PINs are not equally likely and the simple formula overestimates safety. Counting tells you the best case; human habits make it worse. This is exactly the thinking security engineers do.

Real-life example 2, BPL cricket squad: A franchise has 16 players and must pick an 11-player team. Ignoring roles, there are 16C11 = 16C5 = 4,368 possible teams. Now add rules: exactly 4 foreign players out of 6 foreigners, and 7 locals from the 10 locals. That gives 6C4 x 10C7 = 15 x 120 = 1,800 teams. If the batting order of the 11 chosen players also matters, multiply by 11! which is 39,916,800. The numbers explode, which is why team analysts use computers and statistics instead of trying every option.

In computer science: Counting tells you the size of a search space. A string of n bits has 2^n values, so a 128-bit key has 2^128 possibilities, too many to try one by one. The number of subsets of n items is 2^n, which is why some brute-force algorithms take exponential time. The number of orderings is n!, which is even worse. Counting arguments also prove the pigeonhole principle: if 13 people are in a room, at least two share a birth month, because there are only 12 months.

Common mistakes: Using permutation when order does not matter (or the reverse). Ask yourself: if I swap two chosen items, do I get something new? If yes, permutation; if no, combination. Forgetting to divide by repeated letters in word arrangements. Adding when you should multiply: multiply for steps done one after another, add for separate cases. Double counting in "at least" problems; split into exact cases or use the complement. Forgetting that 0! = 1.

What exams ask: arrangements of letters of a word (with repeats, with vowels together, with vowels never together); committee selection with conditions; circular arrangements; proving nCr = nC(n-r) or Pascal's rule; number of diagonals of a polygon (nC2 - n, so a hexagon has 15 - 6 = 9); and simple probability problems that need counting, like drawing balls or cards.

Recap: Multiply for steps in sequence, add for separate cases. n! counts the arrangements of n different things, and 0! = 1. Permutations nPr = n!/(n-r)! count ordered selections; combinations nCr = n!/(r!(n-r)!) count unordered ones. Repetition allowed gives n^r, identical items give n!/(n1! n2! ...), and round tables give (n-1)!. Pascal's triangle stores the combination numbers and the binomial coefficients. With counting in your pocket, you are ready for probability itself in the next lesson.
key_points: Multiplication rule: steps in sequence multiply; addition rule: separate non-overlapping cases add.
n! = n x (n-1) x ... x 1 counts arrangements of n distinct items; 0! = 1.
Permutations nPr = n!/(n-r)! when order matters; with repetition allowed the count is n^r.
Identical items: n!/(n1! n2! ... nk!); circular arrangements: (n-1)!.
Combinations nCr = n!/(r!(n-r)!) = nPr/r! when order does not matter; nCr = nC(n-r).
Pascal's rule nCr = (n-1)C(r-1) + (n-1)Cr builds Pascal's triangle, which gives binomial coefficients.
For 'at least' problems, split into exact cases or subtract the complement from the total.
lessons.tip: Before using any formula, ask one question: if I swap two chosen items, do I get something new? That single question decides permutation or combination.
lessons.task: Take the letters of your own name. Count how many distinct arrangements they have using n!/(repeats!), then list a few by hand to see the idea.

quiz.explain: Posts are different, so order matters: 10P3 = 10 x 9 x 8 = 720.

quiz.q: How many distinct arrangements of the letters of BANANA are there?
quiz.explain: 6! / (3! 2!) = 720 / 12 = 60, dividing for the repeated A's and N's.

quiz.q: Which value equals 10C8?
quiz.explain: nCr = nC(n-r), so 10C8 = 10C2 = 45.

quiz.explain: Circular arrangements: (n-1)! = 4! = 24.
