quiz.explain: Repetition allowed: 10^4 = 10,000.

lessons.title: Basic Probability: Experiments, Sample Spaces and Axioms
lessons.content:
Imagine your cricket team captain walks to the middle for the toss. The coin spins in the air, everyone holds their breath, and nobody knows if it will land heads or tails. But here is something funny: even though nobody knows what will happen this one time, everybody agrees that heads and tails are equally likely. That calm, confident sentence, "it is fifty-fifty", is probability. Probability is the maths of not knowing for sure, but still being smart about it. In this lesson we build the basic words and rules that the whole rest of the course stands on.

Why this matters: Weather apps say "70% chance of rain". Doctors say "this test is 95% accurate". Your phone keyboard guesses the next word you will type. A spam filter guesses if an email is junk. All of these are probability in action. In computer science, probability shows up in randomized algorithms, hashing, networking, machine learning, games and simulations. So before we can do any of that, we need to know exactly what an experiment, an outcome, a sample space and an event are. These words sound fancy, but each one is a simple idea.

Random experiment: A random experiment is any action that can be repeated, where we know all the possible results in advance, but we cannot say which result will come this time. Tossing a coin, rolling a die, drawing a card, checking whether tomorrow's bus is late, or picking a random student from a class are all random experiments. The key words are "possible results known" and "actual result not known". If you already know the answer (like 2 + 2), it is not random.

Outcome and sample space: Each single possible result of an experiment is called an outcome. The set of all outcomes is called the sample space, usually written S (some books use the Greek letter omega). For one coin toss, S = {H, T}. For one die roll, S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. For two coin tosses, S = {HH, HT, TH, TT}, which has 4 outcomes. For two dice, S has 6 x 6 = 36 ordered pairs like (1,1), (1,2), up to (6,6). Notice we used the multiplication rule from the counting lesson to find the size of S.

Discrete and continuous sample spaces: Some sample spaces are finite, like the 36 dice pairs. Some are countably infinite, like "toss a coin until the first head", where S = {H, TH, TTH, TTTH, ...} goes on forever but you can still list it one by one. Others are continuous, like "the exact time you wait for a bus in minutes", where S could be every real number from 0 to 30. Finite and countable ones are called discrete. We handle discrete ones by counting and adding; continuous ones need areas and integrals, which come later in the course.

Event: An event is any subset of the sample space, in plain words, a group of outcomes that we care about. When we roll a die, the event "get an even number" is A = {2, 4, 6}. The event "get more than 4" is B = {5, 6}. An event "happens" if the actual outcome is inside it. If you roll a 4, then A happened but B did not. A single outcome as an event, like {3}, is called a simple or elementary event. The whole S is the sure event (something in S always happens), and the empty set is the impossible event.

Set operations on events: Because events are sets, we can combine them using set operations, the same ones you met in discrete maths. The union A ∪ B means "A or B (or both)". The intersection A ∩ B means "A and B both". The complement A' (also written A^c) means "not A", everything in S that is not in A. The difference A − B means "in A but not in B". With the die example, A ∪ B = {2, 4, 5, 6}, A ∩ B = {6}, A' = {1, 3, 5}, and A − B = {2, 4}.

Mutually exclusive and exhaustive events: Two events are mutually exclusive (or disjoint) if they cannot happen together, that is, A ∩ B is empty. "Roll a 1" and "roll an even number" are mutually exclusive. A group of events is exhaustive if together they cover the whole sample space, so at least one of them must happen. "Even" and "odd" for a die are both mutually exclusive and exhaustive. Such a group is called a partition of S. Partitions become very useful in the lesson on Bayes' theorem.

Venn diagrams: A Venn diagram draws S as a rectangle and each event as a circle inside it. The overlap of two circles is A ∩ B, both circles together is A ∪ B, and the part of the rectangle outside a circle is the complement. Drawing a quick Venn diagram is the best habit for event questions. For example, in a class of 40, 25 like cricket, 18 like football and 10 like both. The circles show 15 only cricket, 8 only football, 10 both, and 40 − 33 = 7 like neither.

Three ways to define probability: Over history, people defined probability in three ways. The classical definition counts equally likely outcomes. The relative frequency definition repeats the experiment many times and watches what fraction of the time the event happens. The axiomatic definition, given by the Russian mathematician Andrey Kolmogorov in 1933, does not say how to find the number at all; it just lists rules that any probability must follow. Modern probability theory is built on Kolmogorov's rules, and the other two are ways to assign numbers that obey them.

Classical definition: If the sample space has n outcomes that are all equally likely, and an event A contains m of them, then P(A) = m / n. Rolling a fair die, P(even) = 3/6 = 1/2. Drawing one card from a standard 52-card deck, P(ace) = 4/52 = 1/13, and P(heart) = 13/52 = 1/4. With two dice, P(sum = 7) = 6/36 = 1/6, because the pairs (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1) give 7. The big catch is "equally likely". If a die is loaded, the classical formula is simply wrong.

A classic trap: With two dice, people sometimes say the possible sums are 2 to 12, that is 11 values, so P(sum = 7) = 1/11. This is wrong, because the 11 sums are not equally likely. A sum of 2 happens only with (1,1), while a sum of 7 happens in 6 ways. Always go back to outcomes that truly are equally likely (the 36 ordered pairs here) before dividing. Another trap: treating (1,2) and (2,1) as the same outcome. With two separate dice, they are different outcomes.

Relative frequency definition: Suppose you cannot assume equal chances, like the chance that a Dhaka bus arrives late, or that a cricketer scores a fifty. Then you repeat or observe the experiment n times and count how many times A happened, say m times. The relative frequency is m / n, and the probability is the value this ratio settles near as n becomes very large. If you watched 200 mornings and the bus was late on 130 of them, your estimate is P(late) ≈ 130/200 = 0.65. With only 10 mornings, the estimate would be much shakier.

Coin experiment with numbers: Toss a fair coin 10 times and you might get 7 heads, a ratio of 0.7. Toss it 100 times and you might get 54, a ratio of 0.54. Toss it 10,000 times and you will very likely be within about 0.01 of 0.5. The ratio wobbles a lot at first and then calms down. This calming down is the law of large numbers, which we study properly in lesson 17. The relative frequency idea is great in practice, but as a definition it is a bit fuzzy, because "very large n" is not exact.

Axiomatic definition, the Kolmogorov axioms: A probability is a function P that gives each event A a number P(A) such that: Axiom 1, P(A) ≥ 0 for every event A. Axiom 2, P(S) = 1. Axiom 3, if A1, A2, A3, ... are mutually exclusive events (no two overlap), then P(A1 ∪ A2 ∪ ...) = P(A1) + P(A2) + .... That is it. Only three rules. Every other rule in probability is proved from these three. Both the classical and relative frequency numbers satisfy these axioms, which is why they are valid ways to get probabilities.

Quick results from the axioms: From the three axioms we can prove some useful facts. The impossible event has probability zero: P(∅) = 0. Probabilities never go above one: 0 ≤ P(A) ≤ 1. The complement rule: P(A') = 1 − P(A), because A and A' are disjoint and together make S. And if A is inside B (A ⊆ B), then P(A) ≤ P(B). For example, "roll a 6" is inside "roll an even number", so its probability 1/6 is less than 1/2. The next lesson builds the full addition and multiplication rules on top of these.

Assigning probabilities on a finite space: For a finite sample space you just give each outcome a number p_i ≥ 0 so that all of them add to 1. Then P(A) is the sum of the p_i of the outcomes in A. The outcomes do not need equal chances. Suppose a loaded die has P(6) = 0.25 and each of 1 to 5 has 0.15. Check: 5 x 0.15 + 0.25 = 1. Then P(even) = P(2) + P(4) + P(6) = 0.15 + 0.15 + 0.25 = 0.55, not 0.5. This is how simulations and games model unfair dice and weighted choices.

Odds versus probability: People in sport often talk in odds. The odds in favour of A are P(A) : P(A'), and the odds against are the reverse. If P(A) = 1/4, the odds in favour are 1/4 : 3/4, which is 1 : 3, and the odds against are 3 : 1. Going back: odds in favour a : b means P(A) = a / (a + b). Do not mix up odds with probability; "odds of 1 to 3" is a probability of 1/4, not 1/3.

Real-life example 1, a Ludo game: In Ludo, many players need a 6 to bring a piece out. With a fair die, P(6) = 1/6 on one throw. What about the chance of not getting a 6 on one throw? By the complement rule, it is 5/6. If your cousin claims his die is lucky and gives a 6 "every other time", you can test it with relative frequency: roll it 120 times and count. A fair die should give around 20 sixes. If you see 60, the die is very likely loaded, and the classical 1/6 is no longer right for it.

Real-life example 2, a load-shedding guess: Suppose your area had power cuts on 18 of the last 30 evenings. Your relative frequency estimate is P(cut this evening) ≈ 18/30 = 0.6, so P(no cut) ≈ 0.4. This is not classical probability, since there is no list of equally likely outcomes, but it still obeys the axioms: both numbers are between 0 and 1 and they add to 1. A software team in Dhaka doing server monitoring uses exactly this kind of estimate, like "on 3% of days we had an outage", to plan backup power and alerts.

In computer science: When a program calls random() to get a number between 0 and 1, it relies on probability ideas. Shuffling a playlist, picking a random pivot in quicksort, choosing which ad to show, or generating a random password all start from a sample space and equally likely outcomes. For a 4-digit PIN, the sample space has 10^4 = 10,000 outcomes, so a single random guess succeeds with probability 1/10,000.

Common mistakes and exam questions: First, forgetting that classical probability needs equally likely outcomes. Second, writing the sample space for two dice or two coins with unordered pairs. Third, giving answers bigger than 1 or negative, which can never be right, so always sanity check. Fourth, mixing up "mutually exclusive" (cannot happen together) with "independent" (one does not affect the other), which we separate in the next lesson. Exams commonly ask: write the sample space for a given experiment, list events using union and intersection, find classical probabilities with cards and dice, state Kolmogorov's axioms, and prove P(A') = 1 − P(A) or P(∅) = 0 from them.

Recap: A random experiment has known possible outcomes but an unknown actual result. The sample space S is the set of all outcomes, and an event is any subset of S. Events combine with union, intersection and complement, and Venn diagrams help. Probability can be assigned classically (m/n for equally likely outcomes), by relative frequency (long-run fraction), and must always obey Kolmogorov's three axioms: non-negative, P(S) = 1, and adding over disjoint events. In the next lesson we turn these into working rules: addition, multiplication, independence and the famous birthday problem.
key_points: A random experiment has known possible outcomes but an unpredictable actual result.
The sample space S is the set of all outcomes; an event is any subset of S.
Events combine with union (or), intersection (and), complement (not); Venn diagrams make this visual.
Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together; an exhaustive set covers all of S; both together form a partition.
Classical probability P(A) = m/n works only when all n outcomes are equally likely.
Relative frequency estimates P(A) as the long-run fraction m/n of trials where A happens.
Kolmogorov axioms: P(A) ≥ 0, P(S) = 1, and probabilities of disjoint events add; every other rule follows from them.
Consequences: P(∅) = 0, 0 ≤ P(A) ≤ 1, P(A') = 1 − P(A).
lessons.tip: Before computing any probability, write the sample space out (or at least its size) and ask: are these outcomes really equally likely? Half of all wrong answers die at that one question.
lessons.task: Toss a coin 50 times (or flip a 1-taka coin while watching TV) and record the running fraction of heads after 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 tosses. Plot it on paper and watch it settle toward 0.5.

quiz.explain: Each die has 6 outcomes, so ordered pairs give 6 x 6 = 36.

quiz.q: Rolling a fair die, A = {2,4,6} and B = {5,6}. What is A ∩ B?
quiz.explain: The intersection keeps outcomes in both events; only 6 is even and greater than 4.

quiz.explain: m/n is the classical formula, valid only for equally likely outcomes; it is not an axiom.

quiz.explain: On time on 15 of 60 days, so 15/60 = 0.25.

quiz.explain: Odds a : b in favour give P = a/(a+b) = 2/5.

lessons.title: Probability Rules: Addition, Multiplication, Independence
lessons.content:
Imagine your class has 23 students. What do you think is the chance that two of them share the same birthday? Most people guess something tiny, like 5 or 6 percent, because there are 365 days in a year. The real answer is a little over 50 percent. Your gut feeling is badly wrong here, and the only way to fix a wrong gut feeling is with clean rules. In the last lesson we met sample spaces, events and Kolmogorov's axioms. In this lesson we turn them into the everyday working rules of probability, and at the end we solve the birthday problem properly.

The toolbox in one line: There are really only a few rules you will use again and again. The complement rule for "not". The addition rule for "or". The multiplication rule for "and". And the idea of independence, which tells you when the multiplication rule becomes simple. Almost every probability problem in this course, from cards to computer networks, is a mix of these few tools. The skill is knowing which tool to pick, and that is what we practise here.

Complement rule: P(A') = 1 − P(A). Since A and "not A" are disjoint and together make the whole sample space, their probabilities must add to 1. This rule looks too simple to matter, but it is the hero of "at least one" problems. "At least one six in four rolls" has many messy cases: exactly one six, exactly two, three, four. The complement, "no six at all in four rolls", is a single clean case. So we find that and subtract from 1. Remember: when you see "at least one", think complement first.

Worked example with the complement: Roll a fair die 4 times. The chance of no six on one roll is 5/6. If the rolls do not affect each other, the chance of no six in all four is (5/6)^4 = 625/1296 ≈ 0.482. So P(at least one six) = 1 − 0.482 ≈ 0.518. A French gambler, the Chevalier de Méré, bet on this in the 1600s and made money, because the chance is a bit above one half. His questions to Pascal and Fermat helped start probability theory as a subject.

Addition rule for mutually exclusive events: If A and B cannot happen together, then P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B). This is just Kolmogorov's third axiom. Draw one card from a deck: P(ace or king) = 4/52 + 4/52 = 8/52 = 2/13, because no card is both an ace and a king. It works for more events too: on a die, P(1 or 2 or 3) = 1/6 + 1/6 + 1/6 = 1/2, since the three outcomes are disjoint.

General addition rule: When A and B can overlap, adding P(A) and P(B) counts the overlap twice, so we subtract it once: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B). Example: draw one card, find P(king or heart). P(king) = 4/52, P(heart) = 13/52, and the king of hearts is in both, P(king and heart) = 1/52. So the answer is 4/52 + 13/52 − 1/52 = 16/52 = 4/13. If you forget to subtract, you get 17/52, which is wrong because the king of hearts was counted twice.

Three events, inclusion-exclusion: For three events the pattern is: add the singles, subtract the pairs, add back the triple. P(A ∪ B ∪ C) = P(A) + P(B) + P(C) − P(A∩B) − P(A∩C) − P(B∩C) + P(A∩B∩C). Example: in a class of 100, 50 use Facebook, 40 use YouTube, 30 use TikTok, 20 use both Facebook and YouTube, 15 Facebook and TikTok, 10 YouTube and TikTok, and 5 use all three. The number using at least one is 50 + 40 + 30 − 20 − 15 − 10 + 5 = 80, so the probability a random student uses at least one is 0.8.

Independent events: Two events are independent if knowing that one happened does not change the chance of the other. Formally, A and B are independent if P(A ∩ B) = P(A) x P(B). Tossing a coin and rolling a die are independent; the coin does not care what the die did. So P(head and six) = 1/2 x 1/6 = 1/12. You can check by counting: the joint sample space has 2 x 6 = 12 equally likely pairs, and only (H, 6) works.

Multiplication rule for independent events: For independent events A1, A2, ..., An, P(all happen) = P(A1) x P(A2) x ... x P(An). Example: a quiz has 3 true/false questions and you guess all of them randomly. P(all correct) = (1/2)^3 = 1/8. A machine part works with probability 0.9, and three parts work independently. P(all three work) = 0.9^3 = 0.729. Notice how "and" makes probabilities smaller: each extra requirement multiplies by a number below 1.

Dependent events and the general multiplication rule: When events do affect each other, we use P(A ∩ B) = P(A) x P(B | A), where P(B | A) means "the probability of B given that A already happened". We study this conditional probability fully in the next lesson, but here is a taste. Draw two cards without putting the first back. P(both aces) = 4/52 x 3/51 = 12/2652 = 1/221. The second fraction is 3/51 because one ace and one card are already gone. With replacement, the draws would be independent and the answer would be (4/52)^2 = 1/169.

Mutually exclusive is not independent: This is the most famous confusion in the whole topic. Mutually exclusive means A and B cannot both happen, so P(A ∩ B) = 0. Independent means P(A ∩ B) = P(A) x P(B). If both P(A) and P(B) are bigger than zero, then P(A) x P(B) is bigger than zero, so disjoint events with positive chances are always dependent. Think about it: if I tell you "you rolled a 1", you instantly know "you did not roll a 6". Knowing one changed the other completely. That is the opposite of independence.

Checking independence with numbers: Roll one die. Let A = even = {2, 4, 6} and B = {1, 2}. P(A) = 1/2, P(B) = 1/3, A ∩ B = {2}, so P(A ∩ B) = 1/6. And P(A) x P(B) = 1/2 x 1/3 = 1/6. They match, so A and B are independent, even though they come from the same die. Now let C = {1, 2, 3}. A ∩ C = {2}, P = 1/6, but P(A) x P(C) = 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4. Not equal, so A and C are dependent. Independence is about the numbers, not about whether the events "look connected".

Pairwise versus mutual independence: For three or more events, independence needs more care. A, B, C are mutually independent if every pair multiplies and also P(A ∩ B ∩ C) = P(A) P(B) P(C). It is possible to have every pair independent but the triple not. Classic example: toss two fair coins. A = first is head, B = second is head, C = both coins show the same face. Each has probability 1/2, each pair has probability 1/4, so all pairs are independent. But if A and B both happen, C must happen, so P(A ∩ B ∩ C) = 1/4, not 1/8. So they are pairwise but not mutually independent.

Reliability: series and parallel systems: Engineers use these rules all the time. In a series system, everything must work, like bulbs on an old fairy-light string. If three parts each work with probability 0.9 independently, the system works with 0.9^3 = 0.729. In a parallel system, the system works if at least one part works, like having two internet connections at an office. Using the complement: P(all fail) = 0.1 x 0.1 = 0.01, so P(system works) = 0.99. Parallel backup makes systems far more reliable, which is why data centres keep spare power and spare servers.

The birthday problem set up: Now the big one. Assume 365 equally likely birthdays (ignore 29 February and twins), and birthdays are independent. With n people, find P(at least two share a birthday). "At least" means complement. The complement is "everyone has a different birthday". The first person can have any day: 365/365. The second must avoid that day: 364/365. The third must avoid two days: 363/365. And so on, until the n-th person: (365 − n + 1)/365.

The birthday problem solved: So P(all different) = (365/365) x (364/365) x (363/365) x ... x ((365 − n + 1)/365), and P(shared) = 1 − that product. Doing it on a computer gives: for 10 people, about 0.117; for 20 people, about 0.411; for 23 people, about 0.507; for 30 people, about 0.706; for 50 people, about 0.970; and for 70 people, about 0.999. So in a classroom of 50, a shared birthday is almost certain. Why so high? Because we are not asking about your birthday; we are comparing every pair. With 23 people there are 23C2 = 253 pairs, and that is a lot of chances for a match.

Your birthday is a different question: If you ask "what is the chance that someone among 22 other people shares MY birthday?", the answer is much smaller: 1 − (364/365)^22 ≈ 0.059, about 6 percent. This is where our gut gets confused. We imagine the question about ourselves, but the birthday problem is about any pair at all. Many exam questions test exactly this difference, so read the wording slowly.

Birthday problem in computer science: The same maths explains hash collisions. If a hash function spreads keys evenly over N buckets, you expect the first collision after only about the square root of N keys, not N keys. For a hash with 2^64 outputs, collisions become likely around 2^32 items, roughly 4 billion. Attackers use this in the "birthday attack" on weak hash functions, which is why secure systems use long hashes like SHA-256. So this "party trick" is actually serious security knowledge.

Real-life example 1, a mobile network tower: Suppose a Grameenphone tower in a village has two independent power sources: the grid, which is available 80 percent of the time, and a generator, which starts successfully 90 percent of the time when needed. The tower goes down only if both fail. P(grid fails) = 0.2, P(generator fails) = 0.1, so P(both fail) = 0.2 x 0.1 = 0.02 and P(tower up) = 0.98. Without the generator it would be only 0.80. This is the parallel-system rule saving the day.

Real-life example 2, an MCQ admission test: A student guesses on 10 MCQ questions, each with 4 options, so P(correct) = 1/4 on each, independently. P(at least one correct) = 1 − (3/4)^10 ≈ 1 − 0.056 = 0.944. P(all correct) = (1/4)^10, which is about 1 in a million. This is why admission tests in Bangladesh often have negative marking: pure guessing almost surely gets some questions right, so negative marking removes the reward for blind guessing. We calculate the exact expected score in the binomial lesson.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Adding probabilities for "or" without subtracting the overlap. Multiplying probabilities for "and" when the events are not independent, like drawing cards without replacement. Thinking mutually exclusive means independent. Working out "at least one" by listing every case instead of using the complement. And in the birthday problem, confusing "anyone shares" with "someone shares mine". Typical exam questions: find P(A ∪ B) from a table or Venn diagram, test if two events are independent, compute reliability of series and parallel systems, and solve the birthday problem for a given n.

Recap: Complement: P(A') = 1 − P(A), and it is the shortcut for "at least one". Addition: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B), with no subtraction needed for disjoint events, and inclusion-exclusion for three events. Multiplication: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) P(B | A) in general, and simply P(A) P(B) when A and B are independent. Disjoint events with positive chances are never independent. Series systems multiply success chances, parallel systems multiply failure chances. In the birthday problem 23 people already give a better than even chance of a shared birthday. Next lesson: conditional probability, tree diagrams and Bayes' theorem.
key_points: Complement rule P(A') = 1 − P(A) is the shortcut for any 'at least one' question.
General addition rule: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B); for disjoint events the overlap term is zero.
Inclusion-exclusion for three events: add singles, subtract pairs, add back the triple.
A and B are independent when P(A ∩ B) = P(A) P(B); then 'and' is a simple product.
General multiplication rule: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) P(B | A), needed for draws without replacement.
Disjoint events with positive probabilities are always dependent; pairwise independence does not imply mutual independence.
Series systems: multiply success probabilities; parallel systems: 1 − product of failure probabilities.
Birthday problem: P(shared) = 1 − 365·364·...·(365−n+1)/365^n, about 0.507 at n = 23; same maths drives hash collisions.
lessons.tip: Translate every word before you calculate: 'or' means add and subtract the overlap, 'and' means multiply (check independence first), 'not' and 'at least one' mean use the complement.
lessons.task: Ask 25 friends, classmates or Facebook contacts their birthday (day and month only) and check whether any two match. Then compute 1 − 365·364·...·341/365^25 on a calculator or phone (about 0.57) and compare.

quiz.q: One card is drawn from a 52-card deck. P(king or heart) is:
quiz.explain: 4/52 + 13/52 − 1/52 = 16/52 = 4/13; the king of hearts must not be counted twice.

quiz.q: Two events with P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.4 are mutually exclusive. Which is true?
quiz.explain: Disjoint means P(A ∩ B) = 0, but P(A)P(B) = 0.12 ≠ 0, so they are dependent; P(A ∪ B) = 0.7.

quiz.q: Three independent servers each fail with probability 0.1. A parallel system of them fails only if all fail. P(system works) is:
Two cards are drawn without replacement. P(both aces) is:
quiz.explain: 4/52 x 3/51 = 12/2652 = 1/221; 1/169 would be with replacement.

quiz.q: About how many people are needed for the chance of a shared birthday to pass 50%?
quiz.explain: At n = 23 the probability is about 0.507; at 57 it is already about 0.99.

lessons.title: Conditional Probability and Bayes' Theorem
lessons.content:
Imagine your friend rolls a die behind a book and asks you to guess the chance it is a 6. You say 1/6. Then she gives you a hint: "It is an even number." Suddenly the possible outcomes shrink to {2, 4, 6}, and the chance of a 6 jumps to 1/3. Nothing about the die changed. What changed is your information. Conditional probability is the maths of updating chances when you learn something new. Bayes' theorem is the famous formula that turns this updating into a machine, and it powers medical tests, spam filters, and a large part of machine learning.

Why it matters: Real life is full of partial information. A doctor sees a positive test, not the disease itself. A spam filter sees words, not the sender's intent. A cricket analyst knows the pitch is dry before guessing whether spin will win. In all these cases we want P(something we cannot see | something we can see). Getting this wrong leads to scary mistakes, like panicking over a positive test for a rare disease. Getting it right is one of the most useful thinking skills you can learn.

Definition of conditional probability: For events A and B with P(B) > 0, the probability of A given B is P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B). Read the bar "|" as "given". The idea: once we know B happened, B becomes our new sample space. Inside it, only the part where A also happens counts. So we take the probability of the overlap and divide by the probability of B, which rescales B to total 1. In the die example, P(6 | even) = P({6}) / P({2,4,6}) = (1/6) / (1/2) = 1/3.

Counting version: When all outcomes are equally likely, conditional probability is just counting inside the smaller world. P(A | B) = (number of outcomes in A ∩ B) / (number of outcomes in B). Roll two dice and suppose you know the sum is 8. The pairs with sum 8 are (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3), (6,2), so 5 outcomes. How many of them have a double? Only (4,4). So P(double | sum = 8) = 1/5. Without the information, P(double) = 6/36 = 1/6.

Order matters: P(A | B) and P(B | A) are usually different numbers. P(cricket fan | Bangladeshi) is high. P(Bangladeshi | cricket fan) is much lower, because there are cricket fans in India, Pakistan, England, Australia and many other countries. Mixing these two up is called the confusion of the inverse, or in courts, the prosecutor's fallacy. Bayes' theorem is exactly the tool for going from one direction to the other correctly.

Multiplication rule from the definition: Rearranging the definition gives P(A ∩ B) = P(B) x P(A | B) = P(A) x P(B | A). For a chain: P(A ∩ B ∩ C) = P(A) x P(B | A) x P(C | A ∩ B). Example: a bag has 5 red and 3 blue marbles; draw three without replacement. P(all red) = 5/8 x 4/7 x 3/6 = 60/336 = 5/28. Each fraction is a conditional probability given what happened before.

Independence in conditional language: Now we can say independence more naturally. A and B are independent when P(A | B) = P(A), that is, learning B does not change the chance of A. This matches last lesson's definition P(A ∩ B) = P(A) P(B): just divide both sides by P(B). In the die example, P(6 | even) = 1/3 but P(6) = 1/6, so "6" and "even" are dependent, as you would expect.

Tree diagrams: A tree diagram is the friendliest way to handle problems with stages. Draw the first stage as branches with their probabilities. From each branch, draw the second stage with conditional probabilities. To get the probability of a full path, multiply along the branches. To get the probability of an event that can happen in several paths, add the matching path probabilities. The probabilities on branches leaving one point must add to 1, which is a great self-check.

Tree example: A factory has three machines. Machine A makes 50 percent of the bulbs, B makes 30 percent, and C makes 20 percent. Their defect rates are 2 percent, 3 percent and 5 percent. First stage branches: A 0.5, B 0.3, C 0.2. Second stage from each: defective or fine. Path A-defective = 0.5 x 0.02 = 0.010. Path B-defective = 0.3 x 0.03 = 0.009. Path C-defective = 0.2 x 0.05 = 0.010. So P(defective) = 0.010 + 0.009 + 0.010 = 0.029, about 2.9 percent of all bulbs.

Law of total probability: What we just did has a name. If B1, B2, ..., Bn form a partition of the sample space (disjoint, and together they cover everything), then for any event A, P(A) = P(A | B1) P(B1) + P(A | B2) P(B2) + ... + P(A | Bn) P(Bn). In words: split the world into cases, find the chance of A in each case, weight by how likely the case is, and add. This is the bottom row of the tree diagram written as a formula.

Bayes' theorem: Now flip the question. A bulb is found defective. What is the chance it came from machine C? We want P(C | D), but we know P(D | C). Bayes' theorem says P(Bi | A) = P(A | Bi) P(Bi) / P(A), where P(A) comes from the law of total probability. So P(C | D) = 0.010 / 0.029 ≈ 0.345. Similarly P(A | D) ≈ 0.345 and P(B | D) = 0.009 / 0.029 ≈ 0.310. Even though C makes only 20 percent of bulbs, it causes about a third of the defects, because it is the sloppiest machine.

Prior, likelihood and posterior: Bayes' theorem has its own vocabulary. P(Bi) is the prior, what you believed before the evidence. P(A | Bi) is the likelihood, how well each case explains the evidence. P(Bi | A) is the posterior, your updated belief after the evidence. The denominator P(A) is the total chance of the evidence, which makes the posteriors add up to 1. A short way to remember it: posterior is proportional to likelihood times prior.

Medical test example, set up: Suppose 1 percent of people in a city have a disease. A test catches 95 percent of real cases (this is called sensitivity), and wrongly says positive for 5 percent of healthy people (the false positive rate). You test positive. How worried should you be? Most people guess 95 percent. Let D be "has disease" and + be "test positive". Prior P(D) = 0.01, P(+ | D) = 0.95, P(+ | not D) = 0.05.

Medical test example, solved: Total probability: P(+) = 0.95 x 0.01 + 0.05 x 0.99 = 0.0095 + 0.0495 = 0.059. Bayes: P(D | +) = 0.0095 / 0.059 ≈ 0.161. Only about 16 percent! Picture 10,000 people: 100 are sick and about 95 of them test positive; 9,900 are healthy and about 495 of them also test positive. Out of about 590 positives, only 95 are truly sick. The disease is so rare that false alarms outnumber real cases. This is called the base rate effect, and ignoring it is called the base rate fallacy.

A second test: Doctors usually confirm with a second test. If the second test is independent given the true condition, your posterior from the first test becomes the new prior. Prior 0.161, then another positive: numerator 0.161 x 0.95 ≈ 0.153; denominator 0.153 + 0.839 x 0.05 ≈ 0.153 + 0.042 = 0.195. So P(D | two positives) ≈ 0.785. Evidence piles up, and Bayes lets you update step by step. This step-by-step updating is exactly how many learning algorithms work.

Spam filter example: Suppose 40 percent of emails are spam. The word "free" appears in 30 percent of spam emails and in 2 percent of normal emails. An email contains "free". P(free) = 0.30 x 0.40 + 0.02 x 0.60 = 0.12 + 0.012 = 0.132. P(spam | free) = 0.12 / 0.132 ≈ 0.909. One word pushes the chance from 40 percent to about 91 percent. A real spam filter combines many words this way; lesson 25 shows the Naive Bayes classifier that does exactly that.

The Monty Hall puzzle: A game show has 3 doors, one hiding a car. You pick door 1. The host, who knows where the car is, always opens a different door with a goat, say door 3, and offers you a switch to door 2. Should you switch? Yes. Your first pick wins with probability 1/3, and that does not change because the host will always open a goat door anyway. So the remaining door has probability 2/3. A tree diagram or 30 rounds played with three cups and a coin will convince you.

Real-life example 1, bKash fraud alert: Imagine 0.1 percent of transactions are fraud. A detection system flags 90 percent of fraud and wrongly flags 1 percent of honest transactions. P(flag) = 0.9 x 0.001 + 0.01 x 0.999 = 0.0009 + 0.00999 ≈ 0.0109. P(fraud | flag) ≈ 0.0009 / 0.0109 ≈ 0.083. So more than 90 percent of flags are honest customers. This is why such systems usually send a confirmation SMS or call instead of freezing the account immediately. These numbers are made up for learning, but the pattern is real for any rare event.

Real-life example 2, weather and traffic: Say 30 percent of days in Dhaka during monsoon are heavy-rain days. On rainy days, your rickshaw ride to university takes over an hour 70 percent of the time; on dry days, only 20 percent of the time. P(late) = 0.7 x 0.3 + 0.2 x 0.7 = 0.21 + 0.14 = 0.35. If you arrived late today, what is the chance it rained? P(rain | late) = 0.21 / 0.35 = 0.6. Your friend can guess the weather from your lateness, a small Bayes detective story.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Confusing P(A | B) with P(B | A). Forgetting to divide by P(B) when finding a conditional probability. Ignoring the base rate in rare-event problems. Using branch probabilities that do not add to 1. Forgetting that after drawing without replacement, the denominators change. Typical exam questions: compute P(A | B) from a table or from dice; draw a tree for a two-stage experiment; use the law of total probability for a factory or urn problem; use Bayes' theorem to find which machine or which urn is responsible; and the medical test question with sensitivity and false positive rate.

Recap: P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B) shrinks the sample space to B. P(A | B) and P(B | A) are different. The multiplication rule P(A ∩ B) = P(B) P(A | B) builds trees: multiply along paths, add across paths. The law of total probability adds up P(A | Bi) P(Bi) over a partition. Bayes' theorem flips the condition: P(Bi | A) = P(A | Bi) P(Bi) / P(A), turning a prior into a posterior. Rare events plus imperfect tests give many false alarms. Next we move from events to random variables, numbers that come out of random experiments.
key_points: P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B): knowing B shrinks the sample space to B.
P(A | B) and P(B | A) are usually different; mixing them up is the prosecutor's fallacy.
Multiplication rule: P(A ∩ B) = P(B) P(A | B); tree diagrams multiply along branches and add across paths.
A and B are independent exactly when P(A | B) = P(A).
Law of total probability: P(A) = Σ P(A | Bi) P(Bi) over a partition B1..Bn.
Bayes' theorem: P(Bi | A) = P(A | Bi) P(Bi) / P(A); posterior is proportional to likelihood x prior.
With a rare condition, even a good test gives mostly false positives (base rate effect).
lessons.tip: For any Bayes question, imagine 10,000 people (or emails, or bulbs) and fill in the counts. Natural counts are much harder to get wrong than formulas full of bars.
lessons.task: Play Monty Hall 30 times with three cups and a coin under one, with a friend acting as host. Always switch for 15 rounds and always stay for 15. Count your wins in each group and compare with 2/3 and 1/3.

quiz.q: A fair die shows an even number. P(it is 6 | even) is:
quiz.explain: (1/6) / (1/2) = 1/3; the sample space shrinks to {2, 4, 6}.

quiz.q: Machines A and B make 60% and 40% of items, with defect rates 1% and 4%. P(defective) is:
In the same factory, an item is defective. P(it came from B) is about:
1% have a disease; a test has 95% sensitivity and 5% false positives. P(disease | positive) is about:
quiz.explain: 0.0095 / (0.0095 + 0.0495) ≈ 0.161; false positives outnumber true ones.

quiz.q: In Monty Hall, the probability of winning if you switch is:
quiz.explain: Your first pick stays at 1/3, so the other unopened door carries 2/3.

lessons.title: Random Variables: PMF, PDF and CDF
lessons.content:
Imagine you are playing Ludo and you only care about one thing: how many steps your piece moves. You do not care if the die rolled on the left side of the board or landed upside down first. You just want the number. A random variable is exactly that: a rule that turns each outcome of a random experiment into a number. Once outcomes become numbers, we can add them, average them, draw graphs of them, and use all the power of algebra and calculus. This lesson is the bridge from "events" to "numbers", and the rest of the course walks on this bridge.

Why it matters: Computers love numbers. The response time of a server, the number of packets lost on a network, the marks a student gets, the number of customers at a bKash agent in an hour, the life of a phone battery in hours: all of these are random variables. Machine learning models, simulations and performance analysis all describe their data with random variables and their distributions. If you understand PMF, PDF and CDF well, the coming lessons on binomial, Poisson and normal distributions become much easier.

Definition: A random variable X is a function from the sample space S to the real numbers. It gives each outcome a number. The name is a bit silly, since X is not "variable" in the algebra sense and it is a function, but the name has stuck. We use capital letters like X, Y for the random variable, and small letters like x, y for particular values it can take. So "X = 2" is an event: the set of all outcomes whose number is 2.

A first example: Toss a coin three times. S has 8 outcomes: HHH, HHT, HTH, THH, HTT, THT, TTH, TTT. Let X = number of heads. Then X(HHH) = 3, X(HHT) = 2, X(HTT) = 1, X(TTT) = 0, and so on. The event "X = 2" is {HHT, HTH, THH}, so P(X = 2) = 3/8. Different random variables can live on the same sample space: Y = number of tails, or Z = 1 if the first toss is heads and 0 otherwise.

Discrete versus continuous: A random variable is discrete if it takes a finite or countable list of values, like 0, 1, 2, 3, or 0, 1, 2, ... forever. Counts are discrete: number of heads, goals, defective chips, emails per hour. A random variable is continuous if it can take any value in an interval, like waiting time, height, temperature or battery life. The two types are handled with slightly different tools: sums and PMFs for discrete, integrals and PDFs for continuous. The CDF works for both.

Probability mass function (PMF): For a discrete X, the PMF is p(x) = P(X = x), the probability that X equals exactly x. For the three-coin example: p(0) = 1/8, p(1) = 3/8, p(2) = 3/8, p(3) = 1/8. A PMF has two properties. First, p(x) ≥ 0 for every x. Second, the p(x) over all possible values add up to 1. Here 1/8 + 3/8 + 3/8 + 1/8 = 1. You can draw a PMF as a bar chart with a bar of height p(x) at each value x.

PMF of the sum of two dice: Let X = sum of two fair dice. The 36 equally likely pairs give: p(2) = 1/36, p(3) = 2/36, p(4) = 3/36, p(5) = 4/36, p(6) = 5/36, p(7) = 6/36, p(8) = 5/36, p(9) = 4/36, p(10) = 3/36, p(11) = 2/36, p(12) = 1/36. The bar chart looks like a tent, highest at 7. That is why 7 is special in many dice games. Adding them gives 36/36 = 1, which is our check.

Finding an unknown constant: Exams love this. Suppose P(X = x) = kx for x = 1, 2, 3, 4. Find k. The probabilities must add to 1, so k(1 + 2 + 3 + 4) = 10k = 1, giving k = 0.1. Then P(X = 3) = 0.3 and P(X ≥ 3) = 0.3 + 0.4 = 0.7. If a question gives a "PMF" with a negative value or values that do not add to 1, it is not a valid PMF, and you should say so.

Cumulative distribution function (CDF): The CDF of any random variable is F(x) = P(X ≤ x), the probability that X is at most x. For a discrete X, you get it by adding the PMF up to x. For three coins: F(0) = 1/8, F(1) = 4/8, F(2) = 7/8, F(3) = 1. In between values, F stays flat: F(1.5) = P(X ≤ 1.5) = P(X ≤ 1) = 4/8. So a discrete CDF is a staircase that jumps at each possible value, and the height of each jump equals p(x) at that point.

Properties of every CDF: F(x) is never decreasing as x grows. F(x) goes to 0 as x goes to minus infinity, and to 1 as x goes to plus infinity. F is right-continuous, which means at a jump the value is taken from the top of the step. And the most useful property: P(a < X ≤ b) = F(b) − F(a). For three coins, P(1 < X ≤ 3) = F(3) − F(1) = 1 − 4/8 = 1/2, which matches p(2) + p(3) = 3/8 + 1/8.

A dice example with the CDF: Roll two dice and let M = the larger of the two numbers. The event M ≤ k means both dice are at most k, which happens in k x k ways. So F(k) = k^2 / 36. Then p(k) = F(k) − F(k − 1) = (k^2 − (k − 1)^2) / 36 = (2k − 1) / 36. So p(1) = 1/36, p(6) = 11/36. This trick, finding the CDF first and then the PMF, is often much easier than counting directly.

Continuous random variables and the PDF: For a continuous X, the chance of any single exact value is zero. The chance your bus comes in exactly 5.000000... minutes is zero, because there are infinitely many possible times. Instead we describe X with a probability density function f(x). Probabilities are areas under f: P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx. A valid PDF has f(x) ≥ 0 everywhere and total area 1: ∫ over all x of f(x) dx = 1.

Density is not probability: This confuses many students. f(x) itself is not a probability, so it can be bigger than 1. If X is uniform between 0 and 0.5, then f(x) = 2 on that interval, because the area 0.5 x 2 = 1. What must stay between 0 and 1 is the area over any interval. Also, because single points have zero probability, for continuous X it does not matter if you write < or ≤: P(a < X < b) = P(a ≤ X ≤ b).

Spinner example: A spinner gives a random number X evenly between 0 and 1, like a game wheel marked from 0 to 1. Its PDF is f(x) = 1 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1 and 0 elsewhere. P(0.2 ≤ X ≤ 0.5) = area of a rectangle of width 0.3 and height 1 = 0.3. The CDF is F(x) = 0 for x < 0, F(x) = x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, and F(x) = 1 for x > 1. It is a smooth ramp, not a staircase. This is the continuous uniform distribution, studied in lesson 14.

Finding the constant for a PDF: Suppose f(x) = c x^2 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 3 and 0 elsewhere. The total area must be 1: ∫ from 0 to 3 of c x^2 dx = c x 27/3 = 9c = 1, so c = 1/9. Then P(X ≤ 1) = ∫ from 0 to 1 of x^2/9 dx = (1/27). The CDF is F(x) = x^3/27 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 3. Check: F(3) = 27/27 = 1. Good.

Link between PDF and CDF: For a continuous X, F(x) = ∫ from minus infinity to x of f(t) dt, and going the other way, f(x) = F'(x), the derivative of the CDF wherever it exists. Example: if F(x) = x^2 on [0, 1], then f(x) = 2x on [0, 1]. Then P(X ≤ 0.5) = F(0.5) = 0.25, and P(0.5 < X ≤ 1) = 1 − 0.25 = 0.75. Values near 1 are more likely than values near 0, as the rising f(x) = 2x shows.

Functions of a random variable: If X is a random variable, then so is Y = g(X). If X is the number of heads in three tosses, and you win 10 taka per head minus a 15 taka entry fee, your profit is Y = 10X − 15, which takes values −15, −5, 5, 15 with probabilities 1/8, 3/8, 3/8, 1/8. For discrete X, just transform each value and carry its probability along, combining values that land on the same number. This idea leads straight to expected value in the next lesson.

Real-life example 1, a tea stall's customers: A tea stall owner near a Dhaka bus stop notes how many customers come in each 5-minute slot. From many days of notes she gets: P(0) = 0.1, P(1) = 0.3, P(2) = 0.3, P(3) = 0.2, P(4) = 0.1. This is a PMF; it adds to 1. The CDF tells her P(X ≤ 2) = 0.7, so in 30 percent of slots three or more customers arrive. If one person can serve only two customers in 5 minutes, she knows how often she needs a helper.

Real-life example 2, app loading time: A team measures how long their app takes to load and models the time T in seconds with a PDF. They care about the CDF value F(2), the chance a user waits at most 2 seconds. If F(2) = 0.9, then 10 percent of users wait longer. Product teams often talk about "90th percentile latency", which is just the x where F(x) = 0.9. So the CDF is not just exam theory; engineering dashboards are full of it.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Treating a PDF value f(x) as a probability. Forgetting that P(X = a) = 0 for continuous variables. Forgetting the CDF is flat between jumps in the discrete case. Not checking that a PMF adds to 1 or a PDF integrates to 1. Writing F(b) − F(a) for P(a ≤ X ≤ b) in the discrete case, where you must also include the jump at a. Typical exam questions: list the PMF of a given experiment, find k so that something is a valid PMF or PDF, draw a CDF, find probabilities from a CDF, and get f from F by differentiating.

Recap: A random variable turns outcomes into numbers. Discrete ones have a PMF p(x) = P(X = x), non-negative and adding to 1. Continuous ones have a PDF f(x), non-negative with total area 1, and probabilities are areas. Every random variable has a CDF F(x) = P(X ≤ x), which never decreases, goes from 0 to 1, and gives P(a < X ≤ b) = F(b) − F(a). For continuous X, f = F'. Next lesson: expected value and variance, the two numbers that summarise a random variable's centre and spread.
key_points: A random variable X is a function from the sample space to real numbers; 'X = x' is an event.
Discrete X takes countable values (counts); continuous X takes any value in an interval (times, heights).
PMF p(x) = P(X = x): every p(x) ≥ 0 and all values add to 1.
PDF f(x) ≥ 0 with total area 1; P(a ≤ X ≤ b) is the area under f; f(x) can exceed 1.
For continuous X, P(X = a) = 0, so < and ≤ give the same probabilities.
CDF F(x) = P(X ≤ x) is non-decreasing, goes from 0 to 1, and P(a < X ≤ b) = F(b) − F(a).
Discrete CDF is a staircase with jumps p(x); continuous CDF is smooth with f(x) = F'(x).
lessons.tip: Always do the 'adds to 1' check: sum the PMF or integrate the PDF before answering anything else. It catches wrong constants and typos in seconds.

lessons.title: Expectation and Variance of Random Variables
lessons.content:
Imagine a game at a village fair: you pay 20 taka, roll a die, and if you get a 6 you win 100 taka. Should you play? On any single roll you might win or lose, so that does not tell you much. The useful question is: if you played this game hundreds of times, how much would you win or lose on average per game? That long-run average is the expected value. And how wildly your results swing around that average is measured by the variance. These two numbers are the most important summary of any random variable.

Why it matters: Expected value is how insurance companies price policies, how casinos make sure they always win in the long run, how algorithm designers state the average running time of quicksort, and how a machine learning model measures its average error. Variance tells you about risk and reliability: two investments can have the same average return but very different risk. In computer science you will meet "expected time", "expected number of collisions" and "variance of the estimate" again and again.

Expected value of a discrete random variable: For discrete X with PMF p(x), the expected value (or mean) is E[X] = Σ x p(x), the sum of each value times its probability. It is a weighted average, where likely values get more weight. For one fair die: E[X] = (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6) x 1/6 = 21/6 = 3.5. Notice that 3.5 is not a possible roll. The expected value is a long-run average, not "the value you expect to see next time". We often write μ (mu) for E[X].

Back to the fair game: Let W = your net win in the 20 taka game. If you roll a 6, W = 100 − 20 = 80, with probability 1/6. Otherwise W = −20, with probability 5/6. E[W] = 80 x 1/6 + (−20) x 5/6 = 80/6 − 100/6 = −20/6 ≈ −3.33 taka. So on average you lose about 3 taka 33 paisa per game. Over 300 games you would expect to lose about 1,000 taka. The stall owner, on the other hand, expects to earn that much, which is exactly how such games stay in business.

Expected value of a continuous random variable: For continuous X with PDF f(x), replace the sum with an integral: E[X] = ∫ x f(x) dx over all x. For the spinner uniform on [0, 1], E[X] = ∫ from 0 to 1 of x dx = 1/2, the middle, as you would guess. For f(x) = 2x on [0, 1], E[X] = ∫ from 0 to 1 of 2x^2 dx = 2/3. The mean leans toward 1 because the density is higher there. You can picture E[X] as the balance point of the PMF bars or of the PDF shape cut from cardboard.

Expected value of a function, E[g(X)]: If Y = g(X), you do not need the PMF of Y. You can use E[g(X)] = Σ g(x) p(x) in the discrete case and ∫ g(x) f(x) dx in the continuous case. This is sometimes called the law of the unconscious statistician, because people use it without thinking. For a die, E[X^2] = (1 + 4 + 9 + 16 + 25 + 36) / 6 = 91/6 ≈ 15.17. Careful: (E[X])^2 = 3.5^2 = 12.25, which is different. In general E[g(X)] is not g(E[X]).

Linearity of expectation: This is the most powerful property. For any constants a and b, E[aX + b] = a E[X] + b. And for any two random variables, E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y], whether or not they are independent. Example: the sum of two dice has expected value 3.5 + 3.5 = 7, with no need for the 11-value PMF. The expected number of heads in 100 tosses is 100 x 0.5 = 50. Linearity turns hard problems into easy ones by breaking a count into small pieces.

Indicator trick: Linearity shines with indicator variables. An indicator I_A equals 1 if event A happens and 0 if not, so E[I_A] = P(A). Example: 10 students put their bags in a pile and each picks one at random. How many expect to get their own bag? Let I_k = 1 if student k gets their own. Each has P = 1/10, so E[number] = 10 x 1/10 = 1. The events are dependent, but linearity does not care. Computer scientists use this trick to analyse hashing and randomized algorithms.

Variance: The mean tells us the centre; the variance tells us the spread. Var(X) = E[(X − μ)^2], the expected squared distance from the mean. The standard deviation is σ = √Var(X), which is in the same units as X. Squaring makes all distances positive and punishes big distances more. A random variable that is always 5 has variance 0. One that is 0 or 10 with equal chances has mean 5 and variance 25, so σ = 5.

The shortcut formula: Expanding the square gives Var(X) = E[X^2] − (E[X])^2. Read it as "mean of the square minus square of the mean". For one die: Var(X) = 91/6 − 12.25 = 35/12 ≈ 2.92, so σ ≈ 1.71. For three coins with X = number of heads: E[X] = 0 x 1/8 + 1 x 3/8 + 2 x 3/8 + 3 x 1/8 = 12/8 = 1.5. E[X^2] = 0 + 3/8 + 12/8 + 9/8 = 24/8 = 3. So Var(X) = 3 − 2.25 = 0.75. This shortcut is the formula exams expect you to use.

A continuous variance: For f(x) = 2x on [0, 1], we found E[X] = 2/3. E[X^2] = ∫ from 0 to 1 of x^2 x 2x dx = ∫ 2x^3 dx = 2/4 = 1/2. So Var(X) = 1/2 − 4/9 = 9/18 − 8/18 = 1/18 ≈ 0.056, and σ ≈ 0.236. Same recipe as the discrete case, with integrals in place of sums.

Properties of variance: Var(aX + b) = a^2 Var(X). Adding a constant b shifts everything but does not change the spread, so b disappears. Multiplying by a stretches distances by a, and squared distances by a^2. So SD(aX + b) = |a| SD(X). If X and Y are independent, Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y). Note the plus sign even for Var(X − Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y), because subtracting an independent random amount adds uncertainty. For dependent variables there is an extra covariance term, which we meet in lesson 16.

Using the properties: In the coin game where profit Y = 10X − 15 and X = heads in three tosses, E[Y] = 10 x 1.5 − 15 = 0 and Var(Y) = 100 x 0.75 = 75, so SD(Y) ≈ 8.66 taka. The game is fair on average but quite risky. For the sum S of two independent dice, Var(S) = 35/12 + 35/12 = 35/6 ≈ 5.83. No PMF of S needed.

Moment generating function, the idea: The k-th moment of X is E[X^k]. The moment generating function (MGF) packs all moments into one function: M(t) = E[e^(tX)]. Taking derivatives at t = 0 gives the moments: M'(0) = E[X], M''(0) = E[X^2]. For a Bernoulli variable that is 1 with probability p and 0 otherwise, M(t) = (1 − p) + p e^t, and M'(0) = p. Two useful facts: if two variables have the same MGF (existing near 0), they have the same distribution; and for independent X and Y, the MGF of X + Y is M_X(t) x M_Y(t). These facts make proofs about sums much easier.

Chebyshev's inequality: What if you know only the mean μ and standard deviation σ, and nothing about the shape? Chebyshev's inequality still gives a guarantee: P(|X − μ| ≥ kσ) ≤ 1/k^2 for any k > 0. With k = 2, at most 1/4 of the probability is 2 or more standard deviations away from the mean, so at least 75 percent is within 2σ. With k = 3, at least 1 − 1/9 ≈ 89 percent is within 3σ. It works for any distribution with finite variance, which is its strength; the bound is often loose, which is its weakness.

Chebyshev example: A food delivery app finds delivery times have mean 40 minutes and standard deviation 5 minutes. What can we say about deliveries outside 30 to 50 minutes? That is 2σ from the mean, so P(outside) ≤ 1/4. If we also knew the times were roughly normal, the real chance would be only about 5 percent. Chebyshev is the safe, shape-free answer; the normal distribution (lesson 15) gives a sharper one when it applies.

Real-life example 1, MCQ negative marking: In an admission test, a correct answer gives 1 mark and a wrong one costs 0.25. If you guess blindly among 4 options, E[score] = 1 x 1/4 + (−0.25) x 3/4 = 0.25 − 0.1875 = 0.0625. So blind guessing still gives a tiny positive expected mark. But if you can rule out two wrong options and guess between the remaining two: E = 1 x 1/2 − 0.25 x 1/2 = 0.375. Expected value tells you when a smart guess is worth it. Check your own exam's rules, since negative marking varies.

Real-life example 2, the tea stall again: The tea stall PMF from last lesson was P(0) = 0.1, P(1) = 0.3, P(2) = 0.3, P(3) = 0.2, P(4) = 0.1 customers per 5 minutes. E[X] = 0 + 0.3 + 0.6 + 0.6 + 0.4 = 1.9 customers. E[X^2] = 0 + 0.3 + 1.2 + 1.8 + 1.6 = 4.9, so Var(X) = 4.9 − 3.61 = 1.29 and σ ≈ 1.14. In an hour (12 slots, assumed independent), the expected number is 12 x 1.9 = 22.8 customers, with variance 12 x 1.29 = 15.48 and σ ≈ 3.9. This helps her decide how much milk and sugar to buy.

In computer science: Randomized quicksort makes about 2n ln n ≈ 1.39 n log2 n comparisons on average, a result proved with indicator variables and linearity. In hashing with n keys and m buckets, the expected number of keys in any bucket is n/m. Load testing reports mean response time and standard deviation. A model's mean squared error is literally an expected value of a squared difference. These are all the same ideas from this lesson.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Thinking E[X] must be a possible value. Writing E[X^2] = (E[X])^2. Writing Var(aX + b) = a Var(X) + b. Forgetting that Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) needs independence, while E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y] does not. Getting a negative variance, which signals an arithmetic error. Typical exam questions: find E[X] and Var(X) from a PMF table or PDF, find the expected profit of a game, use linearity for sums, compute an MGF and get the mean from it, and apply Chebyshev's inequality to bound a probability.

Recap: E[X] = Σ x p(x) or ∫ x f(x) dx is the long-run average. E[g(X)] = Σ g(x) p(x). Linearity: E[aX + b] = aE[X] + b and E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y] always. Var(X) = E[X^2] − (E[X])^2, σ = √Var. Var(aX + b) = a^2 Var(X), and Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) for independent variables. The MGF M(t) = E[e^(tX)] generates moments by differentiation. Chebyshev: P(|X − μ| ≥ kσ) ≤ 1/k^2 for any distribution. Next lesson: our first named distribution, the binomial.
key_points: E[X] = Σ x p(x) (discrete) or ∫ x f(x) dx (continuous) is the long-run weighted average.
E[g(X)] = Σ g(x) p(x); in general E[g(X)] ≠ g(E[X]).
Linearity: E[aX + b] = aE[X] + b and E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y], even for dependent variables.
Var(X) = E[(X − μ)^2] = E[X^2] − (E[X])^2; standard deviation σ = √Var(X).
Var(aX + b) = a^2 Var(X); Var(X ± Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) when X, Y are independent.
MGF M(t) = E[e^(tX)]: M'(0) = E[X], M''(0) = E[X^2]; MGF of an independent sum is the product.
Chebyshev: P(|X − μ| ≥ kσ) ≤ 1/k^2 for any distribution with finite variance.
