lessons.title: Bernoulli and Binomial Distributions
lessons.content:
Imagine you sit for an MCQ test and you did not study at all. There are 10 questions, each with 4 options, and you just guess every single one. How many will you get right? Maybe 2 or 3? Could you get all 10 right by pure luck? Could you get zero? This lesson gives you a tool that answers all of these questions with exact numbers. That tool is the binomial distribution, and it is built from a tiny brick called the Bernoulli trial. Once you understand these two, you will see them everywhere: in coin tosses, in factory quality checks, in network packets, in cricket, and in exam guessing.

Where this fits: In the last two lessons you learned what a random variable is and how to find its expected value and variance. Now we start meeting the famous named distributions. A named distribution is just a ready-made PMF or PDF that shows up so often that people gave it a name and worked out its mean and variance once and for all. Binomial is the first and most important discrete one. Poisson, geometric and hypergeometric come in the next lesson.

The Bernoulli trial: A Bernoulli trial is an experiment with exactly two outcomes. We call one of them success and the other failure. The word success does not mean good; it just means the thing we are counting. If we are counting broken bulbs, a broken bulb is a success! The chance of success is p, and the chance of failure is 1 - p, which people often write as q. Tossing a coin (head or tail), checking if a mango is rotten (yes or no), sending a packet (arrives or lost), a batsman facing one ball (out or not out): all of these are Bernoulli trials.

The Bernoulli random variable: We turn a Bernoulli trial into a number by saying X = 1 for success and X = 0 for failure. So P(X = 1) = p and P(X = 0) = 1 - p. Its expected value is E[X] = 1 x p + 0 x (1 - p) = p. For the variance, notice X squared is the same as X (because 1 x 1 = 1 and 0 x 0 = 0), so E[X^2] = p. Then Var(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2 = p - p^2 = p(1 - p). Example: a fair coin, head = 1, gives mean 0.5 and variance 0.25. Notice the variance is biggest when p = 0.5, which makes sense: a fair coin is the hardest to predict.

From one trial to many: Now repeat the Bernoulli trial n times and count the total number of successes. That count is called a binomial random variable. We write X ~ Bin(n, p). But there are four conditions, and exams love to ask them. First, the number of trials n is fixed in advance. Second, each trial has only two outcomes. Third, the probability of success p stays the same in every trial. Fourth, the trials are independent, so one result does not change another. A short way to remember: BINS, which stands for Binary, Independent, Number fixed, Same p.

Building the formula by hand: Toss a fair coin 3 times and let X be the number of heads. What is P(X = 2)? The sequences with exactly two heads are HHT, HTH and THH. Each sequence has probability (1/2) x (1/2) x (1/2) = 1/8. There are 3 such sequences, so P(X = 2) = 3/8. Look closely at what we did. We counted how many sequences have 2 successes, which is the number of ways to choose 2 positions out of 3, that is 3C2 = 3. Then we multiplied by the probability of one such sequence.

The binomial PMF: Doing the same thing in general gives the formula P(X = k) = nCk x p^k x (1 - p)^(n - k), for k = 0, 1, 2, ..., n. Read it like a sentence. nCk counts in how many orders the k successes can appear among n trials (this is the combinations from Lesson 6). p^k is the chance that those k chosen trials are all successes. (1 - p)^(n - k) is the chance that the remaining n - k trials are all failures. Because the trials are independent, we multiply. If you add P(X = k) for all k from 0 to n, you get (p + (1 - p))^n = 1^n = 1, thanks to the binomial theorem. That is actually where the name binomial comes from.

Mean and variance: The binomial count X is just a sum of n independent Bernoulli variables: X = X1 + X2 + ... + Xn. Expectation is linear, so E[X] = p + p + ... + p = np. Because the trials are independent, variances also add, so Var(X) = np(1 - p). The standard deviation is the square root, sqrt(np(1 - p)). Example: toss a fair coin 100 times. Expected heads = 100 x 0.5 = 50. Variance = 100 x 0.5 x 0.5 = 25, so the standard deviation is 5. This means getting 45 or 55 heads is totally normal, but 80 heads would be very strange.

Worked problem 1, MCQ guessing: Back to the 10-question test, 4 options each, pure guessing. Here n = 10 and p = 1/4 = 0.25. The chance of getting zero right is P(X = 0) = 0.75^10 which is about 0.0563, roughly 5.6 percent. The chance of exactly 2 right is 10C2 x 0.25^2 x 0.75^8 = 45 x 0.0625 x 0.1001 which is about 0.2816. The chance of all 10 right is 0.25^10 = 1/1,048,576, less than one in a million. The expected score is np = 2.5 and the standard deviation is sqrt(10 x 0.25 x 0.75) which is about 1.37.

Worked problem 1, continued: What is the chance of scoring at least 5 out of 10, which might be the pass mark? We add P(X = 5) + P(X = 6) + ... + P(X = 10). The values are about 0.0584, 0.0162, 0.0031, 0.0004 and two tiny numbers near zero. The total is about 0.078, a bit less than 8 percent. So pure guessing passes this test only about 1 time in 13. Now you also see why some exams use negative marking: it cancels the expected gain from guessing. With +1 for right and -1/3 for wrong, the expected mark per guessed question is 0.25 x 1 + 0.75 x (-1/3) = 0.

Worked problem 2, defective items: A factory in Gazipur makes phone chargers, and 5 percent of them are defective. An inspector picks 20 chargers at random. Let X be the number of defective ones, so X ~ Bin(20, 0.05). The chance of no defective charger is P(X = 0) = 0.95^20 which is about 0.358. The chance of exactly one is 20 x 0.05 x 0.95^19 which is about 0.377. So the chance of at least one defective is 1 - 0.358 = 0.642. The expected number of defective chargers is 20 x 0.05 = 1, and the variance is 20 x 0.05 x 0.95 = 0.95.

The at-least trick: Notice how we found at least one by using the complement: P(X >= 1) = 1 - P(X = 0). This trick saves huge amounts of work. Computing P(X >= 1) directly would need 20 separate terms. Whenever a question says at least one, think of 1 minus none. Similarly, at most k means adding from 0 to k, and more than k means 1 minus at most k. Write the words as inequalities before you calculate, because mixing up at least 3 (X >= 3) and more than 3 (X > 3) is one of the most common mistakes.

The shape of the binomial: If p = 0.5 the binomial PMF is perfectly symmetric around n/2. If p is small, like 0.05, the bars pile up near zero and there is a long tail to the right, so it is positively skewed. If p is large, like 0.95, it is skewed to the left. As n grows large, the shape becomes more and more like a smooth bell curve. That observation is the seed of the normal approximation you will meet in Lesson 15. The most likely value (the mode) is near np; more exactly, it is the floor of (n + 1)p.

Using a table or calculator: For small n you can compute by hand. For bigger n, use a calculator with nCr, a binomial table, or one line of code. In Python, math.comb(n, k) * p**k * (1 - p)**(n - k) gives the PMF, and scipy.stats.binom.pmf(k, n, p) or binom.cdf(k, n, p) does it for you. In a spreadsheet, BINOM.DIST(k, n, p, FALSE) gives the PMF and TRUE gives the cumulative. But in an exam hall, you will usually do it by hand, so practise writing the formula neatly with each part labelled.

Computer science example, packet loss: Suppose a mobile network in a crowded area loses each data packet with probability 0.02, independently. A video chunk is sent as 50 packets. The number of lost packets is Bin(50, 0.02). The chance that nothing is lost is 0.98^50 which is about 0.364. So almost two times out of three, at least one packet must be resent. Engineers use exactly this kind of calculation to decide how much error-correction data to add, and how many retries a protocol should allow.

Real life example 1, a cricket batsman: Suppose a batsman hits a boundary on any ball with probability 0.1, and we treat balls as independent (a simplification, but useful). In an over of 6 balls, the number of boundaries is Bin(6, 0.1). The chance of no boundary is 0.9^6 which is about 0.531. The chance of exactly one is 6 x 0.1 x 0.9^5 which is about 0.354. The expected number of boundaries per over is 0.6. Commentators who say he is due a boundary are wrong under this model, because independent trials have no memory.

Real life example 2, seeds in a village farm: A farmer in Rangpur buys seeds from a packet that says 80 percent germination. She plants 10 seeds in one pot. The number that sprout is Bin(10, 0.8). The expected count is 8, the variance is 10 x 0.8 x 0.2 = 1.6, and the standard deviation is about 1.26. The chance that all 10 sprout is 0.8^10 which is about 0.107. The chance that 6 or fewer sprout is small (about 0.12), so if that happens again and again, she has a good reason to suspect the packet label. This is a tiny first taste of hypothesis testing.

When binomial does NOT apply: If you pick cards from a deck without putting them back, p changes after every pick, so the trials are not independent and p is not the same. That is the hypergeometric distribution (next lesson). If you keep trying until the first success, the number of trials is not fixed, so that is the geometric distribution. If you count random events in a time period with no fixed n, like calls per minute, that is Poisson. Checking the BINS conditions first will stop you from using the wrong formula.

A useful rule of thumb: When you sample a small part of a very big population without replacement, the binomial is still a great approximation. For example, picking 20 voters out of a city of a million barely changes p. A common rule is that if the sample is less than 5 percent of the population, using binomial is fine. That is why opinion polls and quality checks happily use binomial even though nobody is put back.

Common mistakes: Forgetting the nCk part and just writing p^k(1 - p)^(n - k), which gives the chance of one particular order only. Swapping p and 1 - p, especially when success means something bad. Using binomial when the trials are not independent. Writing the variance as np instead of np(1 - p). Mixing at least and more than. Also, remember that the possible values are only 0 to n; P(X = n + 1) is zero.

What exams ask: State the four conditions of a binomial experiment. Derive the mean and variance from Bernoulli variables. Given n and p, find P(X = k), P(X <= k) or P(X >= 1). Find n or p from given mean and variance (for example, mean 6 and variance 4.2 gives 1 - p = 0.7, so p = 0.3 and n = 20). Sometimes you are asked for the most probable value. Practise the reverse problem, because many students only practise the forward one.

Recap: A Bernoulli trial has two outcomes with success probability p; its mean is p and variance p(1 - p). Repeat it n times, independently, with the same p, and count successes: that is Bin(n, p), with P(X = k) = nCk p^k (1 - p)^(n - k), mean np and variance np(1 - p). Use the complement for at least one. Check BINS before using it. Next lesson we meet its cousins: Poisson, geometric and hypergeometric.
key_points: A Bernoulli trial has two outcomes; with success = 1 and failure = 0, the mean is p and the variance is p(1 - p).
Binomial conditions (BINS): two outcomes, independent trials, fixed number n, same p every trial.
Binomial PMF: P(X = k) = nCk p^k (1 - p)^(n - k) for k = 0, 1, ..., n.
A binomial is a sum of n Bernoulli variables, so its mean is np and its variance is np(1 - p).
Use the complement for 'at least one': P(X >= 1) = 1 - (1 - p)^n.
The shape is symmetric when p = 0.5, right-skewed for small p, left-skewed for large p, and bell-like for large n.
Without replacement from a small group, use hypergeometric; until the first success, use geometric; counts in time, use Poisson.
lessons.tip: Before touching the formula, write three things in the margin: n = ?, p = ?, and the event as an inequality (X = k, X >= k, X <= k). Half the marks are lost in setting up, not in calculating.
lessons.task: Toss a coin 5 times and count heads. Repeat this 20 times (or ask friends to help) and make a frequency table of the head counts. Compare your table with 20 x P(X = k) from Bin(5, 0.5).

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a condition of a binomial experiment?
options: The number of trials is fixed
The probability of success changes after each trial
quiz.explain: In a binomial experiment p must stay the same in every trial. If it changes, binomial does not apply.

quiz.q: A student guesses 10 MCQs with 4 options each. What is the expected number of correct answers?
For X ~ Bin(20, 0.05), what is P(X >= 1)?
quiz.explain: At least one is the complement of none: 1 - P(X = 0) = 1 - 0.95^20, about 0.642.

quiz.q: A binomial variable has mean 6 and variance 4.2. What are n and p?
quiz.explain: 1 - p = variance/mean = 4.2/6 = 0.7, so p = 0.3 and n = 6/0.3 = 20.

quiz.q: Toss a fair coin 3 times. What is P(exactly 2 heads)?

lessons.title: Poisson, Geometric and Hypergeometric Distributions
lessons.content:
Think about a bKash customer care line. Calls do not arrive on a timetable. Sometimes two come in the same minute, sometimes nobody calls for a while. Now think about a kid rolling a ludo dice again and again, waiting for a six to open a piece. And think about a teacher picking 4 copies out of a pile of 10 to check, without putting any back. These three pictures look different, and each one has its own distribution. In this lesson you meet three cousins of the binomial: Poisson for counting random events in time or space, geometric for waiting until the first success, and hypergeometric for picking without replacement.

Why we need more than binomial: The binomial needs a fixed number of trials, the same p each time, and independence. Real life often breaks one of these. Phone calls have no fixed n. The ludo player does not decide in advance how many times to roll. The teacher's picks change the pile, so p changes. Each new distribution here is what you get when one of the binomial conditions is replaced by something else.

The Poisson distribution: A Poisson random variable counts how many times an event happens in a fixed interval of time, length, area or volume, when events happen independently and at a constant average rate. The single parameter is lambda (written λ), the average number of events in the interval. The PMF is P(X = k) = e^(-λ) λ^k / k!, for k = 0, 1, 2, ... with no upper limit. Here e is about 2.71828. The values k can, in theory, go on forever, but the probabilities get tiny very quickly.

Conditions for Poisson: Events happen one at a time (two events never happen at exactly the same instant). The number of events in non-overlapping intervals are independent. The average rate is constant over the interval. And the chance of an event in a very small interval is proportional to the length of that interval. Typical examples: calls to a helpdesk per minute, typing mistakes per page, cars passing a toll plaza per minute at night, requests hitting a web server per second, earthquakes per year in a region, and flaws per metre of cloth in a garment factory.

Mean equals variance: The most famous property of the Poisson is that E[X] = λ and Var(X) = λ. The mean and the variance are the same number. So the standard deviation is sqrt(λ). This is a quick check you can do on real data: if the sample mean and sample variance of your counts are close, a Poisson model may fit. If the variance is much bigger than the mean, the data is overdispersed and a plain Poisson model is not a good fit.

Worked Poisson example: A helpdesk gets on average 3 calls per minute, so λ = 3. The chance of no call in a minute is e^(-3) which is about 0.0498. The chance of exactly 2 calls is e^(-3) x 3^2 / 2! = 0.0498 x 4.5 which is about 0.224. The chance of 3 or fewer is e^(-3) x (1 + 3 + 4.5 + 4.5) = 13 e^(-3) which is about 0.647. So the chance of 4 or more calls in a minute, the moment when one operator gets overwhelmed, is 1 - 0.647 = 0.353, about 35 percent.

Scaling λ: If the rate is 3 per minute, then over 2 minutes the count is Poisson with λ = 6, and over 30 seconds λ = 1.5. You always scale λ to match the interval in the question. This is a classic exam trap. Example: a proofreader finds on average 1 typo per 2 pages. For one page, λ = 0.5, so P(no typo on a page) = e^(-0.5) which is about 0.607. For a 10-page chapter, λ = 5.

Poisson approximation to binomial: When n is large and p is small, Bin(n, p) is very close to Poisson with λ = np. A common rule is n >= 20 and p <= 0.05, or n >= 100 and np <= 10. Example: a chip has a 0.002 chance of being faulty, and a box has 1000 chips. Exactly, P(no faulty chip) = 0.998^1000 which is about 0.1351. With Poisson, λ = 1000 x 0.002 = 2, and P(0) = e^(-2) which is about 0.1353. For one faulty chip, both methods give about 0.2707. The approximation saves you from raising numbers to the power 1000. This is why Poisson is sometimes called the law of rare events.

The geometric distribution: Now we repeat independent Bernoulli trials with success probability p until we get the first success, and let X be the number of trials needed. Then P(X = k) = (1 - p)^(k - 1) p, for k = 1, 2, 3, .... It says: the first k - 1 trials are failures, and the k-th one is a success. The mean is E[X] = 1/p and the variance is (1 - p)/p^2. Some books define X as the number of failures before the first success instead; then the values start at 0 and the mean is (1 - p)/p. Always check which version your teacher uses.

Geometric worked example: In ludo you need a six to bring a piece out, so p = 1/6. The chance that you first get a six on the 3rd roll is (5/6)^2 x (1/6) = 25/216 which is about 0.116. On average you need 1/p = 6 rolls, and the variance is (5/6)/(1/36) = 30. A useful shortcut: P(X > k) = (1 - p)^k, because X > k means the first k rolls are all failures. So the chance of still waiting after 5 rolls is (5/6)^5 which is about 0.402. And the chance of getting a six within 4 rolls is 1 - (5/6)^4 which is about 0.518.

The memoryless property: The geometric distribution has no memory. P(X > s + t given X > s) = P(X > t). In words: if you have already failed 10 times, the chance of needing at least 3 more tries is exactly the same as for someone just starting. The dice does not remember your bad luck. It is the only discrete distribution with this property. Its continuous partner, the exponential distribution, has the same property, and you will meet it next lesson.

The hypergeometric distribution: Here we have a population of N items, of which K are of a special type (call them successes). We draw n items without replacement and let X be the number of special items in our sample. Then P(X = k) = (KCk x (N - K)C(n - k)) / NCn. Read it as: ways to choose k special items, times ways to choose the rest from the ordinary items, divided by all ways to choose n items. It is pure counting, straight from Lesson 6.

Hypergeometric worked example: A box has 10 bulbs, 3 of them defective. You pick 4 without replacement. The chance of exactly 1 defective is (3C1 x 7C3) / 10C4 = (3 x 35) / 210 = 0.5. The chance of none is 7C4/210 = 35/210 which is about 0.167. The chance of exactly 2 is (3C2 x 7C2)/210 = 63/210 = 0.3. The mean is n x K/N = 4 x 3/10 = 1.2. The variance is n (K/N)(1 - K/N)(N - n)/(N - 1) = 4 x 0.3 x 0.7 x 6/9 = 0.56. Compare with binomial's 4 x 0.3 x 0.7 = 0.84.

The finite population correction: That extra factor (N - n)/(N - 1) is called the finite population correction. It is less than 1, so sampling without replacement gives a smaller variance than with replacement. That makes sense: when you take items out, you learn more about the pile and there is less randomness left. When N is huge compared to n, the factor is almost 1 and the hypergeometric becomes practically binomial with p = K/N. That is the 5 percent rule you saw last lesson.

Computer science uses: Poisson models arrivals of requests at a server, packets at a router and jobs in a queue, which is the base of queueing theory in Lesson 25. Geometric shows up in retry loops: if each attempt to grab a lock or send a packet succeeds with probability p, the expected number of attempts is 1/p. Randomized algorithms like Las Vegas algorithms repeat until success, so their running time is often geometric. Hypergeometric appears in software testing and auditing: if a batch of 500 records has 20 bad ones and you check 30, how likely are you to catch at least one?

Real life example 1, a Dhaka pharmacy at night: A 24-hour pharmacy in Dhanmondi gets on average 4 customers in a 10-minute window late at night, so λ = 4. The owner wants to know how often more than 6 customers come in 10 minutes, because then one person cannot handle the counter. P(X <= 6) is about 0.889, so P(X > 6) is about 0.111, roughly 1 window in 9. If he looks at 48 ten-minute windows in a night shift, he can expect about 5 rush windows. This kind of calculation decides how many staff to keep at night.

Real life example 2, a quality check at a garments factory: A buyer receives a lot of 50 shirts and knows the factory claims at most 5 are faulty. The buyer randomly checks 5 shirts without replacement and accepts the lot only if none are faulty. If exactly 5 are faulty, the chance of accepting is 45C5 / 50C5, which is about 0.577. So more than half the time, a lot with 5 faulty shirts slips through. If the buyer checks 10 shirts instead, the acceptance chance drops to about 0.31. This is exactly how acceptance sampling plans are designed in industry.

How to pick the right one: Ask yourself what is being counted. Number of events in a time or space interval with a known average rate: Poisson. Number of trials until the first success, with constant p: geometric. Number of successes in a sample drawn without replacement from a small known population: hypergeometric. Number of successes in n independent trials with the same p: binomial. Many exam questions are mostly testing whether you choose correctly, so read the story carefully.

Common mistakes: Forgetting to scale λ to the interval asked. Writing the Poisson PMF with k! missing, or using λ^k e^λ instead of e^(-λ). Mixing up the two versions of geometric (trials vs failures). Using binomial for a small batch sampled without replacement. Thinking that a long run of failures makes success more likely next time; for independent trials it does not. And remember Poisson values have no upper limit, so P(X >= 1) = 1 - e^(-λ).

What exams ask: State the conditions of a Poisson process and show that mean = variance = λ. Find P(X = k) or P(X >= k) for a given rate. Use Poisson to approximate a binomial with large n and small p, and compare with the exact answer. Find the probability that the first success happens on the k-th trial, or after k trials. Solve a defective-items problem with hypergeometric and compare with binomial. Prove the memoryless property of the geometric, which takes two lines using P(X > k) = (1 - p)^k.

Recap: Poisson counts random events in an interval, P(X = k) = e^(-λ) λ^k / k!, with mean and variance both λ, and approximates binomial when n is large and p small. Geometric counts trials until the first success, P(X = k) = (1 - p)^(k - 1) p, with mean 1/p, and it is memoryless. Hypergeometric counts successes when drawing without replacement, using combinations, with mean nK/N and a smaller variance than binomial. Next lesson we move to continuous variables: the uniform and the exponential.
key_points: Poisson counts events in a fixed interval at a constant average rate: P(X = k) = e^(-λ) λ^k / k!.
For Poisson, mean = variance = λ; always scale λ to the length of the interval asked.
Bin(n, p) is close to Poisson(np) when n is large and p is small (law of rare events).
Geometric counts trials until the first success: P(X = k) = (1 - p)^(k - 1) p, mean 1/p, variance (1 - p)/p^2.
P(X > k) = (1 - p)^k for the geometric, and it is the only memoryless discrete distribution.
Hypergeometric counts successes drawn without replacement: P(X = k) = KCk (N-K)C(n-k) / NCn, mean nK/N.
Hypergeometric variance has the finite population correction (N - n)/(N - 1); for huge N it becomes binomial.
lessons.tip: Make a one-page table with four columns (binomial, Poisson, geometric, hypergeometric) and rows for 'what is counted', PMF, mean and variance. Revise from that table before every exam.
lessons.task: Stand near a road or watch from a window for 10 one-minute periods and count rickshaws (or cars) passing each minute. Compute the mean and variance of your 10 counts. Are they close, as a Poisson model would predict?

quiz.q: A helpdesk gets on average 3 calls per minute. What is λ for a 2-minute period?
quiz.explain: λ scales with the interval: 3 per minute x 2 minutes = 6.

quiz.q: For a Poisson random variable with λ = 4, what is the variance?
quiz.explain: For Poisson, the variance equals the mean, λ = 4.

quiz.q: You roll a die until the first six. What is the expected number of rolls?
quiz.explain: Geometric with p = 1/6 has mean 1/p = 6.

quiz.q: A box has 10 bulbs, 3 defective. Pick 4 without replacement. P(exactly 1 defective)?
quiz.explain: Hypergeometric: (3C1 x 7C3)/10C4 = (3 x 35)/210 = 0.5.

quiz.q: When does Poisson(np) approximate Bin(n, p) well?
options: Always, for any n and p
quiz.explain: Poisson is the law of rare events: it works when there are many trials with a small success probability.

lessons.title: Continuous Uniform and Exponential Distributions
lessons.content:
You are standing at a bus stop in Mirpur. The board says a bus comes every 15 minutes, but you have no idea when the last one left. How long will you wait? Could be 1 minute, could be 14. Every moment in that window feels equally likely. Now think about a different question: you just bought an LED bulb. How long until it dies? Bulbs do not age the way people do; they fail suddenly and at random. The first picture is the continuous uniform distribution. The second is the exponential distribution. Both are simple, both are everywhere, and together they are a perfect first step into continuous random variables.

Quick reminder about continuous variables: From Lesson 10, a continuous random variable can take any value in an interval, so P(X = exactly 7.000...) is zero. Instead we use a probability density function f(x), and probability is the area under f over an interval: P(a <= X <= b) is the integral of f from a to b. The cumulative distribution function is F(x) = P(X <= x). Total area under f is 1. Mean is the integral of x f(x), and variance is E[X^2] - (E[X])^2. Everything below is just these rules applied to two specific shapes.

The continuous uniform distribution: X ~ U(a, b) means X is equally likely to fall anywhere between a and b. The PDF is a flat rectangle: f(x) = 1/(b - a) for a <= x <= b, and 0 outside. Why 1/(b - a)? Because the rectangle has width b - a and its area must be 1, so its height must be 1/(b - a). The CDF is F(x) = 0 for x < a, (x - a)/(b - a) for a <= x <= b, and 1 for x > b. It is a straight ramp from 0 to 1.

Probabilities with uniform are just lengths: Because the density is flat, the probability of landing in any sub-interval is simply its length divided by the total length. If X ~ U(0, 15), then P(5 <= X <= 8) = (8 - 5)/15 = 3/15 = 0.2. No integration needed, just a ratio of lengths. It also does not matter whether you use < or <=, because single points have zero probability for continuous variables.

Mean and variance of uniform: The mean is right in the middle, E[X] = (a + b)/2, which makes sense because the rectangle is balanced there. The variance is Var(X) = (b - a)^2 / 12. Where does the 12 come from? Compute E[X^2] = (a^2 + ab + b^2)/3, then subtract ((a + b)/2)^2; the algebra simplifies to (b - a)^2/12. For U(0, 1), the mean is 0.5 and the variance is 1/12, so the standard deviation is about 0.289.

Worked uniform example: Buses every 15 minutes and you arrive at a random time, so your wait W ~ U(0, 15). Expected wait = 7.5 minutes. Variance = 15^2/12 = 18.75, so the standard deviation is about 4.33 minutes. P(wait more than 10 minutes) = (15 - 10)/15 = 1/3. P(wait less than 3 minutes) = 3/15 = 0.2. If buses came every 10 minutes instead, your expected wait would drop to 5 minutes. This is one reason transport planners care so much about bus frequency.

Uniform in computers: Almost every programming language has a function like random() in Python or Math.random() in JavaScript that returns a number that behaves like U(0, 1). These are actually pseudo-random numbers made by a deterministic algorithm, but they pass statistical tests well enough for simulations and games. From U(0, 1) you can make U(a, b) by computing a + (b - a) x U. Even more amazing, you can make many other distributions from U(0, 1), as you will see below with the exponential.

The exponential distribution: X ~ Exp(λ) models the waiting time until an event happens, when events occur at a constant rate λ. The PDF is f(x) = λ e^(-λx) for x >= 0, and 0 for x < 0. It starts at height λ at x = 0 and decays smoothly towards zero. Short waits are most likely, but long waits are always possible. The CDF is F(x) = 1 - e^(-λx), and the survival function, the chance of waiting longer than x, is P(X > x) = e^(-λx). That last formula is the one you will use most.

Mean and variance of exponential: The mean is E[X] = 1/λ and the variance is Var(X) = 1/λ^2, so the standard deviation equals the mean, 1/λ. If a bulb lasts on average 1000 hours, then 1/λ = 1000, so λ = 0.001 per hour. Careful: some books write the exponential using the mean θ = 1/λ instead, as f(x) = (1/θ) e^(-x/θ). Same distribution, different label. Always check whether the number given is a rate or a mean.

Worked exponential example: LED bulb lifetime with mean 1000 hours. P(bulb lasts more than 1000 hours) = e^(-0.001 x 1000) = e^(-1) which is about 0.368. Notice that only about 37 percent of bulbs outlive the average, because the distribution is right-skewed with a long tail. P(dies within 500 hours) = 1 - e^(-0.5) which is about 0.393. The median lifetime is where F(x) = 0.5, so x = ln 2 / λ which is about 693 hours. The median is less than the mean, again because of the long right tail.

The memoryless property: For the exponential, P(X > s + t given X > s) = P(X > t). Proof in one line: P(X > s + t)/P(X > s) = e^(-λ(s+t)) / e^(-λs) = e^(-λt). In words: a bulb that has already worked for 500 hours has exactly the same chance of lasting another 1000 hours as a brand-new bulb, e^(-1), about 0.368. It does not get tired. The exponential is the only continuous distribution with this property, just like the geometric was the only discrete one. In fact the exponential is the continuous version of the geometric.

When memoryless is realistic and when it is not: Electronic parts with no wear, radioactive atoms, and arrivals of independent customers are well modelled as memoryless. A radioactive atom does not know how old it is; that is why half-life works, and the half-life is exactly the median ln 2 / λ. But people, car tyres and mechanical parts do wear out, so their lifetimes are not exponential. Engineers then use other models like the Weibull distribution. Saying a mobile phone battery has an exponential lifetime would be a poor model, because batteries clearly age.

The link with Poisson: Here is the beautiful connection. If events happen as a Poisson process with rate λ per unit time, then the number of events in time t is Poisson with mean λt, and the waiting time between consecutive events is Exp(λ). Why? The waiting time until the first event is more than t exactly when zero events happen in time t. Poisson says P(zero events) = e^(-λt). So P(waiting time > t) = e^(-λt), which is exactly the exponential survival function. Counting events gives Poisson; measuring the gaps gives exponential. Same process, two views.

Worked link example: Customers arrive at a tea stall at 6 per hour on average. The number of customers in 1 hour is Poisson(6). The gap between customers is Exp(6 per hour), with mean 1/6 hour = 10 minutes. P(no customer for the next 20 minutes) = e^(-6 x 1/3) = e^(-2) which is about 0.135. Check with Poisson: in 20 minutes λt = 2, and P(0 customers) = e^(-2). Same answer, as it must be.

Making exponential numbers from uniform: If U ~ U(0, 1), then X = -ln(U)/λ follows Exp(λ). This is called the inverse transform method. It works because if F(x) = 1 - e^(-λx), solving F(x) = u gives x = -ln(1 - u)/λ, and 1 - U is also uniform. Simulation programs for networks and queues use exactly this trick to generate random arrival gaps. One line of code: gap = -math.log(random.random()) / rate. (In real code use 1 - random.random() to avoid taking the log of zero.)

Computer science uses: In networking and operating systems, request inter-arrival times and service times are often modelled as exponential; that is the M in the M/M/1 queue you will meet in Lesson 25. Reliability engineers model time to failure of servers and disks with exponential when the failure rate is constant, and then mean time to failure (MTTF) is 1/λ. Uniform is used for random hashing ideas, load balancing by picking a random server, random sampling, and Monte Carlo simulation where you throw random points to estimate areas or integrals.

Real life example 1, the BRTC bus stop: You catch a bus that comes every 15 minutes, five days a week, arriving at random times. Over a 20-day month, your expected total wait is 20 x 7.5 = 150 minutes, two and a half hours. If you learn the timetable and arrive about 2 minutes before the bus, your wait becomes roughly U(0, 4) with mean 2 minutes, and the monthly total drops to about 40 minutes. A simple uniform model tells you that knowing the timetable saves almost two hours a month.

Real life example 2, a bKash agent shop: An agent shop in a small town gets on average 12 customers per hour, arriving independently, so gaps are Exp(12 per hour), with mean 5 minutes. The agent wants to step out for tea for 10 minutes. The chance that no customer comes in those 10 minutes is e^(-12 x 10/60) = e^(-2) which is about 0.135. The chance that the next customer comes within 2 minutes is 1 - e^(-0.4) which is about 0.33. So a 10-minute break will usually miss someone; a helper at the counter is worth it.

Common mistakes: Using λ when the question gives the mean, or the other way round. Forgetting that the exponential PDF is zero for negative x. Thinking a uniform PDF value like 1/15 is a probability; it is a density, and for U(0, 0.5) the density is 2, which is bigger than 1 and perfectly fine. Writing variance of uniform as (b - a)/12 without the square. Assuming everything with a lifetime is memoryless. And forgetting units: if λ is per hour, time must be in hours.

What exams ask: Write the PDF and CDF of U(a, b) and derive its mean and variance. Find interval probabilities for uniform. For exponential, find P(X > t), P(a < X < b), the median, and the mean and variance. Prove the memoryless property. Show that the waiting time in a Poisson process is exponential. Sometimes: given that a part has survived s hours, find the chance it survives t more.

Recap: Uniform U(a, b) has a flat density 1/(b - a), probabilities equal length ratios, mean (a + b)/2 and variance (b - a)^2/12. Exponential Exp(λ) has density λ e^(-λx), survival e^(-λx), mean 1/λ, variance 1/λ^2, median ln 2/λ, and it is memoryless. Poisson counts events at rate λ; exponential measures the gaps between them. Next lesson is the queen of all distributions: the normal distribution.
key_points: Uniform U(a, b): f(x) = 1/(b - a) on [a, b]; probabilities are length ratios.
Uniform mean (a + b)/2 and variance (b - a)^2/12; U(0, 1) has variance 1/12.
Exponential Exp(λ): f(x) = λ e^(-λx) for x >= 0, CDF 1 - e^(-λx), survival P(X > x) = e^(-λx).
Exponential mean 1/λ, variance 1/λ^2, median ln 2/λ (less than the mean).
Memoryless: P(X > s + t | X > s) = P(X > t); exponential is the only continuous distribution with this property.
In a Poisson process with rate λ, counts are Poisson and the gaps between events are Exp(λ).
Inverse transform: X = -ln(U)/λ turns a uniform random number into an exponential one.
lessons.tip: Underline the units in every exponential question. Convert the rate and the time to the same unit (per hour with hours, per minute with minutes) before you plug anything into e^(-λt).
lessons.task: Use a stopwatch on your phone to record the gaps (in seconds) between 20 vehicles passing a road. Compute the average gap, then compare how many gaps are longer than the average with the exponential prediction of about 37 percent.

quiz.explain: For uniform, probability = length/total length = 3/15 = 0.2.

quiz.q: What is the variance of U(2, 8)?
A bulb's lifetime is exponential with mean 1000 hours. P(it lasts more than 1000 hours)?
A part with exponential lifetime has already worked 500 hours. The chance it lasts 200 more hours is:
options: Higher than for a new part
The same as for a new part
Lower than for a new part
quiz.explain: The exponential is memoryless: P(X > 700 | X > 500) = P(X > 200).

quiz.q: Customers arrive as a Poisson process with rate 6 per hour. What is the mean gap between customers?
quiz.explain: Gaps are Exp(6 per hour) with mean 1/6 hour = 10 minutes.

lessons.title: The Normal Distribution
lessons.content:
Line up every student in a big school by height. A few are very short, a few are very tall, and most are somewhere in the middle. If you draw a histogram of their heights, it looks like a smooth hill, highest in the middle and falling off evenly on both sides, like an upside-down bell. Do the same for the weights of 5 kg rice bags from a factory, for the errors in a scale, or for the total of 100 dice rolls, and the same bell shape pops up again and again. This shape is the normal distribution, also called the Gaussian distribution or the bell curve. It is the single most important distribution in all of statistics.

Why it is everywhere: The deep reason is the central limit theorem, which you will meet in Lesson 17. It says that when you add up many small independent random effects, the total tends to be normal, whatever the shape of the small pieces. Height depends on many genes and lots of food and health factors; measurement error comes from many tiny disturbances. Add them up and you get a bell. That is why the normal is the default model for so many things, and why most of the tests in later lessons are built on it.

The normal PDF: A normal random variable X ~ N(μ, σ^2) has two parameters: the mean μ (mu), which sets the centre, and the standard deviation σ (sigma), which sets the spread. The density is f(x) = (1 / (σ sqrt(2π))) e^(-(x - μ)^2 / (2σ^2)), for all real x. You do not need to memorise how to integrate it (in fact it has no simple antiderivative), but you should recognise its parts: the (x - μ)^2 makes it symmetric around μ, the minus sign makes it fall away from the centre, and the 1/(σ sqrt(2π)) in front makes the total area exactly 1.

Properties of the bell: It is perfectly symmetric about μ, so the mean, median and mode are all equal to μ. Its skewness is 0. It never touches the x-axis; the tails go on forever but get very thin very fast. The curve has inflection points (where it changes from curving down to curving up) exactly at μ - σ and μ + σ. Changing μ slides the bell left or right without changing its shape. Making σ bigger flattens and widens the bell; making σ smaller makes it tall and narrow. The area under it is always 1.

Notation trap: N(μ, σ^2) is the usual notation, with the variance as the second number. So N(60, 100) means mean 60 and variance 100, which is standard deviation 10. Some books and software write N(μ, σ) instead. In Python, statistics.NormalDist(60, 10) and scipy.stats.norm(60, 10) both take the standard deviation. Read carefully, because mixing up variance and standard deviation is one of the most common ways to lose marks.

The standard normal Z: Since we cannot integrate the normal by hand, we use a trick. Every normal can be converted into one single standard normal Z ~ N(0, 1), with mean 0 and standard deviation 1, using Z = (X - μ)/σ. This is called standardizing, and the result is the z-score. A z-score tells you how many standard deviations a value is away from the mean. z = 2 means two standard deviations above, z = -1.5 means one and a half below. Then we only need one table, the table of Φ(z) = P(Z <= z).

Reading the z-table: A standard z-table gives Φ(z), the area to the left of z. For example, Φ(1.00) = 0.8413, Φ(1.50) = 0.9332, Φ(1.96) = 0.9750 and Φ(2.00) = 0.9772. Three rules cover almost everything. To find P(Z <= z), read Φ(z) directly. To find P(Z > z), use 1 - Φ(z). To find P(a < Z < b), use Φ(b) - Φ(a). For negative z, use symmetry: Φ(-z) = 1 - Φ(z). So Φ(-1.5) = 1 - 0.9332 = 0.0668. Always draw a quick bell and shade the area you want before you look anything up.

Worked example 1, exam marks: In a large class, marks are approximately N(60, 10^2). What fraction scored below 75? z = (75 - 60)/10 = 1.5, so P(X < 75) = Φ(1.5) = 0.9332, about 93 percent. What fraction scored above 80? z = 2, so P(X > 80) = 1 - 0.9772 = 0.0228, about 2.3 percent. What fraction scored between 50 and 70? z goes from -1 to 1, so the answer is Φ(1) - Φ(-1) = 0.8413 - 0.1587 = 0.6826, about 68 percent.

Going backwards, from probability to value: Sometimes you know the percentage and want the cutoff. Suppose the top 10 percent of the class gets an A. We need z such that Φ(z) = 0.90. From the table, z is about 1.2816. Convert back with X = μ + zσ = 60 + 1.2816 x 10 which is about 72.8. So you need about 73 marks for an A. This reverse lookup is how percentile cutoffs, admission merit lines and quality limits are set.

The 68-95-99.7 rule: For any normal distribution, about 68 percent of values lie within 1 standard deviation of the mean, about 95 percent within 2, and about 99.7 percent within 3. More precisely, 68.27, 95.45 and 99.73 percent. A related number you will use again and again is 1.96: exactly 95 percent of a normal lies within 1.96 standard deviations of the mean. This empirical rule lets you do quick mental checks. If someone says a value is 4 standard deviations from the mean, you know that is extremely rare under a normal model, about 6 in 100,000.

Using z-scores to compare: z-scores let you compare apples and oranges. Rahim got 70 in Physics, where the class mean was 60 and the standard deviation 5. He got 80 in Math, where the mean was 70 and the standard deviation 10. Which result is more impressive? Physics: z = (70 - 60)/5 = 2. Math: z = (80 - 70)/10 = 1. Even though 80 is the higher raw mark, his Physics result is better relative to the class, because he was two standard deviations above the average there.

Sums of normals: If X and Y are independent normals, X + Y is also normal, with mean μX + μY and variance σX^2 + σY^2. Also, aX + b is normal with mean aμ + b and standard deviation |a|σ. Example: a phone's battery and screen take independent times to assemble, N(10, 2^2) and N(15, 3^2) minutes. The total time is N(25, 13), standard deviation about 3.6 minutes. Note that variances add, not standard deviations.

Normal approximation to the binomial: When n is large, Bin(n, p) looks like a bell, so we can approximate it with a normal having the same mean np and variance np(1 - p). A common rule says it works well when np >= 5 and n(1 - p) >= 5 (some books use 10). This saves a lot of work, because adding up dozens of binomial terms is painful.

Continuity correction: There is one catch. The binomial takes only whole numbers, but the normal is continuous. Each whole number k is represented by the interval from k - 0.5 to k + 0.5. So P(X <= 55) becomes P(Y < 55.5), P(X >= 55) becomes P(Y > 54.5), P(X < 55) becomes P(Y < 54.5), and P(X = 50) becomes P(49.5 < Y < 50.5). This small shift of 0.5 is the continuity correction, and it improves the approximation a lot.

Worked approximation: Toss a fair coin 100 times. What is P(at most 55 heads)? Mean np = 50, variance 25, standard deviation 5. With continuity correction, P(X <= 55) is about P(Z < (55.5 - 50)/5) = Φ(1.1) = 0.8643. The exact binomial answer is 0.8644, nearly identical. What about exactly 50 heads? P(49.5 < Y < 50.5) = Φ(0.1) - Φ(-0.1) which is about 0.0797, while the exact value is about 0.0796. Without the correction, P(X = 50) would come out as zero, which is clearly wrong.

Real life example 1, a rice packing machine: A mill in Naogaon fills 5 kg rice bags. The machine's fill weight is N(5.05, 0.03^2) kg. What fraction of bags are under the 5 kg printed on the label? z = (5.00 - 5.05)/0.03 which is about -1.67, so P is about Φ(-1.67) which is about 0.048, nearly 5 percent. If the law says at most 1 percent may be underweight, the owner has two choices: raise the mean or reduce the spread. To get 1 percent, he needs the mean to be at least 2.33 standard deviations above 5 kg, so with σ = 0.03 the mean should be about 5.07 kg. Better maintenance that cuts σ to 0.02 would allow a mean of about 5.047 kg instead, saving rice.

Real life example 2, server response times in CS: A web team measures that the average time for an API to respond is 200 ms, and the response times for the normal part of traffic are roughly N(200, 20^2). They set an alert at 260 ms, which is 3 standard deviations above the mean. Under the normal model, only about 0.13 percent of requests should exceed it. If 5 percent of requests suddenly cross 260 ms, something has really changed, maybe a slow database. This 3-sigma idea is used in monitoring, in manufacturing control charts and in anomaly detection. In practice response times often have a long right tail, so teams also look at percentiles like p95 and p99.

When not to use the normal: Not everything is a bell. Incomes, file sizes, city populations and waiting times are usually right-skewed with long tails. Counts of rare events are Poisson. Anything that cannot be negative but has a mean close to zero is unlikely to be normal. Before assuming normality, draw a histogram or a normal probability plot (also called a Q-Q plot) and check if it looks roughly symmetric and bell shaped.

Common mistakes: Using the variance instead of the standard deviation in z = (x - μ)/σ. Forgetting to subtract from 1 for a greater-than question. Getting the sign of z wrong. Skipping the continuity correction, or applying it in the wrong direction. Using the normal approximation when np or n(1 - p) is small. Treating the 68-95-99.7 rule as exact. And reading the z-table at 1.5 when you needed 1.05; always double-check the row and column.

What exams ask: State the properties of the normal curve. Find probabilities like P(X < a), P(X > b) and P(a < X < b) using the z-table. Find a cutoff value for a given percentage. Compare two scores with z-scores. Use the 68-95-99.7 rule for quick estimates. Approximate a binomial probability with the normal and continuity correction, and say when this is allowed. Find μ or σ when two percentages are given, by setting up two z equations and solving them together.

Recap: The normal N(μ, σ^2) is the symmetric bell curve with mean = median = mode = μ. Standardize with Z = (X - μ)/σ and use Φ(z) from the table, with P(Z > z) = 1 - Φ(z) and Φ(-z) = 1 - Φ(z). About 68, 95 and 99.7 percent of values lie within 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations. Bin(n, p) is approximately N(np, np(1 - p)) for large n, with a 0.5 continuity correction. Next lesson we look at two random variables at the same time: joint distributions.
key_points: N(μ, σ^2) is a symmetric bell curve; mean = median = mode = μ, and σ controls the spread.
Standardize with Z = (X - μ)/σ; the z-score counts standard deviations from the mean.
Use Φ(z) from the table: P(Z > z) = 1 - Φ(z), P(a < Z < b) = Φ(b) - Φ(a), Φ(-z) = 1 - Φ(z).
About 68, 95 and 99.7 percent of values lie within 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations; 1.96 gives exactly 95 percent.
Reverse lookup: the value for a percentile is x = μ + zσ.
Independent normals add: means add and variances add.
Bin(n, p) is approximately N(np, np(1 - p)) when np and n(1 - p) are at least 5; use a 0.5 continuity correction.
lessons.tip: Never touch the z-table without first drawing a tiny bell, marking μ and your x value, and shading the area you want. The sketch tells you whether to use Φ(z), 1 - Φ(z) or a difference.
lessons.task: Ask 20 friends or classmates their height (or measure 20 leaves from the same tree). Compute the mean and standard deviation, then count how many values lie within 1 standard deviation of the mean. Is it close to 68 percent?

quiz.q: Marks are N(60, 10^2). What is the z-score of a mark of 75?
Roughly what percentage of a normal distribution lies within 2 standard deviations of the mean?
quiz.explain: By the 68-95-99.7 rule, about 95 percent lies within 2 standard deviations.

quiz.q: Using the normal approximation with continuity correction, P(X <= 55) for X ~ Bin(100, 0.5) becomes:
quiz.explain: The whole number 55 covers 54.5 to 55.5, so 'at most 55' becomes Y < 55.5.

quiz.q: Physics: 70 (mean 60, SD 5). Math: 80 (mean 70, SD 10). Which is better relative to the class?
quiz.explain: Physics z = (70 - 60)/5 = 2 and Math z = (80 - 70)/10 = 1, so Physics is further above its average.

lessons.title: Joint Distributions, Covariance and Correlation
lessons.content:
So far every random variable we studied lived alone: the number of heads, the waiting time, the height of one student. But real questions often involve two things at once. Do students who sleep more get better marks? When it rains in Dhaka, do Pathao rides go up? When one server is busy, is the other one busy too? To answer these, we need to describe two random variables together, not one at a time. That is what joint distributions do. They are the bridge from single-variable probability to correlation, regression and most of machine learning.

The big idea: A joint distribution gives the probability of every pair of values (x, y) happening together. From it you can get back each variable alone (the marginals), you can ask about one variable when you know the other (the conditionals), and you can measure how strongly they move together (covariance and correlation). We start with the discrete case using a simple table, then move to the continuous case.

The joint PMF: For two discrete random variables X and Y, the joint PMF is p(x, y) = P(X = x and Y = y). Two rules must hold: every p(x, y) is between 0 and 1, and all the p(x, y) values add up to 1. The easiest way to show it is a table, with values of X as rows and values of Y as columns, and each cell holding the probability of that pair.

A small table to work with: A tea stall sells tea with or without a biscuit. Let X be the number of cups a customer buys (1 or 2) and Y be 1 if they also buy a biscuit and 0 if not. From a week of records: P(X = 1, Y = 0) = 0.4, P(X = 1, Y = 1) = 0.2, P(X = 2, Y = 0) = 0.1, P(X = 2, Y = 1) = 0.3. Check: 0.4 + 0.2 + 0.1 + 0.3 = 1. Good, it is a valid joint PMF. We will use this table for the rest of the discrete part.

Marginal distributions: To get the distribution of X alone, add across each row. P(X = 1) = 0.4 + 0.2 = 0.6 and P(X = 2) = 0.1 + 0.3 = 0.4. To get Y alone, add down each column. P(Y = 0) = 0.4 + 0.1 = 0.5 and P(Y = 1) = 0.2 + 0.3 = 0.5. They are called marginal because people used to write these totals in the margins of the table. In formula form: pX(x) = sum over y of p(x, y), and pY(y) = sum over x of p(x, y). This is just the law of total probability from Lesson 9.

Conditional distributions: If we know X, what does that tell us about Y? The conditional PMF is p(y given x) = p(x, y) / pX(x), exactly the conditional probability formula. Customers buying 1 cup: P(Y = 1 given X = 1) = 0.2/0.6 which is about 0.333. Customers buying 2 cups: P(Y = 1 given X = 2) = 0.3/0.4 = 0.75. So people buying two cups are much more likely to also buy a biscuit. Probably they are sitting with a friend and chatting! Each conditional distribution also adds up to 1: for X = 2, 0.25 + 0.75 = 1.

Independence: X and Y are independent if knowing one tells you nothing about the other. Formally, p(x, y) = pX(x) x pY(y) for every pair (x, y). One failing cell is enough to prove they are dependent. In our table, P(X = 1, Y = 0) = 0.4, but pX(1) x pY(0) = 0.6 x 0.5 = 0.3. Not equal, so X and Y are not independent, which matches what the conditionals told us. To prove independence, you must check every cell; to disprove it, one cell is enough.

Joint PDF for continuous variables: For continuous X and Y, the joint density f(x, y) is a surface over the xy-plane. It must be non-negative and the total volume under it must be 1, meaning the double integral over the whole plane is 1. The probability that (X, Y) lands in a region is the volume under the surface over that region. Marginals come from integrating out the other variable: fX(x) = integral of f(x, y) dy. Conditionals are fY|X(y given x) = f(x, y)/fX(x). Independence means f(x, y) = fX(x) fY(y).

A continuous example: Let f(x, y) = x + y for 0 <= x <= 1 and 0 <= y <= 1, and 0 elsewhere. Is it valid? The double integral of x over the unit square is 1/2, and of y is also 1/2, so the total is 1. Yes. The marginal of X is fX(x) = integral from 0 to 1 of (x + y) dy = x + 1/2. By symmetry, fY(y) = y + 1/2. Is f(x, y) equal to (x + 1/2)(y + 1/2)? No, so X and Y are not independent. A quick shortcut: if the region is a rectangle and f factors as g(x) h(y), they are independent; x + y does not factor.

Expectation of a function of two variables: E[g(X, Y)] = sum over all pairs of g(x, y) p(x, y), or the double integral in the continuous case. Two results are important. First, E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y] always, even if X and Y are dependent. Second, E[XY] = E[X] E[Y] if X and Y are independent, but not in general. In our tea table, E[X] = 1 x 0.6 + 2 x 0.4 = 1.4, E[Y] = 0.5, and E[XY] = (1 x 1 x 0.2) + (2 x 1 x 0.3) = 0.8. But E[X] E[Y] = 0.7, so E[XY] is not equal to it, as expected for dependent variables.

Covariance: Covariance measures whether X and Y tend to move together. It is defined as Cov(X, Y) = E[(X - μX)(Y - μY)], and the handy shortcut is Cov(X, Y) = E[XY] - E[X] E[Y]. If big X tends to come with big Y, covariance is positive. If big X comes with small Y, it is negative. If there is no linear pattern, it is near zero. In the tea table, Cov(X, Y) = 0.8 - 1.4 x 0.5 = 0.1, positive, matching our story that two-cup customers buy more biscuits. Note that Cov(X, X) = Var(X).

The correlation coefficient: Covariance has a problem: its size depends on units. Measure height in centimetres instead of metres and covariance jumps by 100. So we scale it: ρ = Cov(X, Y) / (σX σY). This correlation coefficient has no units and always lies between -1 and +1. ρ = +1 means a perfect increasing straight-line relation, ρ = -1 a perfect decreasing one, and ρ = 0 means no linear relation. For the tea table, Var(X) = E[X^2] - 1.4^2 = (1 x 0.6 + 4 x 0.4) - 1.96 = 2.2 - 1.96 = 0.24, Var(Y) = 0.5 - 0.25 = 0.25, so ρ = 0.1 / sqrt(0.24 x 0.25) = 0.1 / 0.245 which is about 0.41, a moderate positive correlation.

Zero correlation does not mean independent: If X and Y are independent, then Cov(X, Y) = 0. But the opposite is false. Classic example: let X be -1, 0 or 1 with equal probability, and Y = X^2. Y is completely determined by X, so they are as dependent as can be. But E[X] = 0 and E[XY] = E[X^3] = 0, so Cov(X, Y) = 0 - 0 = 0. Correlation only measures straight-line relationships. A U-shaped relationship can have zero correlation. Exams love this point.

Variance of a sum: Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) + 2 Cov(X, Y), and Var(X - Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) - 2 Cov(X, Y). More generally, Var(aX + bY) = a^2 Var(X) + b^2 Var(Y) + 2ab Cov(X, Y). When X and Y are independent, the covariance is 0 and the variances simply add, which is what we used for binomial in Lesson 12. In the tea table, Var(X + Y) = 0.24 + 0.25 + 2 x 0.1 = 0.69. You can check this directly: X + Y takes values 1, 2 and 3 with probabilities 0.4, 0.3 and 0.3, mean 1.9, E[(X + Y)^2] = 0.4 + 1.2 + 2.7 = 4.3, and 4.3 - 1.9^2 = 0.69. Same answer.

Notice something surprising: Var(X - Y) is Var(X) + Var(Y) - 2Cov, not Var(X) - Var(Y). Even when you subtract independent variables, the variances add. Example: you weigh a bag on one scale (error variance 4) and an empty bag on another (error variance 4). The difference has error variance 8, not 0. Uncertainties pile up whether you add or subtract.

Real life example 1, servers behind a load balancer: A website runs on two servers. The number of active requests on server A has variance 16, and on server B variance 9. If the loads were independent, the total load would have variance 16 + 9 = 25, standard deviation 5. But a good load balancer sends new requests to whichever server is less busy, so when A is high, B tends to be low. Suppose Cov(A, B) = -6. Then Var(A + B) = 16 + 9 - 12 = 13, standard deviation about 3.6. Negative covariance makes the total steadier, so the team can plan capacity with less spare room.

Real life example 2, a rickshaw puller's day: Think of a rickshaw puller in Sylhet. Let X be hours worked in a day and Y be income. On rainy days, he works fewer hours but each trip pays more because demand is high. Over a month he could note pairs (hours, income), build a joint frequency table, and find the marginal distributions of hours and income, the conditional average income given long or short days, and the correlation. A positive correlation would say longer days earn more, but the conditional view on rainy days might show a different story. This is exactly how researchers study informal income in Bangladesh using survey data.

Where this goes in computer science: In machine learning, a dataset is a joint distribution of features and labels, and a classifier is trying to learn the conditional distribution of the label given the features. The covariance matrix of many features is the heart of principal component analysis (PCA). Naive Bayes, which you will see in Lesson 25, assumes features are conditionally independent given the class, which turns a huge joint table into a product of small ones. In finance software, portfolio risk is Var(sum of assets), full of covariance terms.

Common mistakes: Forgetting to check that the joint table adds to 1. Adding a column when you needed a row for a marginal. Dividing by the wrong marginal in a conditional (always divide by the probability of what is given). Concluding independence from one matching cell. Thinking zero covariance means independent. Writing Var(X - Y) = Var(X) - Var(Y). Forgetting the factor 2 in front of the covariance. And mixing up covariance (has units) with correlation (unitless, between -1 and 1).

What exams ask: Given a joint PMF table, find the marginals, a conditional distribution, E[X], E[Y], E[XY], Cov(X, Y) and ρ. Check whether X and Y are independent. Find a missing value k so that the table is valid. For a joint PDF, find the constant c, the marginal densities, and a probability like P(X < Y) using a double integral. Prove Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) + 2Cov(X, Y). Give an example where covariance is zero but variables are dependent.

Recap: A joint PMF or PDF describes two variables together and must total 1. Marginals come from summing (or integrating) out the other variable; conditionals are joint divided by the marginal of what is given. Independence means the joint equals the product of marginals everywhere. Cov(X, Y) = E[XY] - E[X]E[Y]; ρ = Cov/(σX σY) lies between -1 and 1 and measures linear relation only. Var(X ± Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) ± 2Cov(X, Y). Next lesson: what happens when we average many random variables, the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem.
key_points: A joint PMF p(x, y) = P(X = x, Y = y) (or joint PDF f(x, y)) describes two variables together and totals 1.
Marginals: sum (or integrate) out the other variable; conditionals: joint divided by the marginal of the given variable.
X and Y are independent if the joint equals the product of the marginals for every pair.
E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y] always; E[XY] = E[X]E[Y] only guaranteed under independence.
Cov(X, Y) = E[XY] - E[X]E[Y]; correlation ρ = Cov/(σX σY) is unitless and lies in [-1, 1].
Independence implies zero covariance, but zero covariance does not imply independence (e.g. Y = X^2).
Var(X ± Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) ± 2Cov(X, Y); for independent variables the variances simply add.
lessons.tip: Always add row and column totals to a joint table before answering anything. Those margins give you every marginal probability for free and catch tables that do not sum to 1.
lessons.task: For one week, note each day two numbers: hours you slept and hours you studied (or minutes on your phone). Make a small table, compute the mean of each, the covariance and the correlation. Is the relation positive, negative or near zero?

Add the cells in each row
Add the cells in each column
Divide each cell by the total
quiz.explain: pX(x) is the sum of p(x, y) over all y, which is adding across the row for that x.
Conditional = joint / marginal of the given = 0.3/0.4 = 0.75.

quiz.q: E[XY] = 0.8, E[X] = 1.4, E[Y] = 0.5. What is Cov(X, Y)?
If X and Y are independent with Var(X) = 4 and Var(Y) = 4, what is Var(X - Y)?
quiz.explain: Var(X - Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) - 2Cov = 4 + 4 - 0 = 8. Variances add even when subtracting.

Covariance does not depend on units
Independent variables always have zero covariance
