lessons.title: Law of Large Numbers and the Central Limit Theorem
lessons.content:
Imagine you toss a coin 10 times and get 7 heads. Is the coin unfair? Maybe, maybe not. Ten tosses is a tiny amount, and 7 heads out of 10 happens quite often with a perfectly fair coin. Now imagine you toss it 10,000 times and get 7,000 heads. Now you would be almost sure something is wrong. Why does a bigger number of tosses make you so much more confident? This lesson answers that question with two of the most famous results in all of probability: the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem. Together they explain why averages are so reliable, why polls with only 1,000 people can say something about a whole country, and why the bell curve shows up everywhere.

Where we are in the course: In earlier lessons we learned what a random variable is, how to find its expected value E[X] and variance Var(X), and we met the normal distribution. In this lesson we take many copies of the same random variable, average them, and ask how that average behaves. In the next lessons we will use these ideas for sampling, estimation, confidence intervals and hypothesis tests, so this is the bridge between probability (the theory) and statistics (working with real data).

The setup, i.i.d. variables: Suppose X1, X2, ..., Xn are random variables that are independent and identically distributed, which people shorten to i.i.d. Independent means one result does not affect another, like separate coin tosses. Identically distributed means they all come from the same distribution, so they all have the same mean mu and the same variance sigma squared. Think of them as n separate measurements of the same thing, such as the heights of n randomly chosen students, or n rolls of the same die.

The sample mean: The sample mean is simply the average, X-bar = (X1 + X2 + ... + Xn) / n. Before we collect the data, X-bar is itself a random variable, because it depends on random values. If you roll a die 5 times you might get an average of 3.2; roll another 5 times and you might get 4.0. So X-bar has its own distribution, its own mean and its own variance. Understanding that distribution is the key to everything that follows.

Mean of the sample mean: Using linearity of expectation, E[X-bar] = (E[X1] + ... + E[Xn]) / n = (n x mu) / n = mu. So on average, the sample mean hits the true mean exactly. It does not lean too high or too low. In later lessons we will call this property unbiasedness. Example: a fair die has mu = 3.5. The average of 5 rolls is not always 3.5, but if you repeat the 5-roll experiment many times, the averages of those averages settle at 3.5.

Variance of the sample mean: Because the variables are independent, variances add, and a constant c comes out of variance as c squared. So Var(X-bar) = Var(X1 + ... + Xn) / n squared = (n x sigma squared) / n squared = sigma squared / n. This is a beautiful little formula. It says the spread of the average shrinks as n grows. Double the sample size and the variance halves. Multiply n by 100 and the variance becomes 100 times smaller.

Standard error: The standard deviation of X-bar is the square root of its variance, so SD(X-bar) = sigma / sqrt(n). This number has a special name: the standard error of the mean. It tells you how far, typically, a sample average lands from the true mean. Notice the square root. To make the standard error 2 times smaller you need 4 times as much data, and to make it 10 times smaller you need 100 times as much data. That is why extra accuracy gets expensive quickly.

A worked example of standard error: A fair die has mu = 3.5 and variance sigma squared = 35/12, which is about 2.92, so sigma is about 1.71. If you roll it n = 100 times, the standard error of the average is 1.71 / sqrt(100) = 1.71 / 10 = 0.171. So the average of 100 rolls will usually be within a few tenths of 3.5. With n = 10,000 rolls the standard error is 1.71 / 100 = 0.0171, which is tiny. The average is now nailed down very tightly.

The weak law of large numbers: Here is the first big idea. The weak law of large numbers (WLLN) says that as n grows, the sample mean X-bar gets closer and closer to the true mean mu, in the sense of probability. Formally, for any small positive number epsilon, P(|X-bar - mu| > epsilon) goes to 0 as n goes to infinity. In plain words: pick any tolerance you like, say 0.01, and if you take enough samples, it becomes almost certain that your average is within 0.01 of the truth. This is called convergence in probability.

Proving the weak law with Chebyshev: You already met Chebyshev's inequality: P(|Y - E[Y]| >= k) <= Var(Y) / k squared. Apply it to Y = X-bar. We get P(|X-bar - mu| >= epsilon) <= (sigma squared / n) / epsilon squared = sigma squared / (n x epsilon squared). As n grows, the right side shrinks to 0, so the left side must also go to 0. That is the whole proof, assuming the variance is finite. Example: for a fair coin with heads counted as 1, sigma squared = 0.25. With n = 10,000 and epsilon = 0.05, the bound is 0.25 / (10,000 x 0.0025) = 0.01. So the chance that the fraction of heads is off by 0.05 or more is at most 1 percent.

What the law does NOT say: The law of large numbers does not say that luck evens out in the short run. If a fair coin gives 5 heads in a row, the next toss is still 50-50. Believing tails is now due is called the gambler's fallacy. The law works because the early streak gets diluted by thousands of later tosses, not because the coin remembers anything. Also, the law is about the proportion or average, not the raw count. After 10,000 tosses the number of heads can easily be 50 or so away from 5,000, but 50 out of 10,000 is only 0.5 percent.

Strong law, briefly: There is also a strong law of large numbers, which says X-bar converges to mu with probability 1, a stronger kind of convergence. For this course you only need the idea: in the long run, averages settle at the expected value. The exact difference between weak and strong convergence is a topic for advanced probability courses.

The central limit theorem: The law of large numbers tells you where X-bar ends up. The central limit theorem (CLT) tells you the shape of the randomness around it. It says: if X1, ..., Xn are i.i.d. with mean mu and finite variance sigma squared, then for large n, the sample mean X-bar is approximately normal with mean mu and standard deviation sigma / sqrt(n). Equivalently, Z = (X-bar - mu) / (sigma / sqrt(n)) is approximately standard normal. The same is true for the sum: X1 + ... + Xn is approximately normal with mean n x mu and standard deviation sigma x sqrt(n).

Why the CLT is so surprising: The original variables do not need to be normal at all. A single die roll has a flat distribution, every face equally likely. A waiting time can be very skewed. A coin toss has only two values. Yet when you add or average many of them, the result looks like a bell curve. Try it in your head: the sum of 2 dice already has a triangle shape with 7 most common; the sum of 5 dice already looks quite bell-shaped. This is why heights, measurement errors and exam totals often look normal: they are sums of many small effects.

How large is large n: A common rule of thumb in textbooks is n of at least 30. If the original distribution is already roughly symmetric, much smaller n works. If it is very skewed, you may need more than 30. And if the original data are exactly normal, then X-bar is exactly normal for every n, even n = 2. For proportions, a common rule is that n x p and n x (1 - p) should both be at least 5 (some books say 10), which matches the normal approximation to the binomial you saw earlier.

Worked example 1, average of exam marks: Marks in a large exam have mean mu = 60 and standard deviation sigma = 15. You pick a random sample of n = 36 scripts. What is the chance their average is above 64? Standard error = 15 / sqrt(36) = 15 / 6 = 2.5. Then Z = (64 - 60) / 2.5 = 1.6. From the z-table, P(Z > 1.6) is about 0.0548. So there is roughly a 5.5 percent chance. Notice we did not need the marks themselves to be normal; the CLT handles the average.

Worked example 2, a sum: A rickshaw puller's earning per trip has mean 80 taka and standard deviation 30 taka, and trips are independent. What is the chance that 49 trips earn more than 4,200 taka in total? The total has mean 49 x 80 = 3,920 taka and standard deviation 30 x sqrt(49) = 30 x 7 = 210 taka. Z = (4,200 - 3,920) / 210 = 280 / 210, about 1.33. P(Z > 1.33) is about 0.0918, so roughly 9 percent.

Worked example 3, a proportion: Suppose 40 percent of Dhaka's internet users use a certain app. In a random sample of n = 100, what is the chance the sample proportion is below 0.32? The sample proportion p-hat has mean 0.40 and standard error sqrt(0.4 x 0.6 / 100) = sqrt(0.0024), about 0.049. Z = (0.32 - 0.40) / 0.049, about -1.63. P(Z < -1.63) is about 0.052. A proportion is just the average of 0/1 values, so the CLT covers it too.

Real life example 1, election polls in Bangladesh: A survey company asks 1,500 randomly chosen voters whom they support. Bangladesh has over 100 million voters, so how can 1,500 people be enough? Because of the CLT, the sample proportion is approximately normal, and its standard error is at most sqrt(0.5 x 0.5 / 1,500), which is about 0.013. Roughly 95 percent of the time, the poll lands within about 2 standard errors, so within about 2.6 percentage points of the true value. Notice the formula has no population size in it. What matters is the sample size and that the sample is truly random, not how big the country is.

Real life example 2, computer systems and simulation: When engineers measure how long a web page takes to load, single measurements jump around because of network noise. So they run the test hundreds of times and report the average, and the standard error tells them how much to trust it. Monte Carlo simulation, used in games, finance and physics, works the same way: to estimate something hard, you simulate many random trials and average. The law of large numbers guarantees the average converges, and the CLT says the error shrinks like 1 / sqrt(n). For example, estimating pi by throwing random points into a square needs about 100 times more points to get one more correct decimal digit.

Common mistakes: First, mixing up sigma and sigma / sqrt(n). The spread of individual values is sigma; the spread of the average is sigma / sqrt(n). Many students use sigma in a question about an average and get a wrong answer. Second, thinking the CLT makes the original data normal. It does not; it is about the distribution of the average or sum. Third, applying the CLT when observations are not independent, for example readings from the same patient over and over, or when the variance is infinite. Fourth, believing in the gambler's fallacy, as explained above.

What exams usually ask: State the weak law of large numbers and prove it using Chebyshev's inequality. State the central limit theorem. Find E[X-bar] and Var(X-bar). Compute a probability about a sample mean or a sum using the CLT and a z-table, like the examples above. Find how big n must be so that the standard error is below some value, for instance sigma = 20 and you want standard error at most 2, so sqrt(n) >= 10 and n >= 100.

Recap: For i.i.d. data with mean mu and variance sigma squared, the sample mean has mean mu and variance sigma squared / n, so its standard error is sigma / sqrt(n). The law of large numbers says averages settle at the true mean as n grows. The central limit theorem says averages and sums of many independent values are approximately normal, whatever the original shape. These two results are why statistics works at all: a well-chosen sample of a reasonable size can tell you a lot about a huge population.
key_points: For i.i.d. data, E[X-bar] = mu and Var(X-bar) = sigma^2 / n.
Standard error of the mean = sigma / sqrt(n); 4 times the data halves it.
Weak law of large numbers: P(|X-bar - mu| > epsilon) goes to 0 as n grows; Chebyshev's inequality proves it.
The law of large numbers is about averages in the long run; it does not make luck 'even out' (gambler's fallacy).
Central limit theorem: for large n, X-bar is approximately Normal(mu, sigma / sqrt(n)), whatever the original shape.
The sum of n i.i.d. values is approximately normal with mean n mu and SD sigma sqrt(n).
Rule of thumb: n >= 30; for proportions n p and n(1-p) at least 5 to 10.
lessons.tip: Whenever a question says 'average of n' or 'total of n', stop and replace sigma with sigma / sqrt(n) (or sigma x sqrt(n) for a total) before touching the z-table.
lessons.task: Roll a die (or use a phone dice app) 5 times and write the average. Repeat this 20 times, then draw a dot plot of the 20 averages. Compare its spread with a dot plot of 20 single rolls.

quiz.q: Individual values have sigma = 12. What is the standard error of the mean for n = 36?
quiz.explain: Standard error = sigma / sqrt(n) = 12 / 6 = 2.

quiz.q: Which statement is the central limit theorem?
options: The sample mean always equals the population mean
Every data set is normally distributed
For large n, the sample mean is approximately normal even if the data are not
Variance of the mean grows with n
quiz.explain: The CLT is about the distribution of the average (or sum) becoming approximately normal for large n.

quiz.q: A fair coin shows 6 heads in a row. What is P(tail) on the next toss?
quiz.explain: Tosses are independent; believing a tail is 'due' is the gambler's fallacy.

quiz.q: To make the standard error 3 times smaller, the sample size must be multiplied by:
quiz.explain: SE = sigma / sqrt(n), so dividing SE by 3 needs sqrt(n) times 3, which means n times 9.

quiz.q: Each trip earns mean 80 and SD 30 taka, independently. For 49 trips, the SD of the total is:
quiz.explain: SD of a sum of n i.i.d. values = sigma x sqrt(n) = 30 x 7 = 210.

lessons.title: Sampling and Sampling Distributions
lessons.content:
Imagine your mother is cooking a big pot of khichuri. To check the salt, she does not eat the whole pot. She stirs it well, takes one spoonful, and tastes it. If the spoon is salty, the pot is salty. That spoonful is a sample, and the whole pot is the population. Statistics works exactly like this. But notice one important thing: she stirs first. If she took the spoon only from the top, where the salt was just sprinkled, she would get a wrong idea. This lesson is about taking good spoonfuls, and about how the numbers we calculate from samples behave.

Population, sample, parameter, statistic: The population is the whole group you care about, such as all university students in Bangladesh. A sample is the part you actually measure, say 400 students. A parameter is a number describing the population, like the true average study hours mu or the true proportion p who own a laptop. A statistic is a number computed from the sample, like the sample mean x-bar or the sample proportion p-hat. Parameters are usually unknown and fixed. Statistics are known once you collect data, but they change from sample to sample.

Why not just measure everybody: Measuring the whole population is called a census. Bangladesh does a population census about once every ten years because it is huge, slow and expensive. Sometimes a census is even impossible: if a factory tests every light bulb by burning it until it fails, it would have no bulbs left to sell. A good sample is faster, cheaper, and, if done right, accurate enough.

Simple random sampling: In a simple random sample (SRS) of size n, every possible group of n members has the same chance of being chosen. In practice, you number everyone from 1 to N and use a random number generator or a lottery to pick n numbers. Example: a department has 200 students, numbered 1 to 200. You ask a computer for 20 random numbers in that range without repeats, and those 20 students are your sample. Simple random sampling is the basic method; most formulas in this course assume it.

With or without replacement: If a chosen person can be chosen again, that is sampling with replacement, and the draws are independent. Usually we sample without replacement, so the draws are slightly dependent. When the population is much bigger than the sample (a common rule is n less than 5 percent of N), the difference is tiny and we treat the draws as independent. When the sample is a big chunk of the population, the standard error of the mean is multiplied by the finite population correction sqrt((N - n) / (N - 1)). For N = 200 and n = 50 that factor is sqrt(150/199), about 0.87.

Stratified sampling: Split the population into groups called strata that are different from each other but similar inside, then take a random sample from each stratum. Example: a university has 60 percent male and 40 percent female students, and you want 100 students. You randomly choose 60 men and 40 women. This is called proportional allocation. Stratified samples guarantee that every important group is represented and usually give more precise estimates than an SRS of the same size, because the variation between strata is removed.

Systematic sampling: List the population in some order, pick a random starting point, and then take every k-th member. If N = 1,000 and you want n = 50, then k = 1,000 / 50 = 20. Pick a random start between 1 and 20, say 7, and take members 7, 27, 47, 67, and so on. It is quick and easy, like checking every 20th product on a factory belt. The danger: if the list has a repeating pattern with the same period, for example every 20th item comes from the same faulty machine, the sample can be badly biased.

Cluster sampling: Divide the population into clusters that each look like a mini population, randomly pick a few clusters, and then measure everyone (or a random sample) inside the chosen clusters. Example: to survey school students in a district, you randomly pick 10 schools out of 150 and survey all students in those 10 schools. This saves huge travel cost. The trade-off is that people in the same cluster tend to be similar, so for the same number of people a cluster sample is usually less precise than an SRS. Remember the difference: in stratified sampling you take some from every group; in cluster sampling you take whole groups but only some of them.

Bias in sampling: A sampling method is biased if it systematically favours some outcomes. Selection bias happens when some members have no chance or a smaller chance of being picked, for example a phone survey misses people without phones. Convenience sampling, like asking your friends, is cheap but usually biased. Voluntary response bias happens in online polls, because people with strong opinions are the ones who respond. Non-response bias happens when many chosen people refuse, and those who refuse differ from those who answer. Response bias comes from badly worded or leading questions. A bigger sample does not fix bias; it only makes you more confident about a wrong answer.

A famous bias lesson: In the 1936 US presidential election, the Literary Digest magazine mailed about 10 million ballots and got roughly 2.4 million back. It predicted that Alf Landon would beat Franklin Roosevelt. Roosevelt won by a landslide. The mailing list came largely from telephone directories and car registrations, which in those days leaned toward wealthier people, and the many who did not reply added non-response bias. Meanwhile, George Gallup used a much smaller, better designed sample and called the winner correctly. Lesson: how you sample matters more than how many.

Sampling distribution: If you take many different samples of the same size and compute a statistic each time, the statistic will vary. The probability distribution of that statistic over all possible samples is called its sampling distribution. Tiny example: population {2, 4, 6}, mean 4. All samples of size 2 with replacement are 9 pairs, with means 2, 3, 4, 3, 4, 5, 4, 5, 6. The average of these 9 means is 36 / 9 = 4, exactly the population mean. Their spread is smaller than the population's spread. That is the sampling distribution of x-bar in miniature.

Sampling distribution of the mean: From the last lesson, x-bar has mean mu and standard error sigma / sqrt(n). If the population is normal, x-bar is exactly normal; otherwise, by the central limit theorem, it is approximately normal for large n. We will not repeat the proof here. Just remember the three facts: centre mu, spread sigma / sqrt(n), shape normal (exactly or approximately).

Sampling distribution of a proportion: If p is the true proportion with some property, the sample proportion p-hat = X / n, where X is the number of successes, has mean p and standard error sqrt(p(1 - p) / n). For large n, p-hat is approximately normal. Example: if 30 percent of bKash users in a city also use Nagad, and you sample n = 400, then p-hat has mean 0.30 and standard error sqrt(0.3 x 0.7 / 400) = sqrt(0.000525), about 0.023.

The chi-square distribution: If Z1, ..., Zk are independent standard normal variables, then Z1 squared + ... + Zk squared has a chi-square distribution with k degrees of freedom. It is never negative, it is skewed to the right, its mean is k and its variance is 2k. As k grows it becomes more symmetric. The key use: if the data come from a normal population with variance sigma squared, then (n - 1) s squared / sigma squared follows a chi-square distribution with n - 1 degrees of freedom, where s squared is the sample variance. This lets us make statements about variances, and it powers the chi-square tests in a later lesson.

The t distribution: When we standardise x-bar, we need sigma, but in real life sigma is unknown, so we use the sample standard deviation s instead. The statistic t = (x-bar - mu) / (s / sqrt(n)) is no longer exactly normal. For a normal population it follows Student's t distribution with n - 1 degrees of freedom. This distribution was published in 1908 by William Gosset under the pen name Student, while he worked for the Guinness brewery. The t curve is bell-shaped and symmetric around 0 like Z, but has heavier tails, because s itself is random and adds extra uncertainty.

How t compares with z: With few degrees of freedom the tails are much heavier. For a 95 percent two-sided cut-off, z uses 1.96, but t with 9 degrees of freedom uses about 2.262 and t with 4 degrees of freedom uses about 2.776. As the degrees of freedom grow, t approaches the standard normal; with 30 degrees of freedom the cut-off is about 2.042 and with 120 it is about 1.980. That is why for large samples people often just use z.

The F distribution: If U is chi-square with d1 degrees of freedom and V is chi-square with d2 degrees of freedom, independent of each other, then F = (U / d1) / (V / d2) has an F distribution with (d1, d2) degrees of freedom. It is never negative and is skewed to the right. Its main use: comparing two variances. If two normal populations have equal variances, the ratio of their sample variances s1 squared / s2 squared follows F with (n1 - 1, n2 - 1) degrees of freedom. It is also the heart of ANOVA, which we will see in lesson 23. A neat link: if T has a t distribution with d degrees of freedom, then T squared has an F distribution with (1, d) degrees of freedom.

Degrees of freedom, in simple words: Degrees of freedom count how many values are free to vary. If 5 numbers must have a mean of 10, their total must be 50. You can choose the first 4 freely, but the 5th is then fixed. So there are 4 degrees of freedom. That is why the sample variance divides by n - 1, and why the t and chi-square for one sample use n - 1.

Real life example 1, a Dhaka city health survey: Suppose researchers want the average daily screen time of school children in Dhaka. A list of all children does not exist, but a list of schools does. They use cluster sampling: randomly pick 20 schools. Inside each school, they use stratified sampling by class (six to ten), randomly choosing some students from each class. Within each class, they might even use systematic sampling from the roll register, every 5th student from a random start. Real surveys often mix methods like this to balance cost and accuracy.

Real life example 2, quality control at a garment factory: A garment factory in Gazipur produces 5,000 shirts a day. Checking all of them is too slow, so inspectors take every 50th shirt from the line (systematic), giving 100 shirts. They measure the sleeve length of each. The specification says the mean should be 60 cm. Using the sample mean and sample standard deviation, they compute a t statistic with 99 degrees of freedom to decide if the machine needs adjustment. They also track the sample variance with a chi-square based chart to see if the stitching is becoming inconsistent.

Common mistakes: Confusing stratified and cluster sampling. Thinking that a larger biased sample is better than a smaller random one. Using z instead of t when sigma is unknown and n is small. Forgetting that the t, chi-square and F results above assume the population is normal. Mixing up the degrees of freedom: one sample t uses n - 1, F for two variances uses (n1 - 1, n2 - 1). Writing that chi-square can be negative, which is impossible because it is a sum of squares.

What exams usually ask: Define population, sample, parameter and statistic with examples. Explain and compare simple random, stratified, systematic and cluster sampling, with one advantage and one drawback each. Give examples of bias. Find the mean and standard error of x-bar or p-hat. State how the t, chi-square and F distributions are built, their degrees of freedom and their uses. Small numericals like listing all samples from a tiny population to build a sampling distribution.

Recap: A sample is only as good as the way it is chosen; randomness protects against bias, and a large size cannot cure bias. The four main methods are simple random, stratified, systematic and cluster sampling. Statistics such as x-bar and p-hat have sampling distributions with known centres and standard errors. When sigma is unknown we use t; for variances we use chi-square; for comparing variances we use F. These distributions are the tools for the estimation and testing lessons that come next.
key_points: Parameter = fixed, usually unknown population number; statistic = number computed from a sample, varies sample to sample.
Simple random: every group of size n equally likely; stratified: sample from every stratum; systematic: every k-th after a random start; cluster: pick whole groups at random.
Bias (selection, convenience, voluntary response, non-response, response) is not fixed by a bigger sample.
Sampling distribution of x-bar: mean mu, SE sigma / sqrt(n); of p-hat: mean p, SE sqrt(p(1-p)/n).
Chi-square with k df = sum of k squared standard normals; mean k, variance 2k; (n-1)s^2/sigma^2 ~ chi-square(n-1) for normal data.
t = (x-bar - mu)/(s/sqrt(n)) ~ t(n-1) for normal data; heavier tails than z, approaches z as df grows.
F = (U/d1)/(V/d2); s1^2/s2^2 ~ F(n1-1, n2-1) when normal variances are equal.
lessons.tip: Draw a tiny picture for each sampling method (dots in boxes). Stratified takes a few dots from every box; cluster takes all dots from a few boxes. The picture beats memorising definitions.
lessons.task: Take the population {1, 3, 5, 7}. List all 16 samples of size 2 with replacement, compute each mean, and check that the average of the means is 4 and that the means are less spread out than the original values.

quiz.q: A researcher randomly picks 8 of 120 villages and surveys every household in them. This is:
quiz.explain: Whole groups (villages) are chosen at random and everyone inside is measured: cluster sampling.

quiz.q: Which is a statistic?
quiz.explain: A statistic is computed from the sample; the others are population parameters.

quiz.q: Compared with the standard normal, the t distribution with 5 degrees of freedom has:
quiz.explain: t is symmetric around 0 but has heavier tails, especially at low degrees of freedom.

quiz.q: A chi-square distribution with 6 degrees of freedom has mean and variance:
quiz.explain: Chi-square with k df has mean k and variance 2k.

quiz.q: An online poll on a news site gets 50,000 votes. The main problem is:
quiz.explain: People choose themselves to respond, usually those with strong opinions, so the sample is biased no matter how large.

lessons.title: Point Estimation: Good Guesses from Data
lessons.content:
Imagine a jar full of marbles at a school fair, and the prize goes to whoever guesses closest to the number of marbles. You cannot count them, so you look, think, and write one number. That number is a point estimate: one single best guess for something you do not know. In statistics we do the same thing with data. The true average income in a district, the true chance that a website visitor clicks a button, the true failure rate of a hard disk: all unknown. We collect a sample and turn it into one best number. This lesson is about how to make that guess in a smart, fair way, and how to tell a good guessing rule from a bad one.

Parameter, estimator, estimate: The unknown number is a parameter, often written theta (a Greek letter). An estimator is a rule or formula that turns any sample into a guess, for example the rule 'add the values and divide by n'. Before the data arrive, an estimator is a random variable, written with a hat, like theta-hat. An estimate is the actual number you get when you plug in your data, for example 23.4. So the estimator is the recipe, and the estimate is the dish you cooked today. Exam questions love this difference.

Many estimators for the same thing: For the centre of a population, you could use the sample mean, the sample median, the midrange (average of the smallest and largest), or even just the first observation. All of these are estimators of mu. They are not equally good. To compare them, statisticians use a few properties: unbiasedness, efficiency (small variance), consistency, and the overall mean squared error.

Unbiasedness: An estimator theta-hat is unbiased if its expected value equals the true parameter: E[theta-hat] = theta. Its bias is E[theta-hat] - theta. Think of a dart player: unbiased means the darts are centred on the bull's-eye on average, even if each one misses a bit. The sample mean is unbiased for mu, because E[X-bar] = mu, as we showed in lesson 17. The sample proportion p-hat is unbiased for p. Even the single first observation X1 is unbiased, since E[X1] = mu, which shows unbiasedness alone is not enough.

Why the sample variance divides by n - 1: If you estimate the variance with (1/n) times the sum of (Xi - X-bar) squared, its expected value turns out to be ((n - 1)/n) sigma squared, which is a bit too small. The reason is that the deviations are measured from X-bar, which is pulled toward the data, so they look smaller than deviations from the true mu. Dividing by n - 1 instead fixes this: s squared = (1/(n - 1)) times the sum of (Xi - X-bar) squared has E[s squared] = sigma squared exactly. That is why calculators have two buttons, one for n and one for n - 1. Small note: s itself (the square root) is still slightly biased for sigma, but the bias is small.

Efficiency: Among unbiased estimators, we prefer the one with the smaller variance, because its guesses cluster more tightly around the truth. If theta1-hat and theta2-hat are both unbiased, the relative efficiency of theta1-hat to theta2-hat is Var(theta2-hat) / Var(theta1-hat). Example: X-bar has variance sigma squared / n, while X1 has variance sigma squared. So X-bar is n times as efficient. For a normal population with large n, the sample median has variance about (pi / 2) times sigma squared / n, which is roughly 1.57 times larger than the mean's, so the mean is more efficient there. For data with wild outliers, though, the median can win.

Mean squared error: Sometimes a slightly biased estimator with much smaller variance is better overall. The mean squared error combines both: MSE(theta-hat) = E[(theta-hat - theta) squared] = Var(theta-hat) + bias squared. Example: suppose estimator A is unbiased with variance 4, so MSE = 4. Estimator B has bias 1 and variance 2, so MSE = 2 + 1 = 3. B has lower MSE, so on average it lands closer to the truth, even though it is biased. This trade-off between bias and variance shows up again in machine learning as the famous bias-variance trade-off.

Consistency: An estimator is consistent if it gets closer and closer to the true value as the sample size grows, meaning P(|theta-hat - theta| > epsilon) goes to 0 for every epsilon greater than 0. A simple sufficient condition: if the bias and the variance both go to 0 as n grows, the estimator is consistent. X-bar is consistent because it is unbiased and its variance sigma squared / n goes to 0; this is just the law of large numbers. The silly estimator X1 is unbiased but not consistent, because its variance stays sigma squared no matter how much data you collect. The divide-by-n variance estimator is biased but still consistent, since its bias, minus sigma squared / n, vanishes.

Method of moments, the idea: The method of moments (MoM) is the oldest and simplest way to build estimators. Population moments, like E[X] and E[X squared], depend on the parameters. Sample moments, like (1/n) times the sum of Xi and (1/n) times the sum of Xi squared, are computed from data. The method says: set the sample moments equal to the population moments and solve for the parameters. You use as many moments as there are unknown parameters.

Method of moments, examples: For an exponential distribution with rate lambda, E[X] = 1 / lambda. Setting X-bar = 1 / lambda gives lambda-hat = 1 / X-bar. If customer waiting times are 2, 4 and 6 minutes, X-bar = 4, so lambda-hat = 0.25 per minute. For a uniform distribution on (0, theta), E[X] = theta / 2, so theta-hat = 2 X-bar. With data 2, 5, 3, X-bar = 10/3, so theta-hat is about 6.67. For a Poisson distribution, E[X] = lambda, so lambda-hat = X-bar. For a normal distribution, matching the first two moments gives mu-hat = X-bar and sigma squared hat = (1/n) times the sum of (Xi - X-bar) squared.

Maximum likelihood, the idea: Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE), made popular by Ronald Fisher in the 1920s, asks a different question: which value of the parameter makes the data I actually saw the most probable? The likelihood function is L(theta) = f(x1; theta) x f(x2; theta) x ... x f(xn; theta), the joint probability (or density) of your data, viewed as a function of theta. The MLE is the theta that makes L(theta) as large as possible. Because products are messy, we usually maximise the log-likelihood, ln L(theta), which turns the product into a sum and has its peak at the same place.

MLE example, a coin: You toss a coin 10 times and get 7 heads. With p = probability of heads, the likelihood is L(p) = p^7 (1 - p)^3 (the constant 10C7 does not affect where the peak is, so we can drop it). The log-likelihood is 7 ln p + 3 ln(1 - p). Take the derivative and set it to zero: 7/p - 3/(1 - p) = 0, so 7(1 - p) = 3p, so 7 = 10p, so p-hat = 0.7. In general, with x successes in n trials, the MLE is x / n, exactly the sample proportion your intuition would choose.

MLE example, Poisson: Suppose the number of emails you get per hour follows a Poisson distribution with mean lambda, and over n hours you observe counts x1, ..., xn. The log-likelihood is (sum of xi) ln lambda - n lambda minus terms not depending on lambda. The derivative is (sum of xi) / lambda - n. Setting it to zero gives lambda-hat = (sum of xi) / n = X-bar. If the counts over 4 hours are 3, 5, 2, 6, then lambda-hat = 16 / 4 = 4 emails per hour. For the exponential distribution, the same steps give lambda-hat = 1 / X-bar, the same answer as the method of moments.

MLE example, normal: For normal data, the MLE of mu is X-bar, and the MLE of sigma squared is (1/n) times the sum of (Xi - X-bar) squared, the divide-by-n version. So the MLE of the variance is slightly biased, but it is consistent. This is a good reminder that MLE does not always give unbiased estimators.

When MoM and MLE disagree: For a uniform distribution on (0, theta), the likelihood is 1 / theta^n as long as theta is at least as big as every data value, and 0 otherwise. 1 / theta^n gets bigger as theta gets smaller, so we push theta down as far as allowed: theta-hat = the maximum observation. With data 2, 5, 3 the MLE is 5, while the method of moments gave about 6.67. Notice the MoM answer can even be impossible: with data 1, 1, 10 it gives theta-hat = 8, but we already saw a 10. The MLE never makes that mistake here.

Nice properties of MLE: Under regularity conditions that hold for most common models, MLEs are consistent, approximately normal for large samples, and asymptotically efficient, meaning that with lots of data no other reasonable estimator has a smaller variance. They also have the invariance property: if theta-hat is the MLE of theta, then g(theta-hat) is the MLE of g(theta). For example, if the MLE of sigma squared is 9, the MLE of sigma is 3. The downside: MLE sometimes needs calculus or numerical optimisation, and it can be biased for small samples.

Real life example 1, the German tank problem: During World War II, the Allies wanted to know how many tanks Germany was producing. They noted the serial numbers on captured tanks. If tanks are numbered 1 to N and you see k serial numbers with the largest being m, the MLE of N is just m, which tends to underestimate. A better unbiased estimator is m + m/k - 1. Statisticians' estimates turned out to be much closer to the true production figures found after the war than the estimates from spy reports. A clever estimator beat secret agents.

Real life example 2, an online shop in Bangladesh: Suppose an e-commerce site in Dhaka shows a new 'Buy now' button to 2,000 visitors and 130 of them click. The MLE of the click rate is 130 / 2,000 = 0.065. The data team also models orders per minute during an Eid sale as Poisson; if 600 orders arrive in 60 minutes, lambda-hat = 10 orders per minute. They use these estimates to decide how many servers to run and how many delivery riders to book. Machine learning works the same way: training a logistic regression or a neural network classifier with cross-entropy loss is, under the hood, maximising a likelihood.

Common mistakes: Mixing up estimator (random rule) and estimate (fixed number). Thinking unbiased automatically means good; X1 is unbiased but terrible. Forgetting to take the log before differentiating, which makes the algebra painful. Forgetting to check that the stationary point is a maximum, or forgetting boundary cases like the uniform example, where the derivative never equals zero. Using n instead of n - 1 when the question asks for the unbiased sample variance.

What exams usually ask: Define unbiasedness, efficiency and consistency and give examples. Show that X-bar is unbiased and consistent for mu. Show that the divide-by-n variance is biased. Compute MSE from bias and variance. Find method of moments estimators for exponential, Poisson, uniform or normal. Find the MLE for Bernoulli, binomial, Poisson, exponential or normal, including the steps: write L, take ln, differentiate, set to zero, solve. Compare MoM and MLE for the uniform distribution.

Recap: A point estimate is one best guess for an unknown parameter, produced by an estimator. Good estimators are unbiased or nearly so, have small variance, and are consistent; MSE = variance + bias squared balances both. The method of moments matches sample moments to population moments. Maximum likelihood picks the parameter that makes the observed data most probable and usually gives excellent estimators for large samples. In the next lesson we go one step further and give a whole interval of plausible values, not just one number.
key_points: Estimator = rule (a random variable, theta-hat); estimate = the number you get from your data.
Unbiased: E[theta-hat] = theta; bias = E[theta-hat] - theta. X-bar and p-hat are unbiased.
s^2 with n - 1 is unbiased for sigma^2; dividing by n gives expected value ((n-1)/n) sigma^2.
Efficiency compares variances of unbiased estimators; MSE = variance + bias^2.
Consistent: theta-hat approaches theta as n grows; bias and variance both going to 0 is enough.
Method of moments: set sample moments equal to population moments and solve (exponential: 1/X-bar, uniform(0,theta): 2X-bar).
MLE: maximise L(theta) (usually ln L); Bernoulli x/n, Poisson X-bar, exponential 1/X-bar, uniform(0,theta) max value; invariance property.
lessons.tip: For every MLE problem follow the same four-step chant: write L, take ln, differentiate and set to zero, solve and check. Then sanity-check the answer against common sense.
lessons.task: Toss a coin (or a bottle cap) 20 times and record the results. Write the likelihood L(p), find the MLE p-hat = heads/20, and plot L(p) on paper for p = 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9 to see the peak.

quiz.q: Estimator A: bias 0, variance 5. Estimator B: bias 2, variance 0.5. Which has the smaller MSE?
quiz.explain: MSE = variance + bias^2. A: 5. B: 0.5 + 4 = 4.5.

quiz.q: You see 3 heads in 12 coin tosses. The MLE of p is:
quiz.explain: For a binomial/Bernoulli model the MLE is x/n = 3/12 = 0.25.

quiz.q: Why does the unbiased sample variance divide by n - 1?
options: Deviations from X-bar are on average too small, so dividing by n underestimates sigma^2
Because the data are always normal
quiz.explain: With n, E = ((n-1)/n) sigma^2; using n - 1 corrects this downward bias.

quiz.q: Waiting times 3, 5, 4 minutes are modelled as exponential. The MLE of the rate lambda is:
quiz.explain: For exponential, lambda-hat = 1 / X-bar = 1 / 4 = 0.25 per minute.

quiz.q: Data 2, 7, 4 from Uniform(0, theta). The MLE of theta is:
quiz.explain: The likelihood 1/theta^n is largest at the smallest allowed theta, which is the maximum value, 7. (MoM would give 2 x 13/3 = 8.67.)

lessons.title: Confidence Intervals
lessons.content:
Imagine you ask a friend what time the bus comes, and they say 'exactly 8:17'. That sounds precise, but it is almost certainly a bit wrong. If instead they say 'somewhere between 8:10 and 8:25, and I am pretty sure about that', you get something much more useful: a range plus a level of trust. A confidence interval is exactly that. Instead of one single guess, like in the last lesson, we give a range of plausible values for an unknown parameter, together with a confidence level such as 95 percent. News reports that say 'support is 52 percent, plus or minus 3 points' are giving you a confidence interval.

The general shape: Almost every confidence interval in this course has the same skeleton: estimate plus or minus (critical value) x (standard error). The estimate is your point estimate, like x-bar or p-hat. The standard error measures how much that estimate typically wobbles from sample to sample. The critical value comes from the z or t distribution and depends on how confident you want to be. The part after the plus-or-minus sign is called the margin of error. So: interval = estimate plus or minus margin of error.

Where the formula comes from: Suppose x-bar is normal with mean mu and standard error sigma / sqrt(n). Then Z = (x-bar - mu) / (sigma / sqrt(n)) is standard normal, and P(-1.96 < Z < 1.96) = 0.95. Rearranging the inequality to put mu in the middle gives P(x-bar - 1.96 sigma / sqrt(n) < mu < x-bar + 1.96 sigma / sqrt(n)) = 0.95. The random thing here is x-bar, so the interval moves around from sample to sample, while mu stays fixed.

What 95 percent confidence really means: This is the most misunderstood idea in the whole course. It means: if we repeated the sampling many times and built an interval each time, about 95 percent of those intervals would contain the true mu. It does NOT mean 'there is a 95 percent probability that mu lies in this particular interval'. Once you have computed, say, (68.1, 75.9), mu is either inside it or not; we just do not know which. Picture 100 students each taking their own sample and drawing their own interval on the board. About 95 of the intervals would cover the true value, and about 5 would miss. The confidence is in the method, not in any single result.

Critical values to remember: For z intervals, the common critical values are 1.645 for 90 percent, 1.96 for 95 percent and 2.576 for 99 percent. These are the points that cut off 5 percent, 2.5 percent and 0.5 percent in each tail. Higher confidence means a bigger critical value, so a wider interval. A 100 percent confidence interval would be the whole number line, which is perfectly safe but totally useless.

The z interval for a mean (sigma known): Use x-bar plus or minus z x sigma / sqrt(n) when the population standard deviation sigma is known, and either the population is normal or n is large enough for the central limit theorem. Example: battery life of a phone model has sigma = 14 hours. A test of n = 49 phones gives x-bar = 72 hours. Standard error = 14 / 7 = 2. For 95 percent, margin of error = 1.96 x 2 = 3.92. The interval is 72 plus or minus 3.92, so (68.08, 75.92) hours. In honest words: we are 95 percent confident the true mean battery life is between about 68 and 76 hours.

Knowing sigma is rare: In real life you almost never know the true sigma while not knowing mu. That is why the z interval for a mean is mostly a teaching step. For large samples (often n of at least 30) many books allow replacing sigma by s and still using z, because then t and z are very close. For small samples, use t.

The t interval for a mean (sigma unknown): Use x-bar plus or minus t x s / sqrt(n), where t is the critical value from the t distribution with n - 1 degrees of freedom. This assumes the data come from a roughly normal population, which matters most when n is small. Example: a programmer times a function 10 times and gets mean x-bar = 5.2 milliseconds with s = 0.8. Degrees of freedom = 9, and for 95 percent t is 2.262. Standard error = 0.8 / sqrt(10), about 0.253. Margin of error = 2.262 x 0.253, about 0.572. Interval: (4.63, 5.77) milliseconds. If we had wrongly used z = 1.96, the interval would be narrower than it should be, giving false confidence.

Why t is wider: With a small sample, s might be quite far from sigma, so there is extra uncertainty. The t distribution's heavier tails build that in with larger critical values. For 95 percent: 4 degrees of freedom gives 2.776, 9 gives 2.262, 29 gives 2.045, and as degrees of freedom grow, t moves down toward 1.96.

Interval for a proportion: For a population proportion p, use p-hat plus or minus z x sqrt(p-hat (1 - p-hat) / n). This relies on the normal approximation, so check that n p-hat and n (1 - p-hat) are both at least about 10 (some books say 5). Example: in a survey of 500 university students, 320 say they use mobile banking. p-hat = 320 / 500 = 0.64. Standard error = sqrt(0.64 x 0.36 / 500) = sqrt(0.0004608), about 0.0215. For 95 percent, margin of error = 1.96 x 0.0215, about 0.042. Interval: (0.598, 0.682), so between roughly 60 and 68 percent.

What controls the margin of error: Three things. First, the confidence level: higher confidence means a bigger critical value and a wider interval. Second, the spread of the data, sigma or s: more variable data means a wider interval. Third, the sample size n: a bigger n gives a narrower interval, but only through sqrt(n). To cut the margin of error in half you need four times as many observations. You cannot control sigma, so in practice you choose the confidence level and then pick n.

Choosing the sample size for a mean: Set the margin of error E = z sigma / sqrt(n) and solve for n: n = (z sigma / E) squared, then always round UP. Example: you want to estimate the average daily mobile data use of students within plus or minus 2 MB at 95 percent confidence, and a pilot study suggests sigma is about 15 MB. n = (1.96 x 15 / 2) squared = (14.7) squared = 216.09, so you need at least 217 students. Rounding down to 216 would make the margin slightly bigger than 2.

Choosing the sample size for a proportion: Here n = z squared p (1 - p) / E squared. The trouble is that p is unknown. If you have a rough guess, use it. If not, use p = 0.5, because p (1 - p) is largest at 0.5, so this gives the safest, biggest n. Example: a polling company wants a margin of error of 3 percentage points at 95 percent. n = 1.96 squared x 0.25 / 0.03 squared = 3.8416 x 0.25 / 0.0009, about 1,067.1, so 1,068 people. This is why so many national polls use about 1,000 to 1,500 people.

One-sided bounds, briefly: Sometimes only one direction matters. A food company might only care that the mean weight of a chips packet is at least some value. Then you build a one-sided lower bound, x-bar - z x sigma / sqrt(n), using the one-tailed critical value, which for 95 percent is 1.645 instead of 1.96. Most exam questions, though, are two-sided.

Link to hypothesis testing: Confidence intervals and the tests of the next lesson are two sides of the same coin. A 95 percent two-sided interval contains exactly those values of mu that a two-sided test at the 5 percent level would not reject. So if a 95 percent interval for the average delivery time is (31, 36) minutes, the claim 'the mean is 30 minutes' would be rejected at the 5 percent level, while 'the mean is 33 minutes' would not be.

Real life example 1, internet speed in your area: Suppose you run a speed test on your home broadband at 25 random times over two weeks and get an average download speed of 38 Mbps with s = 6 Mbps. Your provider advertises 40 Mbps. With 24 degrees of freedom, the 95 percent t critical value is about 2.064. Standard error = 6 / 5 = 1.2, margin of error = 2.064 x 1.2, about 2.48. Interval: (35.52, 40.48) Mbps. Because 40 lies inside the interval, the data do not give strong evidence that the true average is below the advertised speed. With 100 tests the interval would be about half as wide, and the answer might change.

Real life example 2, a vaccination survey in a district: A health team in Rangpur wants to know what fraction of children under five have had all their vaccines. They visit 600 randomly chosen households with young children and find 552 fully vaccinated. p-hat = 552 / 600 = 0.92. Standard error = sqrt(0.92 x 0.08 / 600), about 0.0111. The 95 percent margin of error is about 0.022, so the interval is roughly (0.898, 0.942). The team reports: about 90 to 94 percent coverage, and plans extra campaigns if the lower end falls below their target.

Interval for a difference, a peek: The same skeleton works for comparing two groups. For two independent means with known sigmas, the interval for mu1 - mu2 is (x-bar1 - x-bar2) plus or minus z x sqrt(sigma1 squared / n1 + sigma2 squared / n2). If such an interval contains 0, you cannot be confident that the two groups differ. Two-sample methods are covered properly in lesson 22.

Common mistakes: Saying 'there is a 95 percent chance mu is in this interval' for a computed interval. Using z when sigma is unknown and n is small. Using sigma / n instead of sigma / sqrt(n). Rounding the sample size down instead of up. Forgetting to check conditions: randomness, independence, approximate normality or a large enough n, and enough successes and failures for proportions. Believing a bigger sample removes bias; it only narrows the interval around a possibly biased centre.

What exams usually ask: Build a z interval and a t interval for a mean, and an interval for a proportion, with full working. Interpret the interval in words, correctly. Explain how the width changes with confidence level, sigma and n. Compute the minimum sample size for a given margin of error, for a mean and for a proportion (with p = 0.5 if no guess is given). Choose between z and t and justify it.

Recap: A confidence interval is estimate plus or minus critical value times standard error. Use z with known sigma (or large n), t with unknown sigma and n - 1 degrees of freedom, and p-hat plus or minus z sqrt(p-hat (1 - p-hat) / n) for proportions. The 95 percent describes how often the method captures the truth in repeated sampling. Margin of error shrinks with sqrt(n), so sample size formulas are n = (z sigma / E) squared and n = z squared p (1 - p) / E squared, always rounded up.
key_points: Confidence interval = estimate plus or minus (critical value) x (standard error); the second part is the margin of error.
95 percent confidence: about 95 percent of intervals built this way contain the true parameter; not a probability about one computed interval.
Mean, sigma known: x-bar plus or minus z sigma/sqrt(n); sigma unknown: x-bar plus or minus t s/sqrt(n) with n - 1 df.
Proportion: p-hat plus or minus z sqrt(p-hat(1 - p-hat)/n), needing enough successes and failures.
Width grows with confidence level and sigma, shrinks with sqrt(n).
Sample size: n = (z sigma / E)^2 for a mean, n = z^2 p(1 - p) / E^2 for a proportion (use p = 0.5 if unknown); always round up.
lessons.tip: Write the skeleton 'estimate +/- critical value x SE' at the top of every answer, then fill the three blanks. It keeps z, t and proportion problems from getting mixed up.
lessons.task: Ask 30 friends or classmates one yes/no question (for example, do you use bKash?). Compute p-hat, the standard error and a 95 percent confidence interval. Then work out how many people you would need for a margin of error of 5 points.

quiz.q: n = 64, x-bar = 50, sigma = 16. The 95 percent z interval is:
Which interpretation of a 95 percent CI is correct?
options: 95 percent of the data lie in the interval
There is a 95 percent chance mu is in this computed interval
The sample mean is in the interval 95 percent of the time
About 95 percent of intervals built by this method capture mu
quiz.explain: The confidence describes the long-run success rate of the method, not one fixed interval.

quiz.q: Keeping everything else fixed, to halve the margin of error you should:
quiz.explain: Margin is proportional to 1/sqrt(n), so halving it needs 4 times n.

quiz.q: For a t interval with n = 10, the degrees of freedom are:
quiz.explain: One-sample t uses n - 1 = 9 degrees of freedom.

quiz.q: With no prior guess, the sample size for a 95 percent interval for a proportion with margin 0.05 is:

lessons.title: Hypothesis Testing Basics
lessons.content:
Imagine a court case. A person is accused of stealing. The court starts by assuming the person is innocent. Then the prosecutor brings evidence. If the evidence is strong enough that innocence looks very hard to believe, the court says 'guilty'. If not, the court says 'not guilty', which is not the same as proving innocence; it only means the evidence was not strong enough. Hypothesis testing in statistics works exactly like this court. We start with a boring default claim, collect data as evidence, and only throw out the default if the data would be really surprising under it.

What a hypothesis is: A statistical hypothesis is a claim about a population parameter, such as 'the mean delivery time is 30 minutes' or 'this coin has p = 0.5'. It is about the population, never about the sample. We already know the sample mean; we have it in our hands. The question is always what the data say about the unknown truth behind them.

Null and alternative hypotheses: The null hypothesis, H0, is the default, 'nothing special is happening' claim. It always contains an equals sign, like H0: mu = 30 or H0: p = 0.5. The alternative hypothesis, H1 (also written Ha), is what you suspect or want to show, like H1: mu > 30, H1: mu < 30 or H1: mu is not equal to 30. In the court picture, H0 is 'innocent' and H1 is 'guilty'. Important: you choose H0 and H1 before looking at the data, based on the question you want to answer.

Two possible decisions: At the end of a test you either reject H0 (the data give enough evidence for H1) or fail to reject H0 (the evidence is not strong enough). Statisticians avoid saying 'accept H0', because not finding evidence against something does not prove it true. If you test a coin 10 times and get 6 heads, you fail to reject 'the coin is fair', but the coin might still be slightly biased; 10 tosses just could not tell.

The test statistic: A test statistic is a number computed from the sample that measures how far the data are from what H0 predicts, in units of standard error. The common shape is (estimate - value under H0) / standard error. For a mean with known sigma: z = (x-bar - mu0) / (sigma / sqrt(n)). For a proportion: z = (p-hat - p0) / sqrt(p0 (1 - p0) / n). Note that for proportions we use p0, the value under H0, inside the standard error, because we are asking what would happen if H0 were true. A test statistic near 0 means the data agree with H0; a big positive or negative value means they do not.

Significance level alpha: Before testing, you choose how much risk of a false alarm you will accept. This is the significance level, alpha, usually 0.05, sometimes 0.01 or 0.10. Alpha = 0.05 means: if H0 is actually true, we accept a 5 percent chance of wrongly rejecting it. Choosing alpha after seeing the data, to get the answer you like, is cheating.

The p-value: The p-value is the probability, assuming H0 is true, of getting a test statistic at least as extreme as the one you actually observed, in the direction of H1. A small p-value means: if H0 were true, data like ours would be rare, so H0 looks doubtful. The rule: if p-value is at most alpha, reject H0; otherwise fail to reject. The p-value is NOT the probability that H0 is true. It is a probability about the data, calculated assuming H0.

Worked example, a suspicious coin: You toss a coin 100 times and get 60 heads. Is the coin fair? H0: p = 0.5, H1: p is not 0.5 (two-tailed). Standard error under H0 = sqrt(0.5 x 0.5 / 100) = 0.05. Test statistic z = (0.60 - 0.50) / 0.05 = 2.0. The two-tailed p-value is P(|Z| >= 2) = 2 x 0.0228 = 0.0455. Since 0.0455 is less than 0.05, reject H0 at the 5 percent level: there is evidence the coin is not fair. At alpha = 0.01, though, 0.0455 is bigger than 0.01, so we would fail to reject. The conclusion depends on how strict you choose to be.

Critical region approach: Instead of the p-value, you can find the critical values that cut off an area alpha under H0 and reject if the test statistic falls beyond them. The set of values where you reject is the critical region or rejection region. For a two-tailed z test at alpha = 0.05, reject if z is less than -1.96 or greater than 1.96. For a right-tailed test at 0.05, reject if z is greater than 1.645; for a left-tailed test, if z is less than -1.645. In the coin example, z = 2.0 is beyond 1.96, so again reject. The p-value method and the critical value method always give the same decision; the p-value just also tells you how strong the evidence is.

One-tailed versus two-tailed: Use a one-tailed test when the question only cares about one direction, decided in advance. A rice company is accused of underfilling 5 kg bags: H0: mu = 5, H1: mu < 5 (left-tailed). A new app version is hoped to be faster: H1: mu_new < mu_old. Use a two-tailed test when any difference matters: 'is the machine out of calibration in either direction?' A one-tailed p-value is half the two-tailed one (for symmetric tests), which is why switching to one-tailed after seeing the data to get under 0.05 is a classic form of cheating.

Type I and Type II errors: There are two ways to be wrong. A Type I error is rejecting H0 when it is actually true, a false alarm, like convicting an innocent person. Its probability is alpha. A Type II error is failing to reject H0 when it is actually false, a missed detection, like letting a guilty person go. Its probability is called beta. A simple table helps: if H0 is true and you reject, Type I error; if H0 is true and you fail to reject, correct; if H0 is false and you reject, correct; if H0 is false and you fail to reject, Type II error.

The trade-off: For a fixed sample size, making alpha smaller (being stricter about false alarms) makes beta bigger (you miss more real effects). A court that demands extremely strong evidence convicts fewer innocent people but also frees more guilty ones. The only way to reduce both errors at the same time is to collect more data, or reduce noise in the measurements.

Power: The power of a test is 1 - beta, the probability of correctly rejecting H0 when a particular alternative is true. High power means the test is good at catching real effects. Power increases when the true effect is bigger, when the sample size n is larger, when the data are less noisy (smaller sigma), and when alpha is larger. Researchers often design studies to have at least 80 percent power for the smallest effect they care about.

Worked example, computing power: A machine should fill bottles with mu = 100 ml, sigma = 15, and we test n = 25 bottles with H0: mu = 100 against H1: mu > 100 at alpha = 0.05. Standard error = 15 / 5 = 3. We reject if x-bar is greater than 100 + 1.645 x 3 = 104.935. Suppose the true mean is actually 106. Then the chance of rejecting is P(x-bar > 104.935) = P(Z > (104.935 - 106) / 3) = P(Z > -0.355), about 0.64. So power is about 64 percent and beta about 36 percent. With n = 100 the standard error drops to 1.5, the cut-off becomes about 102.47, and the power rises to about P(Z > -2.35), roughly 99 percent.

The steps of any test: First, state H0 and H1. Second, choose alpha. Third, check the conditions (random sample, independence, normality or large n). Fourth, compute the test statistic. Fifth, find the p-value or compare with the critical value. Sixth, decide: reject or fail to reject H0. Seventh, write the conclusion in plain words about the real problem, not just 'reject H0'. Examiners give marks for every step, so write them all.

Statistical versus practical significance: With a huge sample, even a tiny, unimportant difference can give a very small p-value. If a new website design increases average time on page from 120.0 to 120.3 seconds, a test with millions of visitors might call it 'significant', but nobody cares about 0.3 seconds. Always look at the size of the effect too, for example with a confidence interval. Statistically significant means 'unlikely to be pure chance', not 'big' or 'important'.

Real life example 1, A/B testing in a Bangladeshi app: A food delivery app in Dhaka tests a new checkout button. The old button has a known order completion rate of 0.20. The new design is shown to 1,600 users and 352 complete orders, p-hat = 0.22. H0: p = 0.20, H1: p > 0.20, alpha = 0.05. Standard error under H0 = sqrt(0.2 x 0.8 / 1,600) = 0.01. z = (0.22 - 0.20) / 0.01 = 2.0. The one-tailed p-value is about 0.0228, which is less than 0.05, so they reject H0 and conclude the new button likely improves completions. (Real A/B tests usually compare two groups at once, which is the two-sample test of the next lesson.)

Real life example 2, spam and medical screening: A spam filter is like a hypothesis test for each email, with H0 being 'this email is normal'. A Type I error sends an important job offer email to spam; a Type II error lets a scam email into your inbox. A medical screening test for a disease has H0 'the person is healthy'. A Type I error is a false positive that causes worry and more tests; a Type II error is a missed case. Designers choose the threshold based on which error is more costly, exactly like choosing alpha.

The multiple testing trap: If you run 20 independent tests at alpha = 0.05 when every H0 is true, you expect about one false 'significant' result just by chance. The chance of at least one false alarm is 1 - 0.95^20, about 0.64. Running many tests and only reporting the significant ones is called p-hacking. A simple fix is the Bonferroni correction: with m tests, use alpha / m for each.

Common mistakes: Saying the p-value is the probability that H0 is true. Writing 'accept H0'. Putting the claim you want to prove into H0. Writing hypotheses about sample statistics, like H0: x-bar = 30, instead of parameters. Choosing one-tailed after looking at the data. Mixing up Type I and Type II errors. Forgetting to state the conclusion in the context of the problem.

What exams usually ask: Define null and alternative hypotheses, test statistic, critical region, significance level, p-value, Type I and Type II errors and power. Set up H0 and H1 from a word problem and decide one- or two-tailed. Carry out a simple z test for a mean or proportion with both the p-value and the critical value methods. Compute beta and power for a given alternative. Explain the trade-off between alpha and beta.

Recap: Hypothesis testing is a court case for a claim. H0 is the default with an equals sign; H1 is what you suspect. A test statistic measures how far the data are from H0 in standard errors. Reject H0 when the p-value is at most alpha, or equivalently when the statistic falls in the critical region. Type I error (probability alpha) is a false alarm; Type II error (probability beta) is a miss; power = 1 - beta grows with sample size and effect size. In the next lesson we apply this recipe to the most common real tests: z, t, paired and proportion tests.
key_points: H0 is the default claim with an equals sign; H1 is what you suspect; both are about population parameters and set before seeing data.
Decision: reject H0 or fail to reject H0; never 'accept H0'.
Test statistic = (estimate - value under H0) / standard error.
p-value = P(data at least this extreme | H0 true); reject H0 if p-value <= alpha. It is not P(H0 true).
Critical values for z at alpha = 0.05: two-tailed +/-1.96, one-tailed 1.645.
Type I error = rejecting a true H0 (probability alpha); Type II error = not rejecting a false H0 (probability beta).
Power = 1 - beta; it grows with larger n, larger effect, smaller sigma and larger alpha.
lessons.tip: Always say the court analogy to yourself: H0 is 'innocent until proven guilty'. It instantly tells you which hypothesis gets the equals sign, why we never 'accept' H0, and which error is which.
lessons.task: Toss a coin 50 times and count heads. Test H0: p = 0.5 against a two-sided H1 at alpha = 0.05: compute z = (p-hat - 0.5)/sqrt(0.25/50), compare with 1.96, and write a one-sentence conclusion.

quiz.q: A Type I error is:
options: Failing to reject a false H0
quiz.explain: Type I error = false alarm, rejecting H0 when it is true; its probability is alpha.

quiz.q: A test gives p-value = 0.03. At alpha = 0.01 you should:
quiz.explain: 0.03 is greater than 0.01, so the evidence is not strong enough at that level.

quiz.q: A company is accused of underfilling 1 kg sugar packets. The right hypotheses are:
quiz.explain: H0 has the equals sign and is about the parameter mu; the suspicion is underfilling, so H1: mu < 1.

quiz.q: Which change increases the power of a test (all else fixed)?
quiz.explain: A bigger n shrinks the standard error, making real effects easier to detect.

lessons.title: Tests for Means and Proportions
lessons.content:
Imagine a chips company prints "50 g" on every packet. You buy 36 packets from shops in Mirpur, weigh them on a kitchen scale, and the average comes out to 49.2 g. Is the company cheating, or is this just bad luck in your sample? A difference of 0.8 g feels small, but feelings are not proof. In the last lesson we learned the logic of hypothesis testing: start from a null hypothesis, measure how surprising the data is, and reject the null only when the surprise is big enough. In this lesson we put that logic to work on real numbers. We will learn the tests you will use most often: the one-sample z test, the one-sample t test, the two-sample t test, the paired t test and the test for a proportion.

The common recipe: Every test in this lesson follows the same six steps, so learn the steps once and reuse them. Step 1: write H0 and H1. Step 2: choose the significance level alpha, usually 0.05. Step 3: pick the right test and check its conditions. Step 4: compute the test statistic. Step 5: find the critical value or the p-value. Step 6: make a decision (reject H0 or fail to reject H0) and write the conclusion in plain words about the real problem.

The shape of every test statistic: Almost all the statistics here have the same form: (estimate - value claimed by H0) / (standard error of the estimate). The top tells you how far the data is from the claim. The bottom tells you how much wobble you would expect just from random sampling. So the statistic counts "how many standard errors away" the data is. A value near 0 means the data agrees with H0. A value far from 0, like 3 or -3, means the data would be very rare if H0 were true.

One-sample z test for a mean: Use it when you want to compare one sample mean with a claimed value mu0, and the population standard deviation sigma is known (or the sample is large and you treat s as sigma, which many textbooks allow for n of about 30 or more). The statistic is z = (xbar - mu0) / (sigma / sqrt(n)). Under H0 it follows the standard normal distribution. Critical values at alpha = 0.05 are plus or minus 1.96 for a two-tailed test, 1.645 for a right-tailed test and -1.645 for a left-tailed test.

Worked example, the chips packet: Suppose the company says mu = 50 g and from years of quality data we know sigma = 2 g. We weighed n = 36 packets and got xbar = 49.2 g. Step 1: H0: mu = 50, H1: mu is not 50 (two-tailed, since we only ask whether the weight is different). Step 2: alpha = 0.05. Step 3: sigma known, so z test. Step 4: standard error = 2 / sqrt(36) = 2/6 = 0.333. z = (49.2 - 50) / 0.333 = -2.4. Step 5: |z| = 2.4 is bigger than 1.96, so it is in the rejection region. The p-value is 2 x P(Z < -2.4) = 2 x 0.0082 = about 0.016. Step 6: reject H0. In plain words: at the 5% level, the data gives evidence that the average packet weight is not 50 g.

One-sample t test: In real life you almost never know sigma. You only have the sample standard deviation s. When you replace sigma by s, the statistic gets extra wobble, especially for small samples, so it no longer follows the normal curve. It follows Student's t distribution with n - 1 degrees of freedom: t = (xbar - mu0) / (s / sqrt(n)). The t curve looks like the normal curve but with fatter tails, so its critical values are bigger. As n grows, t gets closer and closer to z. The condition: the data should come from a roughly normal population, or n should be large enough that the CLT helps.

Worked example, study hours: A teacher believes students at her college study 50 minutes a day on average. A sample of n = 16 students gives xbar = 52 minutes and s = 4 minutes. H0: mu = 50, H1: mu is not 50, alpha = 0.05. Standard error = 4 / sqrt(16) = 4/4 = 1. t = (52 - 50) / 1 = 2.0, with df = 15. From the t table, the two-tailed critical value for df = 15 at 0.05 is 2.131. Since 2.0 < 2.131, we fail to reject H0. Now notice something interesting: if the question had been one-tailed (H1: mu > 50), the critical value would be 1.753, and 2.0 > 1.753, so we would reject. The same data can give different decisions depending on the alternative, which is exactly why you must choose H1 before looking at the data, not after.

Two-sample t test (independent groups): Now we compare two separate groups, like students taught with method A and students taught with method B. H0: mu1 = mu2 (or mu1 - mu2 = 0). The statistic is t = (xbar1 - xbar2) / SE, where SE is the standard error of the difference. There are two common versions. The pooled version assumes both groups have the same population variance. It first combines the variances: sp^2 = ((n1 - 1) s1^2 + (n2 - 1) s2^2) / (n1 + n2 - 2), then SE = sp x sqrt(1/n1 + 1/n2), with df = n1 + n2 - 2. The Welch version does not assume equal variances: SE = sqrt(s1^2/n1 + s2^2/n2), and the degrees of freedom come from a longer formula (software computes it). Many statisticians use Welch by default because it stays safe when the variances differ.

Worked example, two coaching centres: Coaching centre A has n1 = 10 students with mean test score 75 and s1 = 8. Centre B has n2 = 12 students with mean 68 and s2 = 6. Is there a real difference? H0: mu1 = mu2, H1: mu1 is not mu2, alpha = 0.05. Pooled variance: sp^2 = (9 x 64 + 11 x 36) / 20 = (576 + 396) / 20 = 972 / 20 = 48.6, so sp = about 6.97. SE = 6.97 x sqrt(1/10 + 1/12) = 6.97 x sqrt(0.1833) = 6.97 x 0.428 = about 2.98. t = (75 - 68) / 2.98 = about 2.35, with df = 20. Critical value at df = 20 is 2.086. Since 2.35 > 2.086, reject H0. Plain words: the average scores of the two centres differ at the 5% level. Careful though: this does not prove centre A teaches better. Maybe stronger students chose A in the first place.

Paired t test: Sometimes the two sets of numbers are not independent. The same person is measured twice (before and after a training), or two things are matched in pairs (left hand vs right hand, the same program on two computers). Then the right move is to take the difference d for each pair and do a one-sample t test on those differences, with H0: mean difference = 0. The statistic is t = dbar / (s_d / sqrt(n)), with df = n - 1, where n is the number of pairs. Pairing removes the person-to-person variation, so a paired test is often much more powerful than treating the data as two independent groups.

Worked example, typing speed: Five students take a typing test, practise for a week, then take it again. Their improvements (after minus before, in words per minute) are 3, 5, 2, 4, 6. The mean difference is dbar = 20 / 5 = 4. Deviations from 4 are -1, 1, -2, 0, 2; their squares add to 1 + 1 + 4 + 0 + 4 = 10. So s_d^2 = 10 / 4 = 2.5 and s_d = about 1.58. SE = 1.58 / sqrt(5) = 1.58 / 2.236 = about 0.707. t = 4 / 0.707 = about 5.66, with df = 4. The two-tailed critical value at df = 4 is 2.776. Since 5.66 is far beyond it, reject H0: practice really changed the speed. If you wrongly used a two-sample test here, the large differences between students (some type 20 wpm, some 60) would hide the small but steady improvement.

Test for one proportion: Many questions are about percentages, not averages. What fraction of students use bKash? What fraction of bulbs are defective? Let p0 be the claimed proportion and p-hat = x / n the sample proportion. The statistic is z = (p-hat - p0) / sqrt(p0 (1 - p0) / n). Notice we use p0 (not p-hat) inside the square root, because we compute the standard error assuming H0 is true. The condition: n p0 and n (1 - p0) should both be at least about 10 (some books say 5), so that the normal approximation to the binomial works.

Worked example, mobile banking: A report claims 60% of university students use bKash weekly. You survey n = 200 students and 132 say yes, so p-hat = 0.66. Check: 200 x 0.6 = 120 and 200 x 0.4 = 80, both at least 10. SE = sqrt(0.6 x 0.4 / 200) = sqrt(0.0012) = about 0.0346. z = (0.66 - 0.60) / 0.0346 = about 1.73. For a two-tailed test at 0.05, the critical value is 1.96, and 1.73 < 1.96, so we fail to reject H0. The p-value is about 2 x 0.042 = 0.084. In plain words: 66% looks higher than 60%, but with 200 people that gap could easily be chance. With a bigger sample, the same 6-point gap might become significant.

Choosing the right test, a quick map: Ask three questions. Is the data a mean (numbers) or a proportion (yes/no)? How many groups: one, two independent, or two paired? Is sigma known? Means with sigma known: z test. Means with sigma unknown: t test (one-sample, two-sample or paired). Proportions: z test for proportion. More than two groups: that needs ANOVA, which comes in the next lesson along with chi-square tests for categories.

Real life example 1, internet speed: A broadband company in Chattogram advertises 20 Mbps. A student runs a speed test at 9 pm every night for 25 nights and gets an average of 18.6 Mbps with s = 3 Mbps. H0: mu = 20, H1: mu < 20 (a one-tailed test, because the worry is only about getting less). SE = 3 / 5 = 0.6. t = (18.6 - 20) / 0.6 = about -2.33 with df = 24. The one-tailed critical value at 0.05 is -1.711. Since -2.33 < -1.711, reject H0. The student now has a number-based complaint, not just "my net feels slow".

Real life example 2, software performance: A developer changes a sorting function in an app and wants to know whether it is faster. She runs the same 10 input files with the old code and the new code on the same laptop and records the time for each file. Because each file is measured twice, this is paired data. She computes the 10 differences (old minus new) and runs a paired t test with df = 9. If the mean saving is significantly above 0, she can ship the change with confidence. If she had run the old code on 10 files and the new code on 10 different files, the natural difference in file sizes would drown out the effect.

Common mistakes: Using z when sigma is unknown and n is small (use t). Using a two-sample test on paired data, or a paired test on independent groups. Using p-hat instead of p0 in the standard error of a one-proportion test. Picking one-tailed after seeing which way the data points, which doubles your real Type I error rate. Writing "accept H0". Forgetting the plain-language conclusion. And confusing statistical significance with practical importance: with a huge sample, a 0.1 g difference in chips weight may be significant but nobody cares.

What exams ask: A typical question gives a short story with numbers and says "test at the 5% level". You must state H0 and H1, name the test, compute the statistic, show the critical value from a table, and conclude. Other favourites: explain why t is used instead of z; explain the difference between paired and independent samples with an example; compute a p-value from a z score; and state the conditions for the proportion test.

Recap: Every test follows the same recipe: hypotheses, alpha, choose the test, compute the statistic, compare with a critical value or p-value, conclude in words. The statistic is always (estimate - claim) / standard error. Use z when sigma is known, t with n - 1 degrees of freedom when it is not. For two independent groups use the two-sample t test (pooled or Welch). For before-after or matched data, take differences and use a paired t test. For percentages use z = (p-hat - p0) / sqrt(p0(1 - p0)/n). Next, we move on to tests for categories and for many groups at once: chi-square and ANOVA.
key_points: Every test: hypotheses, alpha, choose test, compute statistic, compare with critical value or p-value, conclude in plain words.
Test statistic = (estimate - claimed value) / standard error.
One-sample z test: z = (xbar - mu0)/(sigma/sqrt(n)) when sigma is known; critical values 1.96 (two-tailed) and 1.645 (one-tailed) at 5%.
One-sample t test: t = (xbar - mu0)/(s/sqrt(n)) with n - 1 degrees of freedom when sigma is unknown.
Two independent groups: two-sample t test, pooled (equal variances, df = n1 + n2 - 2) or Welch (unequal variances).
Paired data (before/after, matched): take differences and run a one-sample t test on them.
One proportion: z = (p-hat - p0)/sqrt(p0(1 - p0)/n), needing n p0 and n(1 - p0) of at least about 10.
Say 'fail to reject H0', never 'accept H0', and remember significant is not the same as important.
lessons.tip: Before touching any formula, write one line: 'means or proportions, how many groups, paired or not, sigma known or not'. That line picks the test for you.
lessons.task: Time how long it takes you to walk a fixed route (or solve 5 sums) on 6 days this week, then 6 days next week after a small change. Treat the days as pairs, compute the differences, and run a paired t test by hand with df = 5 (critical value 2.571).
