quiz.explain: Sigma is unknown and n is small, so use t with n - 1 = 8 degrees of freedom.

quiz.q: With sigma = 2, n = 36, xbar = 49.2 and mu0 = 50, what is z?
The same students are tested before and after a course. Which test should you use?
options: Paired t test on the differences
quiz.explain: Measurements come in pairs from the same person, so take differences and use a paired t test.

quiz.q: In the one-proportion z test, the standard error uses:
quiz.explain: We assume H0 is true when computing the test's standard error, so p0 goes inside the root.

quiz.q: A t test gives t = 2.0 with df = 15. Two-tailed critical value is 2.131, one-tailed is 1.753. What is true?
options: Fail to reject H0 in both cases
Reject only if the one-tailed H1 was chosen before seeing the data
quiz.explain: 2.0 is below 2.131 but above 1.753; a one-tailed test is fair only if H1 was set in advance.

lessons.title: Chi-square Tests and ANOVA
lessons.content:
Imagine a sweet shop in Old Dhaka sells four kinds of mishti: roshogolla, chomchom, kalojam and shondesh. The owner thinks all four are equally popular, so he makes the same amount of each every morning. But at night some trays are empty and some are half full. Is his idea wrong, or is it just a random day? The tests in the last lesson worked with averages and single percentages. Here the data is different: it is counts in categories. For that we need the chi-square test. And when we want to compare the averages of three or more groups at once, we need ANOVA. Both are workhorses of real data analysis.

Categorical data and counts: Categorical data tells you which box each item falls in: blood group, favourite mishti, mobile operator, department. You cannot take an average of "Grameenphone" and "Robi". What you can do is count how many items fall in each box. These counts are called observed counts, written O. The chi-square idea is simple: compare the observed counts with the counts you would expect if H0 were true, called expected counts, written E. If O and E are close, H0 looks fine. If they are far apart, H0 looks wrong.

The chi-square statistic: For every category (or every cell of a table) compute (O - E)^2 / E, then add them all: chi-square = sum of (O - E)^2 / E. Squaring makes every gap positive, so gaps in opposite directions do not cancel. Dividing by E makes the gap relative: being 10 away from an expected 20 is a big deal, but being 10 away from an expected 1,000 is tiny. The statistic is always 0 or bigger, and it is 0 only when every O equals its E.

The chi-square distribution: When H0 is true and the expected counts are not too small, this statistic follows a chi-square distribution. That distribution lives only on positive numbers and is skewed to the right. It has one parameter, the degrees of freedom (df), and its mean equals df. Since big values mean a bad fit, chi-square tests are always right-tailed: we reject H0 when the statistic is larger than the critical value from the chi-square table. Handy values at alpha = 0.05: df 1 gives 3.841, df 2 gives 5.991, df 3 gives 7.815, df 4 gives 9.488 and df 5 gives 11.070.

Goodness of fit test: This test asks whether one categorical variable follows a claimed distribution. H0 says the population proportions are p1, p2, ..., pk. The expected count for category i is E = n x pi, where n is the total count. The degrees of freedom are k - 1 (the number of categories minus one), and you subtract one more for every parameter you had to estimate from the data. The minus one exists because once you know k - 1 of the counts and the total, the last count is fixed.

Worked example, is the die fair: You roll a die 60 times and get the faces 1 to 6 this many times: 8, 12, 9, 11, 6, 14. If the die is fair, each face is expected 60 x 1/6 = 10 times. The gaps O - E are -2, 2, -1, 1, -4, 4. Squares: 4, 4, 1, 1, 16, 16. Divide each by 10 and add: (4 + 4 + 1 + 1 + 16 + 16) / 10 = 42 / 10 = 4.2. df = 6 - 1 = 5, and the critical value is 11.070. Since 4.2 < 11.07, we fail to reject H0. These counts are quite normal for a fair die; 6 and 14 look uneven but random rolls do that all the time.

Back to the mishti shop: Suppose on one day he sold 200 pieces in total: 70 roshogolla, 50 chomchom, 30 kalojam and 50 shondesh. H0: all four equally popular, so E = 50 each. Contributions: (70 - 50)^2/50 = 8, (50 - 50)^2/50 = 0, (30 - 50)^2/50 = 8, 0. Total chi-square = 16, with df = 3. Critical value 7.815. Since 16 > 7.815, reject H0. Roshogolla is more popular and kalojam less, so he should change his morning batch sizes.

Contingency tables: Often we have two categorical variables for each person, like department (CSE or EEE) and whether they prefer online classes (yes or no). We arrange the counts in a table with rows for one variable and columns for the other. This is a contingency table, or cross-tab. A 2 x 2 table has 4 cells; a 3 x 4 table has 12. We add row totals, column totals and the grand total around the edges.

Test of independence: H0 says the two variables are independent, meaning knowing one tells you nothing about the other. H1 says they are associated. If they really were independent, the expected count in a cell would be E = (row total x column total) / grand total. The reason comes from the multiplication rule for independent events: P(row and column) = P(row) x P(column). The statistic is the same sum of (O - E)^2 / E over all cells, and df = (rows - 1) x (columns - 1).

Worked example, online classes: A survey of 200 students gives this table. CSE: 60 yes, 40 no (row total 100). EEE: 30 yes, 70 no (row total 100). Column totals: 90 yes, 110 no. Expected counts: CSE yes = 100 x 90 / 200 = 45, CSE no = 100 x 110 / 200 = 55, EEE yes = 45, EEE no = 55. Every gap is 15 in size. Contributions: 225/45 = 5, 225/55 = about 4.09, 5, 4.09. Total chi-square = about 18.18. df = (2 - 1)(2 - 1) = 1, critical value 3.841. Since 18.18 is far above 3.841, reject H0: preference for online classes depends on department. Note that this tells us there is a link, not why.

Conditions for chi-square tests: The data must be counts (not percentages or averages), each person counted once, and the observations independent. The common rule of thumb is that every expected count should be at least 5. If some are smaller, you can merge neighbouring categories, or for a 2 x 2 table use Fisher's exact test. Some books also apply Yates' continuity correction to 2 x 2 tables, which subtracts 0.5 from each |O - E| before squaring.

Why not just do many t tests: Now switch to numbers. Suppose you want to compare the average marks of students from three coaching centres A, B and C. You could do three t tests: A vs B, A vs C, B vs C. But each test has a 5% chance of a false alarm. With three tests, the chance of at least one false alarm can grow to about 1 - 0.95^3 = 0.143, roughly 14%. With ten groups it gets much worse. ANOVA (analysis of variance) answers the question with one single test.

The ANOVA idea: H0: mu1 = mu2 = ... = mu_k (all group means are equal). H1: at least one mean is different. The clever trick is to look at variance in two places. Between-group variation measures how far the group means are from the overall (grand) mean. Within-group variation measures how spread out the values are inside each group. If the groups truly have the same mean, the between part should be about as big as the within part. If the between part is much bigger, the group means really differ.

The pieces of one-way ANOVA: The total sum of squares SST adds (each value - grand mean)^2. It splits exactly into two parts: SST = SSB + SSW. SSB (between) adds n_i x (group mean - grand mean)^2 for each group. SSW (within) adds (each value - its own group mean)^2. Degrees of freedom: between is k - 1, within is N - k, where N is the total number of values. Mean squares are MSB = SSB / (k - 1) and MSW = SSW / (N - k). Finally F = MSB / MSW, which follows an F distribution with (k - 1, N - k) degrees of freedom under H0. Like chi-square, the test is right-tailed.

Worked example, three small groups: Group A scores 5, 6, 7 (mean 6). Group B scores 8, 9, 10 (mean 9). Group C scores 11, 12, 13 (mean 12). The grand mean is 9. SSB = 3 x ((6 - 9)^2 + (9 - 9)^2 + (12 - 9)^2) = 3 x (9 + 0 + 9) = 54. Inside each group the deviations are -1, 0, 1, giving 2 per group, so SSW = 6. Check: SST adds the squares 16, 9, 4, 1, 0, 1, 4, 9, 16 = 60 = 54 + 6. df between = 2, df within = 9 - 3 = 6. MSB = 54/2 = 27, MSW = 6/6 = 1, so F = 27. The critical value F(2, 6) at 0.05 is 5.14. Since 27 > 5.14, reject H0: the groups do not all have the same mean.

After ANOVA: A significant F only says that at least one mean differs. It does not say which. To find out, statisticians run post-hoc tests such as Tukey's HSD, which compare pairs while keeping the overall false alarm rate at 5%. ANOVA also has conditions: independent observations, roughly normal data in each group, and roughly equal variances across groups. With only two groups, one-way ANOVA gives exactly the same answer as the pooled two-sample t test, because F = t^2.

Real life example 1, rice fertilizer: Agricultural researchers in Bangladesh often test fertilizers on rice. Suppose three fertilizers are each used on 5 equal plots, and the yield of each plot is measured in kg. One-way ANOVA compares the three average yields at once. If F is significant, a Tukey test can show which fertilizer beats which. The farmer in Mymensingh then gets advice based on evidence, not on a salesman's promise.

Real life example 2, app bug reports: A software team gets bug reports from Android, iOS and web users and labels each as crash, slow or visual. They build a 3 x 3 contingency table and run a chi-square test of independence with df = (3 - 1)(3 - 1) = 4, critical value 9.488. If chi-square is large, the type of bug depends on the platform, perhaps the Android app crashes more. That tells the team where to spend testing time. The same test is used to check whether a click on an ad is linked to the user's city, or whether exam pass rates are linked to school type.

Common mistakes: Running chi-square on percentages instead of raw counts (the result changes with sample size, so you must use counts). Forgetting that expected counts should be at least 5. Using the wrong df: k - 1 for goodness of fit, (r - 1)(c - 1) for independence. Treating chi-square as two-tailed; it is right-tailed. In ANOVA, concluding that every mean differs when F is significant, or doing many t tests instead of one ANOVA. And as always, an association is not proof of cause.

What exams ask: Fill in expected counts in a contingency table and compute chi-square; test whether a die or a coin is fair; test a claimed ratio such as 9:3:3:1 in genetics; complete a partly filled ANOVA table (SS, df, MS, F) and conclude; explain why ANOVA is better than multiple t tests; and state the conditions of each test.

Recap: Chi-square tests work on counts in categories: chi-square = sum of (O - E)^2 / E, right-tailed, with expected counts at least 5. Goodness of fit checks one variable against a claimed distribution with df = k - 1. The test of independence uses E = row total x column total / grand total and df = (r - 1)(c - 1). One-way ANOVA compares many means with one test using F = MSB / MSW, where SST = SSB + SSW. A big F means at least one mean differs; post-hoc tests say which. Next we look at how two numeric variables move together: correlation and regression.
key_points: Chi-square = sum of (O - E)^2 / E; it works on counts in categories and is always right-tailed.
Goodness of fit: E = n x p for each category, df = k - 1 (minus one more per estimated parameter).
Test of independence: E = row total x column total / grand total, df = (r - 1)(c - 1).
Expected counts should be at least 5; otherwise merge categories or use Fisher's exact test.
Many t tests inflate false alarms; one-way ANOVA tests H0: all means equal in one go.
SST = SSB + SSW; F = MSB / MSW with (k - 1, N - k) degrees of freedom.
A significant F says at least one mean differs; post-hoc tests like Tukey's HSD say which.
lessons.tip: For chi-square, always draw the table of O and E side by side before computing. For ANOVA, always check SST = SSB + SSW; if it does not add up, you made an arithmetic slip.
lessons.task: Ask 30 friends or classmates their favourite of 3 snacks (for example singara, samosa, puri). Test with a goodness of fit test whether all three are equally popular (E = 10 each, df = 2, critical value 5.991).

lessons.title: Correlation and Regression
lessons.content:
Imagine you ride rickshaws all over Dhaka for a month and write down the distance and the fare each time. Longer trips cost more, of course, but not exactly in a straight line: some rickshawalas bargain hard, some trips are uphill, some are at night. Still, if you plot the points, you will see a clear upward trend. Two big questions come out of this. How strongly are distance and fare linked? That is correlation. And if I know the distance of a new trip, what fare should I expect? That is regression. These two ideas are among the most used tools in all of statistics, and simple linear regression is the very first model you meet in machine learning.

Two numeric variables: In earlier lessons we studied one variable at a time, and in the joint distributions lesson we met covariance and correlation for random variables. Now we work with real paired data: n pairs (x1, y1), (x2, y2), ..., (xn, yn). Usually x is the explanatory variable (the one we think helps predict) and y is the response variable (the one we want to predict). In the rickshaw case, x = distance and y = fare.

Scatter plots: Always start by drawing. Put x on the horizontal axis and y on the vertical axis and draw a dot for each pair. Look for four things: direction (upward means positive, downward means negative), form (a straight line or a curve), strength (dots tight around a line or loosely scattered), and outliers (a dot far away from the rest). A scatter plot can save you from big mistakes, because numbers like r can hide curves and outliers.

The building blocks: Let xbar and ybar be the means. Define three sums. Sxx = sum of (x - xbar)^2, which measures the spread of x. Syy = sum of (y - ybar)^2, the spread of y. Sxy = sum of (x - xbar)(y - ybar), which measures how x and y move together. When a big x usually comes with a big y, both brackets are positive or both negative together, so the products are positive and Sxy is positive. When big x comes with small y, Sxy is negative.

Pearson's correlation coefficient: r = Sxy / sqrt(Sxx x Syy). It always lies between -1 and 1. r = 1 means all points lie exactly on an upward straight line; r = -1 means exactly on a downward line; r near 0 means no straight-line pattern. Roughly, |r| above 0.7 is often called strong, 0.3 to 0.7 moderate and below 0.3 weak, though these labels depend on the field. r has no units, so it does not change if you measure distance in km or metres. It is symmetric: the correlation of x with y equals that of y with x.

Worked example, study hours and marks: Five students report hours studied x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and marks y = 20, 40, 50, 40, 50. Means: xbar = 3, ybar = 40. Deviations of x: -2, -1, 0, 1, 2. Deviations of y: -20, 0, 10, 0, 10. Sxx = 4 + 1 + 0 + 1 + 4 = 10. Syy = 400 + 0 + 100 + 0 + 100 = 600. Sxy = (-2)(-20) + (-1)(0) + 0(10) + 1(0) + 2(10) = 40 + 20 = 60. So r = 60 / sqrt(10 x 600) = 60 / sqrt(6000) = 60 / 77.46 = about 0.77. A fairly strong positive linear relationship.

What r does not see: Pearson's r measures only straight-line relationships. Take x = -2, -1, 0, 1, 2 and y = x^2 = 4, 1, 0, 1, 4. Here y is completely decided by x, yet r = 0, because the U shape has no upward or downward straight trend. Also, a single outlier can push r up or down a lot. That is why you draw the scatter plot first.

Spearman's rank correlation: Sometimes the data are ranks (first, second, third), or the relationship is steady but not straight, or there are outliers. Then we use Spearman's rank correlation. Replace each x by its rank and each y by its rank, find the difference d of ranks for each pair, and compute rs = 1 - 6 x sum(d^2) / (n (n^2 - 1)) when there are no ties. Like r, it runs from -1 to 1. It measures whether y tends to go up when x goes up, not whether it goes up in a straight line.

Worked example, two judges: Two judges rank five teams in a university debate. Judge A gives ranks 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and judge B gives 2, 1, 4, 3, 5 to the same teams. The differences d are -1, 1, -1, 1, 0, so sum(d^2) = 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 0 = 4. With n = 5, n(n^2 - 1) = 5 x 24 = 120. rs = 1 - 6 x 4 / 120 = 1 - 24/120 = 1 - 0.2 = 0.8. The judges agree quite well.

The regression line: Correlation tells us the strength. Regression gives us a formula to predict: y-hat = a + b x, where b is the slope (how much y changes when x goes up by 1) and a is the intercept (the predicted y when x = 0). y-hat (y with a hat) means the predicted value, not the actual one.

Least squares: For each point, the residual e = y - y-hat is the vertical gap between the real dot and the line. Some residuals are positive, some negative. The least squares line is the line that makes the sum of squared residuals as small as possible. Solving that minimisation with a little calculus gives two neat formulas: b = Sxy / Sxx and a = ybar - b x xbar. A nice fact follows: the least squares line always passes through the point (xbar, ybar), and the residuals always add up to 0.

Worked example, the line for study hours: Using our numbers, b = Sxy / Sxx = 60 / 10 = 6, and a = 40 - 6 x 3 = 22. So y-hat = 22 + 6x. Each extra hour of study goes with about 6 more marks. For x = 3 the prediction is 22 + 18 = 40, exactly the means point, as promised. The predictions for x = 1 to 5 are 28, 34, 40, 46, 52, so the residuals are 20 - 28 = -8, 40 - 34 = 6, 50 - 40 = 10, 40 - 46 = -6 and 50 - 52 = -2. They add to 0.

R squared: How good is the line? Compare the leftover error with the total spread. SST = Syy = 600 is the total variation of y. SSE = sum of residuals squared = 64 + 36 + 100 + 36 + 4 = 240 is the part the line could not explain. R^2 = 1 - SSE / SST = 1 - 240/600 = 0.6. So 60% of the variation in marks is explained by hours studied. For simple linear regression R^2 = r^2, and indeed 0.77^2 is about 0.6. R^2 runs from 0 (the line explains nothing) to 1 (perfect fit).

Prediction and its limits: To predict, just plug x into the line. A student who studies 4.5 hours gets y-hat = 22 + 27 = 49. That is interpolation, inside the range of the data, and it is fairly safe. Predicting for x = 20 hours gives 142 marks, which is impossible in a 100-mark exam. That is extrapolation, going outside the data range, and it is dangerous because the straight-line pattern may not continue. Another caution: the line for predicting y from x is not the same as the line for predicting x from y, unless r = 1 or -1.

Correlation is not causation: This is the most famous sentence in statistics. In Dhaka, on days when more umbrellas are sold there are also more traffic jams. Do umbrellas cause jams? No. A third variable, rain, causes both. Such a hidden variable is called a confounder or lurking variable. Sometimes the cause also runs backwards, or the link is pure coincidence in a small sample. To prove cause, you usually need a randomised experiment, where chance decides who gets the treatment. Correlation is a hint to investigate, not a verdict.

Real life example 1, rickshaw fares: Back to the month of rickshaw trips. Suppose the fit comes out as y-hat = 20 + 25x, with x in km and y in taka, and R^2 = 0.8. The slope says each extra km adds about 25 taka; the intercept 20 is roughly the fixed starting charge. Next time a rickshawala asks 150 taka for a 2 km trip, you know the line predicts 70 taka, so you have a fair bargaining number. The residuals tell you which trips were unusually expensive, like night trips.

Real life example 2, machine learning: Linear regression is the hello world of machine learning. A ride-sharing app can predict trip time from distance, a shop can predict next month's sales from advertising spend, and a power company can predict electricity demand from temperature. With many x variables at once it becomes multiple regression, and the same least squares idea is solved with matrices or by gradient descent. When you train a model and check its R^2 or squared error, you are using exactly the ideas of this lesson.

Common mistakes: Computing r without drawing the scatter plot first. Saying r = 0 means no relationship (it means no straight-line relationship). Treating correlation as cause. Mixing up b and r: the slope has units and can be any size, r is unit-free and stays between -1 and 1, though they always have the same sign. Extrapolating far beyond the data. Forgetting that one outlier can change r and the line a lot.

What exams ask: Given a small table of x and y, compute r, the least squares line and R^2, then predict y for a given x. Compute Spearman's rank correlation for two judges or two exams. Interpret the slope and intercept in words. Explain why correlation does not imply causation with an example. Show that the regression line passes through (xbar, ybar). Sometimes you must also find the regression line of x on y and compare.

Recap: Draw a scatter plot first. Pearson's r = Sxy / sqrt(Sxx Syy) measures straight-line strength from -1 to 1. Spearman's rs = 1 - 6 sum(d^2) / (n(n^2 - 1)) works with ranks and steady trends. The least squares line y-hat = a + b x has b = Sxy / Sxx and a = ybar - b xbar, passes through the means, and has residuals adding to 0. R^2 = 1 - SSE/SST tells how much of y's variation is explained, and equals r^2 for one x. Interpolate carefully, avoid extrapolating, and never confuse correlation with causation. In the final lesson we see how all this probability powers computer science.
key_points: Always draw a scatter plot first: look for direction, form, strength and outliers.
Pearson's r = Sxy / sqrt(Sxx Syy) lies in [-1, 1], is unit-free and measures only linear relationships.
Spearman's rs = 1 - 6 sum(d^2) / (n(n^2 - 1)) uses ranks and handles steady non-linear trends and outliers.
Least squares line y-hat = a + b x with b = Sxy / Sxx and a = ybar - b xbar; it passes through (xbar, ybar).
Residuals e = y - y-hat sum to 0; least squares minimises the sum of their squares.
R^2 = 1 - SSE/SST is the share of y's variation explained; for one x, R^2 = r^2.
Interpolation is fairly safe, extrapolation is risky, and correlation does not prove causation.
lessons.tip: Make a little table with columns x, y, x - xbar, y - ybar, their squares and products. Every r, slope and R^2 question becomes simple column sums.
lessons.task: Write down your phone's battery percentage and the minutes of screen time at 5 points in a day. Draw the scatter plot on paper, compute r and the least squares line, and predict the battery level after 3 hours of use.

quiz.q: Which value of r shows the strongest linear relationship?
quiz.explain: Strength depends on |r|; |-0.9| = 0.9 is the largest.

quiz.q: With Sxy = 60, Sxx = 10, xbar = 3 and ybar = 40, the least squares line is:
If r = 0.8 in a simple linear regression, what is R squared?
quiz.explain: For one x variable, R^2 = r^2 = 0.64, so 64% of the variation in y is explained.

quiz.q: For x = -2, -1, 0, 1, 2 and y = x^2, Pearson's r is 0. What does this show?
options: There must be a calculation error
quiz.explain: y is fully decided by x, but the U shape has no linear trend, so r = 0.

quiz.q: Umbrella sales and traffic jams in Dhaka are positively correlated. The best explanation is:
quiz.explain: Rain raises both; correlation alone does not show cause.

lessons.title: Probability in Computer Science and Course Recap
lessons.content:
Imagine you open your email in the morning. The spam folder already caught three fake lottery messages. Your phone keyboard guesses your next word. Google shows the most useful page first. A shopping app quietly shows half its users a red Buy button and the other half a green one. Behind every one of these, there is probability. In this last lesson we connect everything from the course to real computer science: Markov chains, queues, randomized algorithms, hashing, A/B testing and the Naive Bayes classifier. Then we recap the whole course in one place.

Markov chains, the idea: A Markov chain is a system that jumps between states in steps, where the chance of the next state depends only on the current state, not on the full history. This is called the Markov property, or memorylessness: the future depends on the present, not on how you got here. Think of the weather in a simple model: if today is sunny, tomorrow is sunny with probability 0.8 and rainy with probability 0.2. If today is rainy, tomorrow is sunny with probability 0.4 and rainy with probability 0.6.

The transition matrix: We store these chances in a table called the transition matrix P. Row = current state, column = next state. For our weather: row Sunny is (0.8, 0.2) and row Rainy is (0.4, 0.6). Each row adds up to 1, because from any state you must go somewhere. To look two steps ahead, use the law of total probability: if today is sunny, P(sunny the day after tomorrow) = 0.8 x 0.8 + 0.2 x 0.4 = 0.64 + 0.08 = 0.72. In matrix language, the two-step probabilities are the entries of P^2, and n-step probabilities are the entries of P^n.

Steady state: If you run the chain for a long time, for many chains the probability of being in each state settles down to fixed numbers, no matter where you started. This is the steady state (stationary) distribution pi, which satisfies pi = pi P and sums to 1. For the weather: pi_S = 0.8 pi_S + 0.4 pi_R. That gives 0.2 pi_S = 0.4 pi_R, so pi_S = 2 pi_R. With pi_S + pi_R = 1, we get pi_S = 2/3 and pi_R = 1/3. In the long run, two days out of three are sunny in this model.

Where Markov chains appear in CS: Google's original PageRank imagined a random surfer clicking links; a page's rank is its steady state probability in that Markov chain. Phone keyboards and old text generators predict the next word from the current word using transition probabilities. Markov chains also model a CPU switching between busy and idle, network packets moving between routers, and board games like Ludo or Snakes and Ladders.

Queues, the idea: Every system that serves requests has a queue: people at a bKash agent shop, print jobs at a printer, requests at a web server. Queueing theory asks: how long is the line, and how long do people wait? The simplest model is M/M/1. The first M means arrivals form a Poisson process (time between arrivals is exponential, which you met in lessons 13 and 14). The second M means service times are exponential. The 1 means a single server.

M/M/1 formulas: Let lambda be the arrival rate and mu the service rate (both per unit time). The utilisation is rho = lambda / mu, the fraction of time the server is busy. The queue is stable only if rho < 1, meaning work arrives slower than it can be done. Then the average number in the system is L = rho / (1 - rho), the average time a customer spends in the system is W = 1 / (mu - lambda), and the average wait before service is Wq = rho / (mu - lambda). These fit Little's law, L = lambda x W, which holds for almost any stable queue.

Worked example, a bKash agent: Customers arrive at 10 per hour, and the agent serves 12 per hour on average. rho = 10/12 = about 0.83. L = 0.83 / 0.17 = 5 customers in the shop on average. W = 1 / (12 - 10) = 0.5 hour = 30 minutes in the shop, of which Wq = 0.83 / 2 = about 0.42 hour = 25 minutes is waiting. Check Little's law: 10 x 0.5 = 5. Now watch what happens if arrivals rise to 11 per hour: W = 1 / (12 - 11) = 1 hour. A 10% rise in customers doubled the time! Near rho = 1 the queue explodes. This is why servers are not run at 100% load.

Randomized algorithms: Some algorithms flip coins on purpose. Randomized quicksort picks a random pivot, so no particular input can force the worst case, and its expected running time is O(n log n) on every input. There are two families. Las Vegas algorithms always give the correct answer, but their running time is random (randomized quicksort). Monte Carlo algorithms run in a fixed time but may give a wrong answer with small probability.

Monte Carlo example, primality testing: The Miller-Rabin test checks whether a big number is prime. If the number is prime, it always says prime. If it is composite, one round wrongly says prime with probability at most 1/4. Run k independent rounds, and the error chance is at most (1/4)^k by the multiplication rule for independent events. With 20 rounds that is below one in a trillion. This is how cryptography libraries choose huge primes for RSA keys. Another Monte Carlo idea: estimate pi by throwing random points into a square and counting how many land inside the circle.

Hashing and collisions: A hash table puts n keys into m slots using a hash function. If the hash spreads keys uniformly, the load factor alpha = n / m is the expected number of keys per slot, so with chaining a search takes expected O(1 + alpha) time. But collisions come sooner than intuition says. This is exactly the birthday problem from lesson 8: with only 23 keys and 365 slots, the chance of at least one collision is already about 50%. A useful approximation is P(no collision) is about e^(-n(n - 1) / (2m)). The same maths tells security engineers how long a hash output must be so that finding two inputs with the same hash is practically impossible.

A/B testing: Companies like Daraz or Foodpanda test changes on real users. Half of the visitors see version A of a page, half see version B, chosen at random so the groups are alike. Then a two-proportion z test (lesson 22) checks whether the difference in conversion rate is real or just chance. Random assignment is the key: it is what lets us talk about cause, not only correlation (lesson 24).

Worked example, a button colour: Version A: 1,000 visitors, 50 buy (5%). Version B: 1,000 visitors, 70 buy (7%). Pooled p = 120 / 2,000 = 0.06. SE = sqrt(0.06 x 0.94 x (1/1000 + 1/1000)) = sqrt(0.0001128) = about 0.0106. z = (0.07 - 0.05) / 0.0106 = about 1.88. For a two-tailed test at 5%, the critical value is 1.96, so we fail to reject H0. B looks better, but the evidence is not strong enough yet. The team should collect more data, rather than switch to a one-tailed test after seeing the result, which would be cheating.

Naive Bayes classifier: Bayes' theorem (lesson 9) can classify text. For a spam filter, we want P(spam | words). Naive Bayes makes a simplifying ("naive") assumption: given the class, the words appear independently. Then P(spam | words) is proportional to P(spam) x P(word1 | spam) x P(word2 | spam) x ..., and the same for not-spam (ham). We compute both scores and pick the bigger, or divide to get a probability.

Worked example, two words: Suppose 40% of emails are spam. The word "free" appears in 30% of spam and 2% of ham. The word "offer" appears in 20% of spam and 5% of ham. An email contains both. Spam score = 0.4 x 0.3 x 0.2 = 0.024. Ham score = 0.6 x 0.02 x 0.05 = 0.0006. P(spam | both words) = 0.024 / (0.024 + 0.0006) = 0.024 / 0.0246 = about 0.976. The filter is about 97.6% sure it is spam. Real filters use thousands of words and add logs of probabilities instead of multiplying, so the numbers do not underflow to zero.

Real life example 1, a Dhaka web server: An online exam result site gets a flood of requests on result day. Engineers model requests as Poisson arrivals and the server as a queue. If one server handles 100 requests per second and 90 arrive, rho = 0.9 and W = 1 / (100 - 90) = 0.1 second. On result day 99 per second arrive, and W jumps to 1 second, and any more makes the queue unstable. So they add servers and a load balancer before the big day, using the formulas, not guesses.

Real life example 2, mobile fraud detection: A mobile banking company wants to flag suspicious transactions. It uses past data to estimate how often features like a new device, a late-night transfer, or an unusual amount appear in fraud vs normal cases, then applies a Bayes-style score. Because fraud is rare, base rates matter a lot, exactly as in the medical test example of lesson 9: even a good detector produces many false alarms. Engineers then A/B test new rules on a small random share of users before rolling them out.

Common mistakes: Forgetting that each row of a transition matrix must add to 1. Using M/M/1 formulas when rho is 1 or more (the queue grows forever). Thinking a Monte Carlo algorithm is useless because it can be wrong; repeating it makes the error tiny. Underestimating collisions in hashing. Peeking at A/B test results every hour and stopping as soon as p < 0.05, which inflates false alarms. In Naive Bayes, letting one zero probability wipe out a score; real systems use Laplace (add-one) smoothing.

What exams ask: Find two-step probabilities and the steady state of a 2-state Markov chain; compute rho, L, W and Wq for an M/M/1 queue and check Little's law; explain Las Vegas vs Monte Carlo with examples; compute a Naive Bayes posterior from a small table; and explain how a hypothesis test is used in A/B testing.

Course recap, part 1: We began with data: populations, samples, types of variables, tables and charts. We summarised data with the mean, median and mode, with spread measures like variance and standard deviation, and with shape measures like skewness and kurtosis. Then counting rules (permutations and combinations) led us into probability: sample spaces, the axioms, the addition and multiplication rules, conditional probability and Bayes' theorem.

Course recap, part 2: Random variables gave us PMFs, PDFs, CDFs, expectation and variance. We met the main distributions: Bernoulli, binomial, Poisson, geometric, hypergeometric, uniform, exponential and normal, plus joint distributions, covariance and correlation. The law of large numbers and the central limit theorem explained why sample means behave so nicely, and sampling distributions opened the door to inference.

Course recap, part 3: In inference we estimated parameters (unbiasedness, maximum likelihood), built confidence intervals, and tested hypotheses with z, t, chi-square and F tests, always keeping Type I and Type II errors in mind. Correlation and regression let us measure and predict relationships. And today we saw that all of it powers search engines, servers, cryptography, spam filters and product decisions. Probability is not just a maths course; it is how computers make smart guesses under uncertainty.
key_points: Markov chain: the next state depends only on the current one; rows of the transition matrix add to 1 and P^n gives n-step probabilities.
Steady state pi solves pi = pi P with entries summing to 1; PageRank is a steady state of a random-surfer chain.
M/M/1 queue: rho = lambda/mu < 1, L = rho/(1 - rho), W = 1/(mu - lambda), and Little's law L = lambda W.
Las Vegas algorithms are always correct with random time; Monte Carlo algorithms have fixed time and a small, shrinkable error.
Hash collisions follow the birthday problem: about 50% chance with 23 keys in 365 slots; load factor alpha = n/m.
A/B testing = random assignment + a two-proportion z test; decide the test before looking at the data.
Naive Bayes multiplies the prior by per-word likelihoods, assuming words are independent given the class.
lessons.tip: When you meet any new CS system, ask: what is random here, and which distribution fits it? Arrivals are often Poisson, waiting times exponential, yes/no events binomial. That one question links this course to the rest of your degree.
lessons.task: Model your own day as a 2-state Markov chain (for example Studying and Phone). For a week, note every hour which state you were in, estimate the transition probabilities, and compute the steady state. Does it match how you actually spend your time?

quiz.q: Weather chain: Sunny to Sunny 0.8, Sunny to Rainy 0.2, Rainy to Sunny 0.4, Rainy to Rainy 0.6. What is the long-run share of sunny days?
quiz.explain: Solve pi_S = 0.8 pi_S + 0.4 pi_R with pi_S + pi_R = 1: pi_S = 2/3.

quiz.q: An M/M/1 queue has lambda = 10 per hour and mu = 12 per hour. Average time in the system W is:
quiz.explain: W = 1/(mu - lambda) = 1/2 hour = 30 minutes.

quiz.q: Which statement about Monte Carlo algorithms is correct?
options: They always give the right answer but take random time
They are always slower than deterministic algorithms
They may be wrong with small probability, which repetition can shrink
quiz.explain: Monte Carlo has fixed time and a small error chance; independent repeats like Miller-Rabin rounds make it (1/4)^k or less.

quiz.q: In Little's law L = lambda x W, if 20 requests arrive per second and each spends 0.5 s in the system, how many are in the system on average?
What is the 'naive' assumption in Naive Bayes?
options: Words are independent given the class
quiz.explain: It assumes features (words) are conditionally independent given the class, so their probabilities can be multiplied.
